cost: the auth step has now been non-executable in every local build; at least the second consecutive deferral
what: Build step `auth` is `pac auth create --githubFederated --applicationId $APP_ID --tenant $TENANT_ID --environment $ENV_URL_DEV`. It requires ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL and ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN, which exist only inside a GitHub Actions run, so it CANNOT execute in a local build - ever, by construction. It was deferred again here. The build still completed because an interactive/cert pac profile was already active, and `lint` used that.
expected: a step either executes or is declared as conditional on an environment that can run it
root_cause: The step encodes one execution context (CI) as if it were the only one. agents/build-agent.md's own rule says a step that is never executable in this environment is mis-declared or belongs behind an explicit environment condition, not deferred indefinitely - and this is at least the second consecutive deferral.
why_it_was_never_caught: the preflight validates shell syntax, step order and input types, but not whether a step's required env vars can exist in the context the build is running in; and the previous manifest claimed 'no deferred steps' while IMP-0004 records auth and lint deferred across builds #1-#4
lesson: The `auth` step cannot run outside GitHub Actions - it needs the OIDC token env vars. Locally, an existing `pac auth` profile serves the same purpose and `lint` works from it. Declare the step conditional on the CI context rather than deferring it every local build, and do not let a manifest claim 'no deferred steps' when a step was skipped.

cost: one failed Stage 0.5 run; would have failed identically on the first run into TST/ACC and PRD
what: ensure-schema.ps1 created alternate keys (its section 3) BEFORE relationships (section 4). A key on a LOOKUP column therefore fails, because the lookup column is created BY the relationship. Live error from Dataverse: code 0x80040203, 'Attribute(s) rev_applicationid not found for the Entity', for rev_grant.rev_grant_applicationid.
expected: a prerequisite script creates components in an order where each one's dependencies already exist
root_cause: The order was correct for the schema that existed when it was written: rev_setting keys on rev_name and rev_application keys on rev_sourcesubmissionid, both plain string columns created in section 2. The first key targeting a lookup exposed the latent ordering bug. Same shape as the build config's lint step, which consumed an artefact a later step produced (IMP-0004).
why_it_was_never_caught: the Pester suite mocks the Dataverse API, so section order is invisible to it - a mocked POST to /Keys succeeds whether or not the target column exists. Only a live run could catch it, and no live run had ever had a key on a lookup
lesson: In ensure-schema.ps1, RELATIONSHIPS must run before ALTERNATE KEYS: a key on a lookup column cannot be created before the relationship that creates that column (Dataverse 0x80040203). cost: latent: no exposure today, but it ships a defect into Phase 3/4 and the fix gets expensive once the table holds rows
what: Every Money column in Dataverse gets an automatic companion column <name>_base holding the same value converted to the org's base currency, plus table-level transactioncurrencyid and exchangerate. rev_grant.rev_amountawarded is IsSecured=True; its twin rev_amountawarded_base is IsSecured=False AND CanBeSecuredForRead=False - the platform refuses to secure it at all. So the value of a column-secured financial field is readable from an unsecurable copy by anyone holding Read on the table.
expected: securing a column secures the value it holds
root_cause: Money is a compound type: the platform creates a system-maintained base-currency twin that is read-only and not securable. Column security applies to the authored column only. Nothing in this project noticed because rev_application's money columns are all deliberately UNSECURED (costs and amount requested are trustee-visible by design) - rev_grant is the first table in the solution with a SECURED money column.
why_it_was_never_caught: verify-field-security-coverage.py reads IsSecured=1 from SOURCE and cross-checks the profile. The _base twin does not exist in source - the platform creates it on the live column - so the gate reports 51/51 clean while a 52nd column carries the same value unsecured. A gate that reads only source cannot see a component the platform adds.
lesson: A Money column is TWO columns: <name> and an automatic <name>_base. The _base twin CANNOT be secured (CanBeSecuredForRead=False), so column security on a Money field does not protect its value from anyone with table Read. For an amount that must be restricted, use Decimal instead - single-currency orgs gain nothing from Money and lose the ability to secure the value. Verified live on rev_grant.rev_amountawarded 2026-08-19.

proposed_change.summary: REVISED after the reviewer's decision. Do NOT make a secured Money column fail the build - that is now an accepted pattern here. Instead: (1) knowledge line recording that Money is a compound type whose _base twin cannot be secured (CanBeSecuredForRead=False), so column security on Money is not a confidentiality control; (2) the coverage gate should emit a WARNING naming each secured Money column and the compensating table-privilege requirement, so the fact reaches whoever builds a new role rather than sitting in a log; (3) a test asserting no role outside the profile's membership holds Read on rev_grant.

reviewer_decision: 2026-08-19, reviewer: keep Money, accept the risk - 'the views and forms won't contain those columns/fields'. NOTED, WITH ONE CORRECTION RECORDED: form/view omission is not the control. A column absent from every form and view is still readable via Advanced Find, the personal-view column picker, Excel export, the Web API and any flow - which is the exact reason this project chose column security over app-layer filtering (ADR-002). The control that actually holds is the TABLE PRIVILEGE: only REV Admin and REV Service Automation have Read on rev_grant, and both are entitled to the amount. Accepted on that basis.
compensating_control: REV Trustee must never be granted Read on rev_grant. WBS 6.1 builds that role; if it gets table Read, rev_amountawarded_base exposes the awarded amount and column security cannot prevent it. The current design grants trustees no privilege on this table.
applied_by: TWO targets, both now accounted for (the second arrived four days late, which is the defect IMP-0251 records). (1) knowledge/technology/dataverse.md - the Money/_base twin, CanBeSecuredForRead=False on the base column, and the 'use Decimal for a restricted amount' guidance; applied 2026-08-19. (2) scripts/verify-field-security-coverage.py - improvement review 20 change 1 adds the WARNING this finding's own proposed_change part 2 asked for, naming each secured Money column, its unsecurable _base twin and the compensating table-privilege requirement; C-TECH-070 states the rule. cost: would have failed the first TST/ACC deploy at its 14th step; undetected since the promote jobs were written on 2026-08-12
what: The promote-tst-acc and promote-prd jobs exported PROVISION_APP_ID and PROVISION_CERT_THUMBPRINT but nothing ever installed the certificate on the runner. A thumbprint is a lookup key into a certificate store, not a credential, and the store on a fresh ubuntu-latest runner is empty. All 14 `pwsh provisioning/**` steps across pre_deploy, post_deploy and smoke_tests for those two environments would have thrown inside Connect-MgGraph / Connect-PnPOnline.
expected: the ci.yml comment stated the provisioning identity was 'Certificate-based, so also C-TECH-044-compliant', implying it worked

why_it_was_never_caught: nothing — no environment above DEV has been deployed to, and there is no gate that asserts a credential resolves before the steps that need it run
lesson: A certificate THUMBPRINT is a lookup key, not a credential. Any job running provisioning/**/*.ps1 must also import the .pfx into the runner's CurrentUser/My store and prove the thumbprint resolves WITH a private key before the first step that uses it. Use X509Store, never Import-PfxCertificate or Cert:\ — both are Windows-only (C-TECH-054).

cost: the secret-scan gate failed on this machine on every local build run since 2026-08-18
what: `gitleaks detect --source . --no-git` scans the whole working tree, including build/artifacts/ — the build's OWN output. Three findings were reported in a previous run's deploy-logs/importjob-data.xml, all three matching generic-api-key against the literal text `ParameterKey=""` — an EMPTY attribute value in a Dataverse import-job record. The C-TECH-001 HARD gate was failing, on nothing, in a gitignored directory, from a run three weeks old.
expected: the secret scan asserts that no credential reaches the artifact from source
root_cause: the scan's scope was `.` — everything — with no distinction between what the build READS and what it WRITES. Build output is never an input, so a secret cannot enter the repository through it, but it is full of tool-generated text that trips generic detectors.
why_it_was_never_caught: the gate is only run by the build, and every build to date ran on CI (where build/artifacts is empty at scan time) or was run by an agent that did not reach this step. A gate that fails only on a developer machine, on output from a previous run, is invisible to CI by construction.
lesson: Scope a secret scan to what the build READS, never to `.`. Scanning build output means scanning tool-generated text with generic detectors, and the false positives land on a HARD gate. A gate that fires on nothing teaches people to ignore it — the mirror of a gate that cannot fire. When narrowing any security gate, add a test proving the narrowing did not remove the case it exists for.

proposed_change.summary: a gitleaks config that EXTENDS the default rules and allowlists ^build/ only; the build step passes --config; three tests assert the config is used, that it extends rather than replaces the rule set, and that a credential under provisioning/ still fails the scan (IMP-0003's case)

cost: three full rewrites of one report before it was usable
what: A completion report was rejected three times by the reviewer — not for its content, which was correct each time, but for its shape. Draft 1 was a wall of prose with identifiers like C-TECH-062 written as bare code spans, so nothing was clickable and every reference meant opening a file and searching it. cost: a CI mechanism built on a wrong assumption about where the credential lives
what: IMP-0048's fix assumed the provisioning certificate could be exported into a CI secret. The reviewer corrected that on 2026-08-19: it is a SELF-SIGNED certificate on the app registration, held in this Mac's login keychain, and the instruction was to always read the keychain. Verified live: X509Store('My','CurrentUser') on macOS IS the keychain and returns CN=REV-Provisioning-SP with its private key, expiring 2027-08-14.
expected: a certificate used by CI can be supplied to CI
root_cause: the fix was designed from the CI job's point of view (what does the runner need?) rather than from the credential's (where does it actually live, and can it leave?). A self-signed keychain identity is deliberately not exportable into a secret store.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing — the certificate's location was recorded in the digest as a capability (IMP-0022) but no document said whether it could or should be copied
lesson: On macOS, X509Store('My','CurrentUser') IS the login keychain — no separate keychain API is needed, and Get-ProvisioningCertificate resolves the identity directly. Provisioning for this project therefore runs FROM THE MAC, not from a Linux runner; the CI cert-install action is the optional Linux path and the promote jobs now run it only when the .pfx secret exists, failing fast with the real reason when it does not.

cost: 25 unit tests turned into tests that could only pass on the machine holding the production credential
what: Making Connect-ProvisioningGraph and Connect-ProvisioningPnP resolve the certificate broke 89 provisioning tests. Pester's Mock could not intercept Get-ProvisioningCertificate because provisioning-common.ps1 is DOT-SOURCED: each script re-defines the function in its own child scope, shadowing any mock registered in the test's scope. Pester reports 'Could not find Command Get-ProvisioningCertificate'.
expected: a function with a documented 'thin, mockable wrapper' comment is mockable
root_cause: mockability depends on SCOPE, not on intent. A dot-sourced function lives in the caller's scope; only a MODULE's functions are registered in a session state that Pester can patch from anywhere.
why_it_was_never_caught: the wrapper was only ever exercised by the Dataverse path, whose tests dot-source the common file into the TEST scope before mocking — which works, and hid the fact that the same mock is impossible from an integration-style test that invokes a script
lesson: If a function must be mockable from a test that INVOKES a script (rather than dot-sourcing it), the function must live in a .psm1 and be imported — a dot-sourced definition is re-created in the script's own scope and shadows the mock. When mocking a function that a module calls internally, Pester needs -ModuleName <module> to patch that module's session state.

proposed_change.summary: certificate resolution extracted into a module so the security seam is mockable on purpose in one place, rather than via a flag that could be set in production by accident

applied_by: provisioning-cert.psm1 with a header explaining the scope rule; test mocks repointed at Get-ProvisioningCertificate, and the resolver's own tests use -ModuleName provisioning-cert

cost: the first schedule report read OK on every line while understating the constraint fourfold
what: scripts/schedule-risk.py's first version computed each phase's headroom against the full capacity available between today and that phase's own date. Phase 1 got 86h of capacity, Phase 2 134h, Phase 3 230h - the same hours counted four times. Every phase reported OK. Computing it cumulatively (to hit phase N you must also finish 0..N-1) is what makes the number mean anything. Separately, IMP-0031 attributed Phase 1's stall to conversational routing; the ready set shows the dominant cause is that all of Phase 1 is blocked on the Client (DocuSign licence, WP plugin confirmation) - 106 of 179 remaining hours across the engagement are client-blocked.
expected: a per-phase capacity calculation is independent
root_cause: Capacity is a SHARED resource across a sequence of phases; treating each phase as having exclusive access to all remaining time is the same error as double-booking a room. And a plan that reads green on every line is more dangerous than one that reads red, because nobody looks twice.
why_it_was_never_caught: the script was new; the flaw was visible only because the output was read against the known fact that Phase 1 had not started
lesson: When a schedule computes headroom per phase, check whether the same capacity is being counted for more than one phase - it must be cumulative, because finishing phase N requires finishing 0..N-1 too. And distinguish 'late because nobody started it' from 'late because it is blocked on the client': the first needs a queue, the second needs a phone call.
commercial_impact: 106 of 179 remaining estimated hours are blocked on client-side preconditions, three of which have owners and ages recorded and ten of which have never been confirmed at all

proposed_change.summary: Cumulative headroom and a BLOCKED ON CLIENT verdict; contract/external-dependencies.json carries each precondition's state, owner and first_seen so blockers age visibly. Fixed at the point of discovery.

applied_by: scripts/schedule-risk.py headroom is now cumulative; contract/external-dependencies.json carries each precondition's state, owner and age

cost: every push since 88dd590 produced a workflow run with ZERO jobs; CI was dead for a day and the only signal was a GitHub notification email to the reviewer
what: The provisioning-certificate guard added to .github/workflows/ci.yml on 2026-08-19 branched on `if: ${{ secrets.PROVISION_CERT_PFX_BASE64 != '' }}` in four step-level `if:` expressions (two jobs x install + guard). `secrets` is not an allowed context in any `if:`, so GitHub rejected the ENTIRE file with 'Unrecognized named-value: secrets' and ran no jobs at all on any push.
expected: a step could ask whether an environment secret exists, the way it can read one in `with:` or `env:`
root_cause: GitHub's context-availability table was assumed rather than read. `secrets` is available in `jobs.<id>.env`, `jobs.<id>.with` and step `with:`/`env:`/`run:`, and is absent from EVERY `if:` row - step-level `if` permits github, needs, strategy, matrix, job, runner, env, vars, steps, inputs. Because workflow parsing is all-or-nothing, one disallowed named-value in one expression disables the whole file rather than the one step that used it.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing - this repository has no workflow-file validation of any kind (no actionlint, no yaml/schema check, no self-check job), and this is the one defect class CI structurally cannot report: an invalid ci.yml means no job runs, so there is no failing check, no red X on the commit, and no gate output. The build gate-over-the-gates (scripts/verify-build-config.py) covers config/<slug>-build.yml and never looks at .github/.
lesson: `secrets` is not available in ANY `if:` expression - GitHub rejects the WHOLE workflow file and every run shows zero jobs, with no failing check to notice. To branch on whether a secret exists, project it into a job-level `env` boolean (job `env` MAY read secrets) and test `env.FLAG == 'true'` in the step `if:`. And validate .github/workflows/*.yml before pushing: an invalid workflow file is the only defect class CI cannot tell you about, because nothing runs.

proposed_change.summary: Add a pinned actionlint run over .github/workflows/ and .github/actions/ as the FIRST job in ci.yml, plus a local preflight the lead agent runs before committing any .github/ change (the CI copy cannot catch the case where the file itself fails to parse - only the local one can). Per IMP-0024/IMP-0050, ship it with a negative-test fixture asserting the gate FAILS on a `secrets`-in-`if` expression, assembled at runtime so the fixture is not itself an invalid workflow at rest.

applied_by: scripts/verify-workflow-syntax.py (new) encodes GitHub's context-availability table per KEY and rejects `secrets` in any `if:`; wired as the FIRST step of .github/workflows/ci.yml -> validate, with --selftest running on every CI run; C-TECH-063 added, binding the LOCAL run because the CI copy is unreachable in the exact failure it exists for; four negative tests in src/tests/build/BuildGates.Tests.ps1. Coverage proof: the gate reports all four errors against 88dd590's ci.yml at lines 725, 732, 864 and 871 — the same four lines GitHub named — and exits 0 against the fixed tree

cost: a duplicate finding id and a stale digest were committed and pushed, then repaired in a follow-up commit
what: Two sessions appended to logs/improvement-log.jsonl within seven minutes. Both read the next id the way skills/how-to-log-an-improvement.md instructs — from the LAST line, IMP-0073 — and both wrote IMP-0074. Commit 6158243 captured the colliding state together with a digest generated from 74 entries while the log in the same commit carried 77.
expected: an append-only log tolerates two writers; that is most of the point of append-only
root_cause: Append-only removes the read-modify-write conflict on existing lines but not the ID ALLOCATION race, and the skill's own command makes it worse: `tail -1` reads one line, so it cannot even see a higher id further up the file. Nothing reserves an id, and `git add` was run minutes after the generator, so both halves of the same commit were snapshots of different moments.

lesson: Allocate a finding id from the MAXIMUM id in the whole log, never from `tail -1`, and re-read immediately before appending — two sessions can be live in this repository at once, and this one is on a synced SharePoint path. Then run scripts/verify-improvement-log.py BEFORE committing: it detects duplicate ids exactly, and it is worthless if it only ever runs in CI. proposed_change.summary: Replace the `tail -1` id command with a max-over-all-ids command, state that ids are not reserved and the gate is what catches a collision, and require running verify-improvement-log.py locally before the commit rather than trusting CI.

what: `preflight-build-config` reported `[dead-target]` on the `lint` step, which is correct as declared and not a defect: lint tees the solution checker's stdout into $ARTIFACT_DIR/solution-checker/ and then asserts the file is non-empty with `test -s`, in the SAME command. The preflight read the assertion as consuming a path no EARLIER step produces. It only surfaced when the build ran against a FRESH artifact directory — every prior run reused a directory in which that log already existed, so the check passed on a leftover file.
expected: a step that writes a file and then asserts on it in one command is well-formed, and a preflight either accepts it or rejects it consistently regardless of what happens to be on disk
root_cause: extract_paths dispatches per shell command and had no branch for `tee` (which WRITES its argument) or for `test`/`[` (which ASSERT on one). Both fell through to the generic branch, where a bare path-shaped token is classified as an input. So the step's own output was recorded as a foreign input.
why_it_was_never_caught: the gate-over-the-gates had no test that runs it against an artifact directory that does not exist yet, so a check whose result depended on leftover state looked deterministic. This is the same shape as the defects it exists to catch: it passed while reading something other than what it claimed to read.
lesson: A preflight result that depends on files left behind by a previous run is not a result. `tee PATH` PRODUCES that path and `test -s PATH` asserts on it — both now have branches in extract_paths — and any new intra-step write-then-assert pattern needs one too. When changing the preflight, run it with ARTIFACT_DIR pointing at a directory that does NOT exist; on a reused directory it will agree with you for the wrong reason.

cost: three failed shapes for one sub-area attribute across two days; the reviewer had reasonably concluded it was a platform limitation
what: A site-map SubArea's Url attribute is a URL, not a set of parameters to append. Three shapes were tried and failed: (1) Entity= alongside Url="?pagetype=..." — opened the table's default view; (2) Url="&pagetype=...&viewType=1039" with no Entity, which the SITE MAP designer itself wrote — the sub-pages vanished from play mode entirely and the APP designer rejected the value saying it expects a web resource. That error was the answer. GROUND TRUTH came from a Microsoft-authored MANAGED sitemap in the same environment: the 'Power Platform Environment Settings' app carries 25 sub-areas with Url values, every one of them a ROOT-RELATIVE path — Url="/main.aspx?pagetype=control&controlName=..." and Url="/tools/externappmanagement/externappmanagement.aspx".
expected: the site map designer's own output would be a valid value for the attribute it writes
root_cause: The Url attribute was inferred from the shape of a querystring rather than read off a real instance. The site map designer compounded it by persisting a fragment the app designer then rejects, so the platform disagreed with itself and both halves were trusted in turn.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing validates a SubArea Url. `verify-shipped-content.py` reads etn= out of it to prove the table is reachable, which passes on any string containing etn=<name> — including two shapes that render nothing at all.
lesson: A site-map SubArea Url must be a ROOT-RELATIVE URL — a leading slash, then ?, then the query string: Url="/main.aspx?pagetype=entitylist&etn=<table>&viewid=<guid>". A bare `&pagetype=...` fragment is not a URL; the app designer rejects it with 'expects a web resource' and the sub-area disappears from play mode. Read the shape off a Microsoft-authored managed sitemap in the same org — 'Power Platform Environment Settings' has 25 examples — rather than inferring it. AND NOTE: a leading-slash URL carries no host, so it is environment-independent and does NOT breach C-TECH-047; the solution-awareness objection to hardcoding a URL is answered by the relative form, not by avoiding URLs.

proposed_change.summary: Assert the SHAPE of every SubArea Url, not just that etn= appears in it: it must begin with '/' and contain '?', and if it names a viewid that GUID must exist in SavedQueries/ for the entity it names. cost: a HARD coverage constraint fell from 89.13% to 67.78% and stayed unreported for a day and three deploys
what: The first full build since 2026-08-19 failed C-TECH-014: coverage 67.78% against an 80% threshold. The cause is that the four test-data scripts added on 2026-08-20 (remove-test-data.ps1, seed-test-data.ps1, test-data-common.psm1, verify-test-data.ps1) contribute 661 instructions with ZERO coverage. Excluding those four, coverage is 1870 of 2098 = 89.13% - identical to 08-19. The three targeted DEV builds on 08-20 all ran the same suite and recorded 'unit-tests: 782 passed, 1 failed, 1 skipped' in their manifests WITHOUT the coverage figure, so a HARD constraint went from passing to failing and no artifact says so.
expected: a manifest records the result of every gate a step contains, and a HARD constraint that starts failing is visible in the record on the day it starts failing
root_cause: unit-tests is ONE build step carrying TWO gates - a test-count gate and a coverage gate - and the manifest's gates_executed key holds one string per step. A partial result therefore fits the schema: writing the test counts and omitting the coverage number produces a manifest that looks complete. The step's own runner exits non-zero on either, so nothing was bypassed technically; the RECORD was incomplete, and the record is what the next session reads. Compounded by adding provisioning code under a path the coverage scope names while its only tests are contract-level (they assert the script's output vocabulary, not its behaviour), which lifts the test count and not the coverage.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing asserts that a manifest's gates_executed accounts for every gate inside a step. A step that carries two gates can report one. verify-build-config.py counts gates in the CONFIG and never compares that count against what a manifest claims.
lesson: unit-tests is TWO gates in one step - the test count and the 80% coverage threshold - and a manifest that records only the counts hides a HARD C-TECH-014 failure. Record BOTH numbers, always. And when you add a .ps1 under provisioning/{common,entra,dataverse}, coverage scope includes it the moment it lands: contract tests that assert a script's output vocabulary lift the test count and cover almost none of its lines, so the suite goes greener while the constraint goes red. Check the coverage figure, not the pass count, after adding provisioning code.

The reviewer lifted them by hand in DEV, the next import overwrote the hand fix from source, and the reviewer had to lift them again.
expected: a flow that packs, imports and reports Activated can be turned on
root_cause: Initialize variable is top-level-only in the workflow definition language - not inside a Scope, condition, Apply to each or Switch. Nothing in the repository recorded that, so the shape was authored from the general assumption that any action may nest. It packs and imports cleanly, so every gate up to and including the deploy reported green; the restriction is enforced only by the designer's save, which no agent executes.

lesson: Initialize variable is legal ONLY at the top level of a Power Automate flow - never inside a Scope, condition, Apply to each or Switch. A nested one packs, imports and reports Activated, then the designer refuses to save and the flow cannot be turned on. When a nested declaration has to be lifted, move the runAfter guard it sat behind onto the action that CONSUMES the variable, not onto the declaration.

cost: unknown — the FAILED-coverage message has printed a broken line since coverage enforcement was written; nobody has seen a real local coverage failure closely enough to notice
what: src/tests/Invoke-Tests.ps1's FAILED-coverage branch was written as 'Write-Output ("a {0}" -f $x, $y) + "b"' — PowerShell's -f operator binds TIGHTER than +, so this evaluates as ("a {0}") + ("b" -f nothing), not the intended concatenation, and the placeholder is left LITERALLY as '{0}' in the printed line while a bare '+' appears as its own output line. The same shape was then copied into this session's own first draft of the new 'measured, not enforced' branch (IMP-0134) and reproduced the identical break, caught only by actually running the script rather than reading the diff.
expected: a format string with substitutions actually substitutes
root_cause: Write-Output is a cmdlet call, not an expression; PowerShell parses 'Write-Output (expr) + string' as (Write-Output (expr)) + string rather than Write-Output ((expr) + string), so the concatenation happens outside the call and the -f binds to only the trailing fragment. This is a precedence trap specific to piping a multi-part format expression into a cmdlet across a line break.
why_it_was_never_caught: no test asserts the literal text of a FAILED/RESULT line, only exit codes and the presence of a keyword substring — a substring match on 'RESULT: FAILED' still passes when the number beside it is a broken '{0}'
lesson: Never write `Write-Output ("a {0}" -f $x) + "b"` across a line break — `-f` binds tighter than `+`, so PowerShell concatenates `"b"` to the RESULT of `("a {0}" -f $x)`'s own trailing fragment only when parenthesised that way, and the outer `Write-Output (...) + ...` shape sends the first piece to the pipeline and evaluates `+` on the cmdlet's return separately, splitting the message across two output lines with a bare `+` between them. Build the whole template with string `+` FIRST inside one set of outer parens, then apply `-f` to the concatenated whole: `(("a {0} " + "b") -f $x)`.

proposed_change.summary: Add the PowerShell -f/+ precedence trap to the PowerShell section, with the working pattern, so the next multi-line formatted Write-Output does not repeat it.

cost: none yet - every real provisioning script declares parameters multi-line, so no live step is affected. Surfaced only when a new known-bad fixture was first written on one line and the gate reported a parameter that was plainly there.
what: powershell_params() in scripts/verify-pipeline-config.py extracts the param() block as text[start:end] where end is the index of the CLOSING parenthesis, so the closing ')' is excluded from the searched text. The parameter-name regex requires a lookahead of [,)=\r\n], so the LAST parameter of a single-line param() block - the one immediately followed by that excluded ')' - is never matched. `param([Parameter(Mandatory)][string]$Env)` therefore reports 'Declared: (none)' and check 6 fails the step with 'has no parameter -Env'.
expected: check 6 reports the parameters a script declares, whatever the block's line layout
root_cause: an off-by-one between the slice bound and the lookahead: the regex needs the terminator to be INSIDE the slice, and for the final parameter the only terminator is the parenthesis the slice stops at.
why_it_was_never_caught: every .ps1 under provisioning/ declares parameters multi-line, so the final parameter is always followed by a newline that IS inside the slice. No fixture had ever used the single-line form.
lesson: In scripts/verify-pipeline-config.py, powershell_params() cannot see the last parameter of a SINGLE-LINE param() block, because the closing parenthesis it needs as a terminator is outside the slice it searches. The failure direction is a false FAIL in a HARD gate - it blocks a deploy step that is actually correct - which is the expensive direction the function's own comment says it avoids. Fix is one character (end + 1) plus a fixture with a single-line param block. Until then, declare provisioning script parameters multi-line, as every existing one does.

proposed_change.summary: slice the param() block inclusive of its closing parenthesis (text[start:end + 1]) so the final parameter has a terminator, and add a single-line param() fixture to the known-bad tree to prove the case.

revisit_when: the next improvement review, or the first time a provisioning script is written with a single-line param() block - whichever comes first
applied_by: scripts/verify-pipeline-config.py — powershell_params() now slices INCLUSIVE of the closing parenthesis, so a single-line param() block's last parameter keeps a terminator inside the slice (review 5 item 6)

what: lead-agent's own dispatch instruction told development-agent to 'bind REV Trustee to the existing REV_TrusteeRestricted field security profile'. That is backwards: REV_TrusteeRestricted GRANTS read on all 39 secured columns (incl. rev_narrativeraw, Art. 9) to its members, and the control today is that NOBODY is a member. what: provisioning/dataverse/verify-environment-access.ps1 line 105 calls Invoke-DataverseApi with -Method 'GET' (single-quoted) where every other script in provisioning/{dataverse,entra}/*.ps1 (14+ call sites checked) writes the bareword -Method GET. src/tests/provisioning/ScriptContract.Tests.ps1:236 asserts the AST argument's raw Extent.Text matches the regex '(?i)^GET$', which a quoted literal never can (Extent.Text for 'GET' includes the quote characters), so this one script fails a check every other verify-*.ps1 script passes. lesson: src/tests/provisioning/ScriptContract.Tests.ps1's Dataverse-write check (line 236) matches an AST argument's raw Extent.Text against '^GET$', so -Method 'GET' (quoted) fails where -Method GET (bareword) passes even though both send an identical, safe read-only request - a false FAIL, not a caught defect. provisioning/dataverse/verify-environment-access.ps1 is the one script in this repo written with the quoted form, and it is also missing from provisioning/README.md's script inventory (a second, independent contract gap in the same file). what: The approved TAD contradicts itself about trustee access. So the two statements are mutually unsatisfiable, and FR-034's 'region' - which is rev_applicant.rev_locationarea, there being no region column on rev_application - was unreachable by the persona the requirement is written for.

root_cause: section 3.1 was written as a per-column data-classification table and section 6.2 as a per-role privilege table, by different passes, and nothing reconciles a column-level visibility claim against the role-level privilege that would be needed to honour it. why_it_was_never_caught: nothing compares TAD section 3.1 against TAD section 6.2, or either against Roles/*.xml. The architecture gate reviews the TAD as prose; no executable check reads it. cost: very nearly a fabricated blocker in a gate report - caught before it reached the reviewer, twice in one session
what: Measuring a gate's exit code as `cmd | tail -25; echo $?` reported exit=0 for scripts/verify-pipeline-config.py while the script printed 'PIPELINE CONFIG PREFLIGHT: FAILED'. The 0 was tail's exit status, not the script's; run directly the script exits 1, correctly. Left unchecked this would have been reported as a HARD C-TECH-062 gate that prints FAILED and returns success - a fabricated instance of this project's most-recorded defect class. The same trap recurred minutes later with `${PIPESTATUS[0]}`, which is a bash array and is silently EMPTY in this session's zsh.
expected: a shell measurement of a gate's exit code reports the gate's exit code
root_cause: in a pipeline, `$?` is the last command's status, and the habit of piping gate output through tail/grep to keep it short puts a filter between the gate and the measurement. PIPESTATUS looks like the fix and is bash-only; zsh spells it pipestatus, so the bash form expands to nothing and any test against it reads as success.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing checks how an agent measures an exit code. This class of error produces a FINDING rather than a defect, so it would have been caught only by whoever tried to reproduce the claimed gate bug - and a false report in the gate-cannot-fail family is expensive precisely because this project takes that class seriously.
lesson: Never measure a gate's exit code through a pipe: `cmd | tail; echo $?` reports tail's status, and it will make a correctly-failing gate look like a gate that exits 0 while printing FAILED - a fabricated instance of the gate-cannot-fail class. PIPESTATUS is not the fix here either: this session's shell is zsh, where the bash spelling expands to empty and any test on it passes. Capture with `out=$(cmd 2>&1); rc=$?` and print rc, or run the gate bare.

proposed_change.summary: Add one line to the constraint-check procedure: capture a gate's exit code with `out=$(cmd 2>&1); rc=$?`, never through a pipe, and never via PIPESTATUS (bash-only; this environment is zsh). Before reporting any gate as behaving inconsistently with its output, re-run it bare and confirm.

what: scripts/verify-guid-syntax.py reports `OK - 284 GUID(s) across 70 file(s) all parse as UUIDs` against a solution tree that contains `{PENDING-ROLE-ID-REV-TRUSTEE}` where a GUID is required. expected: a gate named verify-guid-syntax fails when an element that must carry a GUID carries something that is not one

cost: one strategic-tier improvement-agent dispatch (reviews 4, 5, 6 applied together + IMP-0170/171 routed alongside) left incomplete: substantial real work landed (C-TECH-023 retired, C-TECH-064 extended, new C-TECH-066 added, 4 new/rewritten gate scripts each independently self-tested and verified working), but the batch's own reconciliation step never ran — IMP-0170 and IMP-0171 are still status NEW / state 'unread', IMP-0170's own proposed_change (a pointer in agents/development-agent.md) was never applied, and none of the three review documents were marked processed
what: The dispatched improvement-agent (task a4e31aded088dd067) fanned out into at least six of its own sub-agent dispatches to parallelise the reviews' proposed changes (scripts/verify-workflow-syntax.py, scripts/verify-derived-counts.py + registry, scripts/verify-tad-coverage.py + contract/tad-deferrals.json, scripts/verify-improvement-log.py's four-state rewrite, scripts/verify-guid-syntax.py's UUID-shape check, and a provisioning/pipeline-config false-FAIL fix). The parent and two of the six sub-agents terminated with 'You've hit your individual spend limit' mid-task; the parent's last visible action was 'Now retiring C-TECH-023.' The other four sub-agents completed normally, each fully self-verified (selftest suites, bare exit codes, negative fixtures) before finishing. The two agents that hit the limit had ALREADY WRITTEN their file edits before dying mid-verification, not left in a half-written state — confirmed after the fact by direct inspection (py_compile, pwsh AST parse, running each script against real data): nothing was left syntactically broken, but nothing about those two edits carries the same self-test evidence the four completed agents produced.
expected: an improvement-agent dispatch either reaches its own gate (fully reconciled, APPROVE IMPROVEMENTS-ready) or reports BLOCKED — not a mix of silently-completed sub-work and a dead parent that never reports anything, discovered only because the lead session happened to check disk state and ListAgents itself
root_cause: the account's individual spend limit is a hard ceiling enforced by the API layer itself, independent of and invisible to this system's own gates. Nothing in agents/WORKFLOW.md's Session Boundaries or Handoff Contract anticipates a dispatched agent (or one of its own children) being terminated by a resource limit rather than finishing, failing its own constraint check, or hitting a harness permission refusal (the existing harness-blocks-destructive-call class) — so there is no defined recovery path, and each already-launched child kept running and reporting independently of its dead parent, arriving as separate notifications with no single place that says 'this batch is N/6 complete, here is what's left'
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing tracks the sub-agent count or completion state of a dispatch that fans out internally — the Handoff Contract's five fields describe one agent's own gate, not a tree of them, and ListAgents/task-notifications are the only way to discover a child is still running or already finished after its parent died
lesson: A parent agent's FAILED notification (API spend limit or any other terminal error) does NOT mean its own sub-dispatches stopped — they were already launched and keep running independently, and their completions arrive as separate, later notifications. Before concluding an improvement-agent (or any agent that itself uses the Agent tool) batch did 'nothing', run ListAgents to see every child's status, and verify each touched file directly (compile/parse/selftest/run against real data) rather than trusting only the parent's last words. When the spend limit is hit, do not immediately re-dispatch the same scale of work — it will likely fail identically; surface it to the reviewer (the error names the remedy: /usage-credits, ask the admin for a higher limit) and, if anything must proceed before that, do the smallest remaining reconciliation as a single narrow dispatch, not another wide fan-out.

proposed_change.summary: Add a spend-limit / partial-orchestration-failure case to Session Boundaries: when a dispatched agent's own sub-dispatches may still be running or complete after it reports FAILED, the dispatcher must reconcile via ListAgents/notifications before treating the batch as fully failed, and log each verified outcome individually rather than one pass/fail for the whole tree.

what: The exact live write IMP-0170 recorded as refused an hour earlier - `pwsh provisioning/dataverse/ensure-schema.ps1 -Env dev` with the same PROVISION_APP_ID/PROVISION_CERT_THUMBPRINT triplet, against the same DEV org - was run again, this time directly in the lead-agent's own foreground Bash tool call (not dispatched to a background Agent-tool subagent). why_it_was_never_caught: agents/development-agent.md and agents/pipeline-agent.md's 'Reviewer-Executed Operations' protocol (just generalised this session per IMP-0170) still assumes the only route past a refusal is handing the exact command to the reviewer's own shell - it does not name 'retry from the lead-agent's own foreground session, not a dispatched sub-agent' as a step to try first, because until this instance nobody had a case where that distinction mattered

This resolved A-TR-2 (REV Trustee role creation) in one attempt after identity-agent's background dispatch (IMP-0170) was refused for the exact same command against the exact same environment. what: scripts/verify-improvement-log.py evaluates evidence_grep for APPLIED entries and for the 'already-fixed' NEW state (needle PRESENT), but never for the inverse: a NEW entry whose needle is ABSENT while its deferred_reason records that the change was APPROVED. Four such entries exist right now - IMP-0148 (provisioning/dataverse/verify-flow-trigger.ps1), IMP-0161 (the getClient(dataSourcesInfo) ground truth in knowledge/technology/code-apps.md), IMP-0162 ('sole enforcement surface' in config/models.yml) and IMP-0166 (EX-004 in contract/known-exceptions.json) - and the gate reports all four on one line as '7 finding(s) deferred with a recorded reason, accepted as a reviewed deferral'. Separately, docs/improvements/2026-08-21-improvement-review-6.md's status header states 'Nothing in section 3 has been applied' while 9 of its 12 items and its one retirement ARE on disk.
expected: a finding whose fix was approved and is demonstrably not on disk should be the loudest thing the log gate says, not folded into an accepted-deferral note; and the four broken needles should have produced that list mechanically instead of by a hand audit of three review documents
root_cause: the deferred_reason field carries three distinct meanings - a reviewer chose to defer, a review processed this and awaits approval, and this was approved and nobody did it - and the gate's four states model only the first two. Review 6 cluster G added the 'already-fixed' state for a needle that IS present and explicitly recorded that it was 'the second review in a row forced to overload one field to mean two things'; the mirror case was not modelled because at that moment no review had been approved. Review 7 then approved ten items, which created the state the vocabulary lacked.
why_it_was_never_caught: the gate's precedence at scripts/verify-improvement-log.py L40 puts reviewer-deferred ABOVE awaiting-approval and unread, so any entry carrying a deferred_reason goes quiet regardless of what its evidence_grep would say - and check_evidence_grep is not called for that state at all. The failure direction is a confident wrong answer rather than silence, which is why three reviews in a row believed their predecessors' proposals were unapplied when 27 of 33 were on disk.
lesson: An evidence_grep needle that is ABSENT is as informative as one that is present, and nothing reads it that way: the log gate checks needles for APPLIED entries and for the already-fixed state only, so four items of APPROVED, unapplied work read as 'accepted reviewed deferrals'. Third generation of one substrate defect in three days - IMP-0154 is a REVIEW leaving no trace, IMP-0169 a DELIVERY FIX leaving no trace, this one an APPROVAL leaving no trace. Two consequences worth remembering independently of the fix: a review document's own status header is a CLAIM (review 6 says nothing was applied; 9 of 12 items were), so verify a review's proposals against the working tree and never against its prose; and only 26 of 164 APPLIED entries carry a needle at all, so the requirement has to bind going forward rather than retroactively or it reports 138 errors about work that is done.

Then require an evidence_grep on any entry moved to APPLIED whose proposed_change.type is not 'none', enforced from review 8 forward, with the 138 legacy entries reported once as a dated NOTE. Review 8 item 1.

expected: a finding named only in a review's 'Findings left unprocessed' table to read as a DECLARED DEFERRAL by that review - a legitimate, informative state - not as an unstamped processing claim
root_cause: the gate matches IMP- ids by scanning the whole review document with no notion of the position they appear in, while the two rules it sits between pull opposite ways: the promotion skill REQUIRES naming every deferral, and IMP-0154's stamping rule (which this gate enforces) requires a stamp for every named id. Complying with the first violates the second, so the gate penalises the compliant review and rewards the one that stays quiet.
why_it_was_never_caught: no prior review named its deferrals as ids in a table - reviews 8 and 9 described their deferred sets in prose, which the scanner does not match, so the conflict between the two rules had never been exercised
lesson: verify-improvement-log.py flags every IMP- id named anywhere in a review document as needing a reviewed_in stamp, including ids the review names ONLY to declare them deferred under the no-silent-caps rule. Do not silence it by stamping a finding the review did not actually dispose of - that is a false claim and IMP-0154's warning is the lesser evil. Name the deferrals, expect one WARNING each, and explain them in the document. THIRD instance of gate-fires-on-nothing (IMP-0057, IMP-0164), so the fix is to teach the gate about citation POSITION - a 'Findings left unprocessed' row means declared-deferred, a 'Cites' row means processed - rather than another per-review explanation.

proposed_change.summary: Distinguish citation position. An id appearing only in a review's 'Findings left unprocessed' table is a declared deferral and needs no reviewed_in; an id in a 'Cites' position or a proposed-change row is processed and does. Alternatively accept a lighter 'deferred_to' stamp for the first case, so the no-silent-caps rule and the stamping rule stop contradicting each other.

cost: one wrong number in an approved review's digest-impact table, caught by measuring after applying rather than by anyone reading it; the routing change it justified was 4/5 overstated
what: Improvement review 10's digest-impact table predicted the Unrouted section would fall from 31 lessons to 26 when platform-fact-groundtruthed and environment-feature-flag-undeclared were added to the routing table in scripts/generate-known-failure-modes.py. Measured after applying: 31 -> 30. The four platform-fact-groundtruthed findings (IMP-0185, IMP-0193, IMP-0194, IMP-0195) were never in Unrouted - all four carry capability:true, and that flag routes a lesson to the 'Capabilities established in earlier sessions' section ahead of the class routing table. Only IMP-0182 actually moved.
expected: a class listed in the digest's recurring-classes table and absent from the routing table to have its findings sitting in the Unrouted section, so adding the class to the routing table moves them
root_cause: the digest generator has TWO independent routing mechanisms - the class-to-section table and the capability:true flag - and the flag takes precedence silently. Neither the rendered digest nor the recurring-classes table shows which mechanism placed a given lesson, so a review that reads the class table infers an Unrouted membership that is not there.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing - no gate compares a review's predicted digest impact against the measured one, and the prediction is written before the change is applied, so the only check is whoever remembers to re-measure afterwards
lesson: The digest routes a lesson by class table OR by capability:true, and the capability flag WINS - a finding with capability:true is never in Unrouted whatever its class. Before claiming that adding a class to the routing table in scripts/generate-known-failure-modes.py will move findings out of Unrouted, grep the rendered digest for those specific IMP ids and see which section actually holds them; the recurring-classes table does not tell you. And measure a predicted digest delta after regenerating, not before - review 10 predicted 31->26 and got 31->30.

proposed_change.summary: Make the routing mechanism visible: annotate each lesson (or each section's header note) with why it landed there - class table or capability flag - so a review can tell an unrouted finding from a capability-routed one without reading the generator. Cheaper alternative: have --check print a per-class breakdown of where that class's lessons currently render.

what: knowledge/technology/code-apps.md (uncommitted edit) states 'pa is not installed on this machine.' npm list -g shows @microsoft/power-apps-cli@1.0.0 IS installed, and /Users/xvl/.npm-global/bin/pa is a real, executable symlink to it (installed 2026-08-22). npm's configured global prefix is /Users/xvl/.npm-global, and that bin directory is absent from $PATH and from ~/.zshrc, ~/.zprofile and ~/.bash_profile -- so a plain `pa` on this machine resolves to 'command not found' despite the package being present.
expected: a globally-installed npm CLI package's bin is reachable by its bare command name
root_cause: npm's configured global prefix (~/.npm-global) is a non-standard location whose bin/ subdirectory was never added to PATH in any shell profile on this machine
why_it_was_never_caught: the knowledge doc's author ran `which pa` (or similar) and reported absence without also checking `npm list -g` / `npm config get prefix` -- a PATH gap and a missing install look identical from a bare 'not found'
lesson: On this Mac, `pa` (Power Apps CLI, @microsoft/power-apps-cli) IS installed globally via npm but is NOT on PATH because npm's global prefix is ~/.npm-global, whose bin/ is in no shell profile. Fix: add `export PATH="$HOME/.npm-global/bin:$PATH"` to ~/.zshrc (or invoke via the full path / `npx @microsoft/power-apps-cli`) before treating any `pa` command as unexecuted ground truth.

what: Dispatched to migrate the trustee-review-portal's hand-rolled Dataverse client to the four generated typed services. Before switching any write path, read the installed @microsoft/power-apps@1.3.0 SDK's own shipped source (the exact version pinned in this app's package.json) for what the generated Rev_reviewsService.update() actually sends. It issues a plain PATCH via a fixed 3-argument updateRecordAsync(tableName, id, changes) with no headers parameter anywhere in the call chain (Data.types.d.ts, both DataOperationExecutors, RuntimeDataClient._createHeaders) - it structurally cannot send If-Match, unlike the hand-rolled client's executeAsync({operationName:'UpdateOnlyRecord', parameters:{If_Match:'*',...}}) which this app relies on to guarantee rev_review is never accidentally created.
expected: docs/development/revitalise-grant-automation-dev-summary.md's own register (A-TR-10) and src/code-apps/trustee-review-portal/src/dataverse/README.md section 1 both correctly flagged this as UNVERIFIED for the generated client and named it as the reason not to swap without checking first - the dispatch instruction itself named this exact risk and authorised stopping if it did not verify.
root_cause: The generated service's high-level updateRecordAsync wraps a plain Dataverse PATCH (upsert-capable) with no way to attach If-Match; only the low-level executeAsync(connectorOperation) surface - which both the generated services and the hand-rolled client share the same getClient(dataSourcesInfo) object for - can set arbitrary connector-operation headers.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing - this is the first time anyone checked, and the dispatch explicitly asked for it to be checked before the swap rather than after
lesson: To verify a Power Apps Code App generated service's write semantics, read the installed @microsoft/power-apps package's own shipped source under node_modules/@microsoft/power-apps/dist/ for the exact pinned version (Data.types.d.ts for the public signature, the two DataOperationExecutor.js files, and runtimeDataClient.js's _createHeaders) rather than assuming symmetry with a hand-rolled connector-operation call. The generated update(tableName, id, changes) has no headers parameter and sends a plain PATCH - it cannot enforce update-only (If-Match) semantics, so it must not replace a hand-rolled UpdateOnlyRecord + If-Match:'*' write path without a different mechanism.

expected: knowledge/technology/build-and-deploy.md (§'Running pac solution check Locally') documents ~35 seconds for this exact command against this repository, uploading the packed managed .zip and printing a severity table to stdout.
root_cause: Not established. The managed zip is small (120KB) and well-formed (source-validate, component-shape, guid-syntax all pass), auth profile is active, and network reachability to the checker's host resolves and responds in <1s for a plain request — so this is not an auth, packaging, or basic connectivity defect on our side. Most likely either transient unavailability/backlog in the Microsoft-hosted Power Apps Checker service (Europe geo), or a client-side hang in this `pac` version's polling loop once the service is slow to ack — not distinguished here because pac itself never surfaced an error to distinguish the two.
why_it_was_never_caught: Nothing in this repo's gates guards against a hosted third-party dependency that accepts a request and then never responds — verify-build-config.py's preflight explicitly exempts `lint` from negative-test coverage as a 'third-party hosted analyser', and there is no client-side timeout or retry-with-backoff around this specific step's invocation in build.yml or in scripts/ci/run-config-steps.sh.
lesson: `pac solution check` against the Microsoft-hosted Solution Checker can hang indefinitely past its documented ~35s duration with no error and no output beyond 'Checking these solution files'. Before re-running it a third time, check `ps` for a still-alive `pac` process from a prior attempt (a killed shell wrapper can leave the underlying `pac` process running), and treat two identical hangs as the signal to stop and report rather than keep re-attempting — wrap the step with an explicit client-side timeout (e.g. `timeout 120 pac solution check ...`) so a stall produces a clean, fast, diagnosable failure instead of consuming minutes per attempt with no new information.

proposed_change.summary: Wrap the `lint` step's `pac solution check` invocation with an explicit timeout (e.g. `timeout 180 pac ...`) and a documented retry-once policy, so a hosted-checker stall fails the step in minutes with a clear message rather than hanging with no signal; note in the step's comment that pac 2.4.1 has no built-in timeout for this call.

applied_by: review 15: the client-side timeout is applied, PORTABLY, which the proposed fix was not. scripts/run-with-timeout.sh (new) wraps the lint step's pac solution check at 180s (~5x the documented ~35s), preserving `set -o pipefail`, the tee into the artifact and the `test -s` assertion; a stall now exits 124 in three minutes instead of consuming ~4.5 minutes with no output. THE PROPOSED `timeout 180 pac ...` WOULD HAVE BROKEN THE BUILD ON THIS MACHINE: `timeout` is GNU coreutils and neither it nor gtimeout exists on this Mac, while CI runs ubuntu-latest -- so the literal fix would pass in CI and fail with 'command not found' on the machine that actually runs builds (IMP-0061), which is C-TECH-054 and V6 in one line. The wrapper uses timeout/gtimeout when present and a portable poll-TERM-then-KILL fallback otherwise, with 5 selftest cases green on this host's fallback path (a hang killed at budget in 3s, exit codes preserved, stdout still pipeable, bad budget refused). cost: IMP-0215 spent 5 attempts and ~13.5+ minutes on a hypothesis the wrong side of a ten-second control, and was one step from a Microsoft support ticket against a healthy service; the second time this project has reached for the vendor before running a local control (IMP-0208 was the first)
what: IMP-0215 concluded that five identical `pac solution check` hangs were a Microsoft-hosted Solution Checker outage, and was logged with class `hosted-service-unresponsive`. Three probes run while processing it contradict that. (1) `pac auth list` — local, no token — returned instantly. (2) `pac org who` — pac's network+cached-token path — hung with ZERO output and had to be killed. (3) The cert-based control that bypasses pac entirely (Get-DataverseAccessToken + Invoke-DataverseApi against organizations?$select=name) succeeded: Entra token in 4172ms, Dataverse responded in 5557ms. So Entra ID and Dataverse were both healthy from this machine at the moment pac was hanging. Prime suspect found by `pgrep -fl pac`: a `pac --non-interactive` process alive 15h34m, spawned by the VS Code Power Platform extension (microsoft-isvexptools.powerplatform-vscode, which bundles its own pac binary separate from ~/.dotnet/tools/pac), predating all five hangs and holding the shared MSAL token cache.
expected: five identical no-output hangs against a Microsoft-hosted endpoint meant the hosted endpoint was unresponsive
root_cause: no control was run that separated 'the hosted service is down' from 'this tool's local state is stuck'. Every one of the five attempts exercised the SAME pac code path, so five identical results were one observation repeated, not five pieces of evidence — and the discriminating probes (a local-only pac command, and a non-pac call to the same platform) cost seconds and were never run.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing in this repo's knowledge told anyone which probes discriminate a hosted outage from a stuck local tool, and pac's failure mode gives no signal to reason from: an indefinite hang with no error and no correlation id looks exactly like a dead remote service from the caller's side.
lesson: Five identical failures through ONE code path are one observation, not five — repetition is not corroboration. Before concluding a Microsoft-hosted service is unresponsive, run the two controls that discriminate: a LOCAL-only command of the same tool (`pac auth list` is instant even with no network) and a call to the same platform that BYPASSES the tool (cert-based Get-DataverseAccessToken + Invoke-DataverseApi). On 2026-08-23 those proved Entra ID and Dataverse healthy while `pac org who` hung, so five `pac solution check` hangs were never an outage. Then run `pgrep -fl pac`: a long-lived pac process — including one bundled inside the VS Code Power Platform extension, which is a DIFFERENT binary from ~/.dotnet/tools/pac — holds the shared MSAL token cache and makes every other pac call that needs a token hang forever. And note what an unattributable hang costs you even if it IS the vendor: with no correlation id there is nothing for Microsoft to trace, so wait-and-retry is the response and a ticket is not.

proposed_change.summary: Under 'Running pac solution check Locally', add the discriminator: the three probes and what each proves, the stray-pac-process check including the VS Code extension's separate binary, and the rule that no correlation id means wait-and-retry rather than a support ticket. Cross-reference IMP-0208 as the first instance of reaching for the vendor before running a local control.

what: IMP-0216's applied diagnosis (a stray VS Code-extension `pac --non-interactive` process holding the shared MSAL token cache) was itself reported incorrect: killing that process (PID 4389) did not fix the hang — `pac org who` hung identically afterward. The reviewer then found and answered a macOS Keychain access permission prompt (a GUI dialog pac was silently blocked on, invisible to any automated probe), after which both `pac org who` (~51s, mostly the prompt) and the `lint` step (~35s, the documented normal duration) completed cleanly on the first subsequent try. root_cause: IMP-0216 inferred causation from correlation and timing (the stray process predated all five hangs, and holds the token cache pac needs) without actually running the causal test — kill the process, retry the exact failing call, confirm success — before the finding was applied to the knowledge base. The correlation was real (the stray process was a genuine anomaly worth killing) but not sufficient, because a second, unrelated blocker (a stuck OS-level Keychain prompt, which also silently blocks any pac call needing to read the credential store, with the identical symptom: connects, then silence, no correlation id) was present at the same time.
why_it_was_never_caught: review 15's process accepted a plausible, well-argued mechanism as sufficient grounds to edit knowledge/technology/build-and-deploy.md without requiring the kill-and-retry test to actually be run and observed first. Nothing in skills/how-to-promote-a-finding.md or the improvement-agent review process currently requires a causal fix to be confirmed (not just argued) before it is written into a knowledge file that future sessions will treat as procedure.
lesson: A hang that 'connects, then goes silent, with no correlation id' on macOS can have more than one simultaneous cause that produces the identical symptom: a stray process holding the MSAL token cache (IMP-0216) AND a stuck OS-level Keychain access permission prompt (a GUI dialog, invisible to any shell-based probe) are BOTH candidates, and fixing one does not rule out the other — test the fix by actually retrying the failing call, not by the plausibility of the mechanism alone. When `pac org who` or `pac solution check` hangs on a Mac with no output and no error, check Console.app / the user's screen for a pending Keychain access prompt (a modal dialog with no automated way to detect or dismiss it) in addition to `pgrep -fl pac`, and do not write a diagnosis into a knowledge file until the specific failing call has actually been re-run and observed to succeed.

what: The evidence_grep closure check added by improvement review 8 (scripts/verify-improvement-log.py, the 'An APPLIED status without a needle' block around line 681) accepts any needle whose {file, contains} pair matches the tree. IMP-0208's needle was {file: knowledge/technology/code-apps.md, contains: 'This is the fix, and it is confirmed working'} -- a sentence WRITTEN BY review 12 as part of closing IMP-0208. The needle therefore matched by construction, and the gate reported the closure as evidenced. The same review closed IMP-0209 on {contains: 'the per-table typed route is NOT closed'}, also its own prose. Neither needle asserted anything about the running app, and the org-url-null error was still live for a real signed-in trustee on 2026-08-23 (IMP-0224).
expected: improvement review 8's rationale for the needle requirement was that 'an APPLIED status is a claim (C-COM-005 applied to this log), and without a needle nothing can ever check it' -- i.e. that the needle would make a closure checkable.
root_cause: A needle proves an artefact CONTAINS a string. For a finding whose proposed_change.type is knowledge/skill/agent/constraint that is exactly right -- the prose IS the deliverable. But for a finding recording a live runtime DEFECT, the deliverable is the defect being gone, and no string in any repository file can assert that. The check has no notion of the verification level at which the defect was observable (C-TECH-053's V1-V5 ladder), so it cannot distinguish 'the lesson was written down' from 'the symptom stopped', and it reports both as evidenced.
why_it_was_never_caught: review 8 designed the needle against the failure it had in front of it -- four APPROVED items that were never implemented, where 'does the artefact exist' was the right question. Nothing since asked whether a needle could be satisfied by the review's own output. The self-test fixtures for this check all use needles pointing at artefacts a third party produced, so the circular case was never exercised.
lesson: An `evidence_grep` needle pointing into knowledge/, docs/, agents/, skills/ or constraints/ can be satisfied by the very sentence the closing review just wrote, so for a finding recording a LIVE RUNTIME defect it proves nothing -- it is a check on the artefact, never on the symptom. Before marking such a finding APPLIED, record the level at which the defect was actually visible (C-TECH-053's V1-V5) and close it with evidence at that level: for a V4 defect that means a named person re-running the original reproduction step and observing the symptom absent, with a timestamp later than the finding. A clean build, a clean lint, a zero CLI exit and a diff full of generated files are V2/V3 evidence and can never close a V4 defect.

cost: ~15 minutes: one deterministic CLI validation error plus one diagnostic regeneration cycle, cheap once the stray-pac-process class (IMP-0216) was recognised and applied a third time
what: Investigated whether either Power Apps CLI can regenerate the GENERIC (non-table) 'commondataserviceforapps' Dataverse connector data source with an explicit org URL, as an alternative to migrating this app's reads to the typed per-table services (see IMP-0227). Checked directly rather than assumed, per dispatch instruction: (1) `pa app add data-source --connector dataverse -c <connection-id> -u <org-url>` WITHOUT --table fails immediately and deterministically, exit code 2, 'Missing required option --table' -- this CLI's -u/--org-url flag has no path that ever reaches a non-table-scoped connector data source. (2) `pac code add-data-source -a shared_commondataserviceforapps -c <connection-id> -env <org-url>` (the older CLI's equivalent flag, undocumented in this project's own knowledge/technology/code-apps.md) hung indefinitely on first attempt -- a THIRD instance of the stray-pac-process class IMP-0216 diagnosed (a `pac --non-interactive` process bundled inside the VS Code Power Platform extension, PID 62791, alive 34m37s, holding the shared MSAL token cache; `pgrep -fl pac` found it exactly where IMP-0216 said to look). Killing it and retrying (IMP-0216's own remedy) let the command complete in ~90s and report 'Data source added successfully', regenerating `.power/schemas/appschemas/dataSourcesInfo.ts` with a much larger `apis` block for the generic connector (3574 lines vs 1858). But `commondataserviceforapps`'s `tableId`/`version`/`primaryKey` fields stayed empty strings exactly as before, and the literal org URL string appears NOWHERE in the regenerated file (grepped). The diagnostic regeneration was reverted (`git checkout --`) after reading it, per C-TECH-056.
expected: IMP-0208/IMP-0209 established that `-u/--org-url` on `pa app add data-source --table <t>` fixes this exact symptom class for a per-table dataset, which raised the question this dispatch was asked to settle directly: whether an equivalent existed for the generic, non-table-scoped connector data source that this app's read AND write calls actually used before this dispatch.
root_cause: A `dataSourceType: "Connector"` entry in the generated dataSourcesInfo.ts (the shape `commondataserviceforapps` has) structurally carries no field for an organisation URL -- `tableId`/`version`/`primaryKey` are always empty strings for this type, populated only for `dataSourceType: "Dataverse"` per-table entries. Regenerating the file with an explicit org URL (old CLI's `-env`) changes only which connector SCHEMA VERSION is fetched (the api operation list), never anything that could carry a resolved org URL at runtime. `-u/--org-url` on the new CLI's `--table` form works by producing a `"Dataverse"`-type entry instead, which resolves its instance URL through a completely different runtime mechanism (the app's own launch-time metadata, per `dataverseDataOperationExecutor.js` -- see IMP-0227). So no CLI flag on either tool can fix the generic connector's runtime org-url-null defect: the fix is a different data-source TYPE, not a different flag on the same one.
why_it_was_never_caught: no prior session tried the older CLI's `-env` flag against the generic (non-table) form specifically, or inspected whether the regenerated file actually carried an org URL anywhere rather than merely exiting cleanly -- exactly the class of gap IMP-0224 itself names (a clean CLI exit is V2/V3 evidence about the artefact, not evidence about the specific value the symptom names as missing).
lesson: Before trying to fix a Code App's GENERIC (non-table) Dataverse connector data source's org-url-null symptom via CLI regeneration: (1) the new `pa` CLI's `app add data-source --connector dataverse` hard-requires --table in non-interactive mode, so it can never target the generic form at all; (2) the old `pac code add-data-source -env <org-url>` DOES run against the generic form, but grep the regenerated dataSourcesInfo.ts for the org URL string and for a non-empty tableId/version on the target block before believing anything was fixed -- a `dataSourceType: "Connector"` entry has no field to hold one, so a clean 'Data source added successfully' proves the schema was refreshed, not that org-url resolution changed. And when any `pac` command hangs past its documented duration with only a partial banner printed, check `pgrep -fl pac` for a stray long-lived `pac --non-interactive` process (including the one VS Code's own Power Platform extension bundles at .../microsoft-isvexptools.powerplatform-vscode/pac/pac, a DIFFERENT binary from ~/.dotnet/tools/pac) before concluding the command itself is broken -- this is the third command this stray-process class has been observed blocking (IMP-0215's `pac solution check`, IMP-0216's `pac org who`, now `pac code add-data-source`).

what: Adding a second <FieldSecurityProfile> element (REV_FinanceOnly) to Other/FieldSecurityProfiles.xml, alongside the existing REV_TrusteeRestricted, makes provisioning/dataverse/ensure-schema-helpers.psm1's Get-RevFieldSecurityProfileDefinition/ConvertFrom-RevFieldSecurityProfileXml return a broken value built from PowerShell's array member-enumeration over both XML nodes, and ensure-schema.ps1 step 6 (which reads the result as a single $fsp) then issues 0 field-permission calls instead of the expected 69 - verified by running src/tests/provisioning/EnsureSchema.Tests.ps1, which reported 'Expected 51, but got 0' on the field-permission-call-count test and the drift-patch test.
expected: ensure-schema-helpers.psm1's own docstring says it 'Parses the one Phase 1 field security profile (REV_TrusteeRestricted) and its 34 field permissions' - true while there was exactly one profile. Adding a second, TAD-required profile (section 6.1/6.2's REV_FinanceOnly) should not silently zero out permission provisioning for every profile in the file, including the one that already worked.
root_cause: ConvertFrom-RevFieldSecurityProfileXml does `$profile = $xml.FieldSecurityProfiles.FieldSecurityProfile` assuming exactly one <FieldSecurityProfile> child. With two, PowerShell's XML property adapter returns an array, so $profile.name and $profile.FieldPermissions.FieldPermission become mis-shaped array-of-array values instead of scalars/flat lists, and the pscustomobject built from them carries a broken Name and Permissions. ensure-schema.ps1 step 6 (line 598) reads the result as a single profile ($fsp), so both the GET-or-CREATE-profile call and every one of the 69 expected field-permission calls resolve against corrupted values.
why_it_was_never_caught: no gate exercises ensure-schema-helpers.psm1 against more than one <FieldSecurityProfile> element, because until this feature there was only ever one in the solution; src/tests/provisioning/EnsureSchema.Tests.ps1 DID catch it the moment it was run against the two-profile source, but nothing in config/revitalise-grant-automation-build.yml runs the Pester suite automatically, so it would not have been caught before a live ensure-schema.ps1 run against DEV
lesson: A PowerShell helper that reads '$xml.Parent.Child' to get 'the one' instance of a repeatable XML element (here <FieldSecurityProfile>) returns a broken array-shaped value instead of erroring the moment a second instance exists - test it, or write it as a foreach over the child collection, before assuming cardinality one is safe for a component type the platform allows to repeat.

what: Fixed IMP-0238 (identity-agent, this same session): Get-RevFieldSecurityProfileDefinition / ConvertFrom-RevFieldSecurityProfileXml (provisioning/dataverse/ensure-schema-helpers.psm1) now returns an ARRAY of profile definitions, one per <FieldSecurityProfile> element, instead of assuming exactly one. ensure-schema.ps1 step 6 now loops over every profile returned rather than processing a single one. expected: a helper parsing a solution component that can legitimately have more than one instance (roles, option sets, and now field security profiles) should return a collection from the start, not assume singularity until it breaks
root_cause: the original function was written when exactly one <FieldSecurityProfile> existed in source and read $xml.FieldSecurityProfiles.FieldSecurityProfile directly as if it always resolves to a single element - PowerShell's XML adapter returns a scalar for exactly one matching child and an array for more than one, so the bug was invisible until a second profile existed

lesson: In PowerShell, $xml.Parent.Child returns a SCALAR XmlElement when exactly one <Child> exists and an ARRAY when more than one does - any helper reading a repeatable XML element (role, option set, field security profile, relationship) must wrap the read in @(...) and iterate, even when only one instance exists today, or it silently breaks the moment a second instance is added with no error at all. Get-RevRoleDefinitions and Get-RevOptionSetDefinitions in the same module already iterate correctly for this reason; Get-RevFieldSecurityProfileDefinition did not, until now.

what: scripts/verify-wbs-chain.py's staleness guard (IMP-0180) compared ANY --state file's mtime against every file under contract/ and src/solutions/, including hand-written fixtures. src/tests/fixtures/known-bad/wbs-chain/clean-state.json is a committed fixture with a fixed mtime, so the moment contract/evidence-map.json was edited, 52 contract files became 'newer than' it and the gate returned 2 — refusing to run — for both the section 4 clean-fixture assertion and the section 7 superseded-seed check.
