what: An Agent-tool dispatch to automation-agent (background), whose prompt described creating a live cloud flow and attempting a live Web API/pwsh write against DEV, was refused outright by the Auto-Mode classifier before the sub-agent ever started (ninth recorded instance of this class, and matches IMP-0252 exactly: dispatch-level refusal, not a refusal of a call the sub-agent later tried). If the dispatching agent already has its own working, unrefused live access this session (confirmed by a prior successful Bash-tool live call), do the operation directly in the dispatching agents own foreground Bash session instead of re-dispatching at the same scope — this resolved the whole flow-authoring task in this instance.

what: Two platform facts confirmed live/via official docs while building the 'REV | Portal | Round Statistics' flow (WBS 6.9, ADR-030). cost: three of four new gates in one review were green on their own selftests and wrong on the real tree: five distinct false-positive classes and one MASKED TRUE POSITIVE. All six were found by running the gates against the repository before wiring them; none was found by the fixtures.
what: Review 28 built four gates, each with runtime selftest fixtures, each passing. Run against the actual tree: (1) verify-change-order-requirements.py reported FR-059 as withdrawn because FR-059's SDD row CITES NFR-027's withdrawal in prose; (2) the same gate would have reported every superseded change order forever, since this project never edits an approved commercial document in place; (3) verify-review-document.py matched 'asks' inside 'tasks'; (4) it matched 'declined'/'carries' in sentences looking BACK at what a section did rather than deferring to it; (5) it read 'TAD section 9.3' and '§11 of the same document' as dangling self-references. Worst, (6) verify-routing-reconciliation.py's FIFO terminal-matching reported 0 unreconciled dispatches while MASKING the one real stall in the log (IMP-0291's 09:23 architect-agent dispatch) and flagging a healthy dispatch as in-flight instead. LIFO matching reports the real stall from the log alone.
expected: a gate proven able to fail against its own fixtures is also correct on the corpus it will run against
root_cause: A gate's selftest fixtures are written by the same author, in the same sitting, from the same mental model as the regex — so they encode the author's assumptions rather than testing them. The fixtures prove the gate CAN fail, which is the property verify-build-config.py requires and the property IMP-0007's class is about; they say nothing about whether it fails on the RIGHT things. Every one of the six defects above needed the real corpus: real prose that cites other requirements' dispositions, a real log where three dispatches to one agent compete for two terminal lines, real documents that reference other documents' sections.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing would have caught it. verify-build-config.py's check_negative_tests() runs a new gate's --selftest and accepts exit 0 as proof — the stronger of its two paths, and still only a can-it-fail proof. No check anywhere measures a new gate's PRECISION against the corpus it is about to be wired over, and a gate wired with false positives is the failure mode that teaches people to configure gates away.
lesson: Before wiring a new gate, run it against the WHOLE real corpus and read every finding, one by one, deciding true or false positive — the selftest proves the gate can fail, the corpus proves it fails on the right things, and these are different questions. Budget for it: three of four gates in one review were wrong on first contact with real data, and the most dangerous defect was not a false positive but a false NEGATIVE that a plausible matching rule produced (FIFO pairing of dispatches to terminal lines hid the one genuine stall while inventing a fake one). Where a gate reports 0 findings against a corpus you know contains an instance, that is the tell. State the measured precision in the review document — 'N findings across M documents, K true positives' — so the number is on the record rather than an impression.

cost: one extra edit-and-rerun cycle, caught in-session before commit (WBS 6.3)
what: src/code-apps/trustee-review-portal/src/dataverse/schema.test.ts's 'names no secured column is named anywhere in this app' check used content.includes(column) — a plain substring test — so binding the three new …redacted care-support columns (TAD sec3.2.1) failed this local check even though they are IsSecured=0 and safe, because each redacted column's name is its secured source's own name with 'redacted' appended directly, no separator, making the secured name a literal substring of the safe one.
expected: TAD sec3.2.1 and the dispatching agent's own instruction treat binding the three …redacted columns as settled-safe; the app's own test suite should agree, the same way the official build gate does.
root_cause: the official gate (scripts/verify-code-app-column-bindings.py) was rewritten in improvement review 19 (C-TECH-069) to match forbidden column names with a whole-identifier regex, '(?<![A-Za-z0-9_])column(?![A-Za-z0-9_])', specifically to stop a secured name that is a prefix of a safe identifier from false-positiving. schema.test.ts carries a separate, older duplicate of that same check and was never updated when the real gate was fixed, so the two drifted.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing cross-checks that a local vitest duplicate of an official build gate's logic stays in sync with a correctness fix applied to the official gate; the real Python gate would have passed this exact binding.
lesson: Any check that matches a forbidden Dataverse column name against source text must use a whole-identifier boundary, (?<![A-Za-z0-9_])name(?![A-Za-z0-9_]) over [a-z0-9_], never String.includes or a bare substring/regex search — a secured column's name can be, and for every …redacted column in this app IS, a strict prefix of a safe identifier with a suffix appended and no separator.

proposed_change.summary: already self-fixed in this session (schema.test.ts now uses the same whole-identifier regex as scripts/verify-code-app-column-bindings.py). what: scripts/verify-improvement-log.py's check_missing_stamps() warns that IMP-0316 and IMP-0319 are 'cited by 2026-08-25-improvement-review-2.md and carry NO reviewed_in ... stamp it with the review that processed it'. That review processed NEITHER. It APPENDED IMP-0319 as its own new finding (its section 10 says 'logged as IMP-0319' and 'this review appended 2 (IMP-0318, IMP-0319)'), and it names IMP-0316 only in a paragraph about its own id allocation shifting from IMP-0316/0317 to IMP-0318/0319 while it was being applied. The stamp the gate demands cannot be written truthfully, because no review processed either entry.
expected: a warning that instructs an action names an action that is true to perform; check_missing_stamps()'s own docstring reserves it for entries that 'read as unread' because a review processed them silently
root_cause: The check decides 'substantive' by SUBTRACTION, not by detection. It takes every id in the document, removes the ids sitting under a deferral heading and the ids in a paragraph that disclaims scope (split_deferral_citations), and treats the remainder as a processing claim. Two positions therefore fall through that no exemption covers: an id a review LOGGED itself, and an id mentioned as numbering/provenance history. Both are guaranteed to occur, because a review that appends its own findings always writes their ids in a non-deferral position -- so this warning fires against every review that logs a finding, by construction. This is the THIRD false-positive shape in the same predicate: IMP-0196 added the deferral-heading exemption, and improvement review 19 change 7 added the disclaiming-paragraph exemption after it warned on the two literal ends of a written-out range.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing. verify-improvement-log.py --selftest carries 53 fixtures and none covers an id the citing document appended or mentioned as provenance -- every fixture for this predicate is built from the processed-vs-deferred distinction, which is the distinction the check already handles. The gate cannot detect its own false positives because a citation genuinely is ambiguous in prose, which is the argument for a declared field rather than a sharper heuristic.
lesson: Before acting on a 'cited by a review and carries no reviewed_in' warning, open the citing document and find WHAT it says about that id: a review that APPENDED the finding, or that mentions it only as id-allocation history, has not processed it and must not be stamped -- stamping it would make the queue claim a disposition that exists nowhere. It asks only whether the action fires when it SHOULD; it does not ask whether it fires when it should not. Its own cheapest-verification step - force a failure and confirm a status:error body - would pass while the success-path double-response defect survived, closing the row as CONFIRMED over a live P1.
expected: An assumption whose subject is a conditional branch states the condition in both directions, so closing it proves the branch is correctly gated and not merely reachable.
root_cause: The row was written to record the novelty of the shape (a PowerApp-kind Response reached from a failure branch, unprecedented in this solution) rather than the property the design needs. Novelty framing produces one-sided claims: it asks whether the new thing works, not whether it is correctly bounded.
why_it_was_never_caught: verify-assumption-markers.py resolves each OPEN row's marker to a real file containing its id - a presence check on the marker, which cannot read the claim's logic.
lesson: When an Unvalidated Assumptions Register row is about a CONDITIONAL branch, word the claim and its verification in both directions - fires when it should AND does not fire when it should not. A one-sided row can be closed CONFIRMED by a test that exercises only the happy half, certifying the opposite defect as verified.

proposed_change.summary: In the Unvalidated Assumptions Register section, instruct that a row about a conditional or error branch states the negative case too, and that its cheapest-verification column names both observations.

cost: one gate would have shipped at 60% precision; another would have shipped blind to the only instance it was built for
what: Applying improvement review 30, two of the five changes carrying a corpus measurement did not reproduce that measurement when the SHIPPED implementation was built. (1) Change 1's draft recorded '3 findings / 3 true / 0 false across 33 documents'; the shipped check measured 5 findings / 3 true / 2 FALSE across 35 - a re-quoted CLUSTER block in an Addendum, and a class carried forward with (x0 new members. Two narrowings fixed it. (2) Change 2's draft recorded '17 resolvable citations, 1 true positive'; the shipped gate's first run resolved 5 and reported a CLEAN RUN over the live instance it was built for, because this repo writes every path in a code span and the regex did not allow a closing backtick. The draft's own section 6 listed two measurement bugs it had already fixed in its probe (repo-relative paths, bold status values) and this was a third, present only in the shipped artefact.
expected: A corpus measurement recorded in a review document should hold for the artefact that ships, or the review should say plainly that it measured a probe and that the shipped gate's precision is unmeasured until application.
root_cause: The corpus-precision obligation (agents/improvement-agent.md, review 29 change 5) says to run a new gate against the real corpus and record the precision - but a DRAFT has no shipped gate to run, so the figure is necessarily produced by a throwaway probe. The probe and the gate are different artefacts written at different times, and nothing carried the obligation forward to the moment the real one exists. Both defects here were in the shipped regex, not in the design: one too loose, one too tight.
why_it_was_never_caught: Both artefacts passed their own --selftest. A gate's fixtures are written by the same author in the same sitting from the same mental model as the regex, so they encode the author's assumptions rather than testing them - which is exactly what the corpus obligation exists to catch, and exactly what a probe-stage measurement cannot deliver for the shipped code.
lesson: A corpus measurement in a review DRAFT is a property of the throwaway probe, not of the gate that ships. Re-measure the shipped artefact against the real corpus at application time and adjudicate every finding again - the figures will differ, and both directions are dangerous: too loose ships a gate that cries wolf (5 findings, 2 false), too tight ships one that reports a clean run over the instance it was built for (5 citations resolved instead of 16). Where a re-measurement contradicts the draft, that is NARROW-AND-REPORT, not a reason to trust the draft.

proposed_change.summary: In the 'run it against the REAL CORPUS before you wire it' section, state that a DRAFT's corpus figure is a probe measurement and must be labelled as one, and that activation step 8 re-runs the measurement against the shipped artefact and re-adjudicates every finding before wiring. Consider requiring the review document to carry both numbers (probe at draft, shipped at application) so a silent divergence is visible - review 30's section 10 does this by hand. The mechanical half worth exploring: verify-build-config.py already runs each new gate's --selftest and accepts exit 0; it could additionally require a recorded corpus-precision line for any gate step added in the same commit.

cost: On the single most likely runtime failure of the new trustee-facing flow (List_applications_in_round, the up-to-1000-row read), the failure alert and the rev_errorlog row will name 'Switch_on_open_round_count' with the platform's wrapper text 'An action failed. No dependent actions succeeded.' instead of the action that failed. The only diagnostic the trustee-facing path produces is therefore useless for 8 of the 10 actions that can fail.
what: REVPortalRoundStatistics's Find_the_failed_action filters @result('Compute_statistics') for the child whose status is Failed - correctly avoiding the result(scope)[0] trap that IMP-0109 recorded. But Compute_statistics has only TWO immediate children, and the second is a Switch containing 8 descendants. result() returns immediate children only, so any failure inside the Switch surfaces as the Switch's own wrapper result, not the leaf. The flow implements the first half of IMP-0109's lesson and not the second half ('when that child is itself a scope, call result() on the inner scope to reach the leaf').
expected: The failure alert names the action that actually failed, which is what the Find_the_failed_action pattern exists to achieve and what its own description claims it does.
root_cause: The pattern was copied from REVScoringDailySummary's Summarise scope, whose six immediate children are ALL leaf actions - so filtering result() for the Failed child always reaches the leaf there. Compute_statistics wraps a Switch instead. The notes.md explicitly records the choice to wrap the whole body in one scope 'rather than attaching a failure branch to each of the two OpenApiConnection actions separately', and cites Summarise as the model, without noting that the two scopes differ in nesting depth - the one property the pattern depends on. This is structurally the SAME error as D-10: a shape copied from a flow whose precondition differs in exactly the way that matters (there, the Response count; here, whether the scope's children are leaves).
why_it_was_never_caught: verify-flow-definition-language.py check 5 says in its own output that it 'proves a failure path EXISTS, never that it works'. The packer, the hosted Solution Checker and all 1248 tests are equally blind: no test in src/tests/ references any part of this flow's failure path (defect D-11, still open for a third cycle). Only tracing result()'s scoping semantics by hand against the action tree finds it - or a deliberate failure once the flow is live.
lesson: Filtering result(scope) for the child whose status is Failed only reaches the real failure when that scope's immediate children are all leaf actions. result() returns immediate children ONLY, so a Scope, Switch, If or Foreach among them collapses everything inside it into one wrapper result whose message is 'An action failed. No dependent actions succeeded.' Before copying this error-diagnosis pattern between flows, compare the two scopes' NESTING, not just their shape: recurse result() into the failed child when that child is itself a container.

proposed_change.summary: Add a check: in any flow whose failure branch filters @result('<scope>') for a Failed child, flag it when that scope has a container (Scope/Switch/If/Foreach/Until) among its immediate children and no follow-on result() call against that container. Pure shape check over the action tree, no fuzzy matching. Measure against all 5 flows before wiring HARD - REVIntakeWordPressToDataverse and REVScoringCalculateAndFlag both have containers among their catch-scope's children too, so this is very likely a 3-instance pre-existing finding, not a single-flow one, and the altitude call belongs to improvement-agent.

what: docs/development/trustee-portal-visual-refresh-dev-summary.md line 106 and docs/tests/trustee-portal-visual-refresh-test-report-v2.md section 4 both describe REVPortalRoundStatistics as a four-Response flow. cost: caught before any push; would have shipped a WCAG 2.1 AA failure on all three primary buttons
what: Fluent UI v9's own default light theme is NOT accessible for an arbitrary brand ramp. Building the real Revitalise theme from #ED008C put colorBrandBackground (= brand[80] = #ed008c) behind colorNeutralForegroundOnBrand (a hard-coded white) as normal-size button label text at 4.22:1, below the 4.5:1 AA floor, on all three Button appearance="primary" instances (VerdictForm.tsx, ApplicationsTable.tsx, LandingPage.tsx). Separately, the reviewer's own supplied rule 'use white when text sits over one of the other colours' was wrong for one of the four colours: white on the accent #14ADBB is 2.72:1, which fails normal text AND fails the 3:1 large-text/UI-graphic floor, so no size of white text is usable on it. Both were found only by computing every pair individually.
expected: TAD ADR-026 states that 'Fluent's own default theme is already accessible by design', and theme.ts's header repeated the claim as arithmetic confirmation. A supplied brand rule was expected to hold for the colours it named.
root_cause: ADR-026's accessibility claim was true of Fluent's OWN blue ramp (brand[80] = #0f6cbd, 5.38:1) and was generalised to any ramp. Fluent's alias layer (@fluentui/tokens/lib/alias/lightColor.js) pins colorBrandBackground and colorBrandBackgroundStatic to brand[80] while colorNeutralForegroundOnBrand is a fixed white, so AA compliance of the primary button is a property of the RAMP, not of Fluent. Any brand whose shade 80 falls between 3:1 and 4.5:1 against white ships a failing button. The accent half has the same shape: a general rule about a colour family, applied without computing the member.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing — this repo has no automated contrast check of any kind. ADR-026 and TAD 8.2 both REQUIRE a contrast check on every brand pair, but the check existed only as prose in theme.ts's header comment, which nothing re-executes, and the placeholder ramp made that prose trivially true.
lesson: Fluent v9's createLightTheme does not guarantee AA: colorBrandBackground and colorBrandBackgroundStatic are brand[80] behind a hard-coded white, so a brand whose shade 80 is under 4.5:1 against white ships a failing primary button. Compute white-on-brand[80] before adopting any ramp, and if it is under 4.5:1 move BOTH rest tokens to brand[70] and shift Hover/Pressed/Selected one step too (brand[60]/[30]/[50]), or rest and hover become the same colour and the button loses all hover feedback. Never accept a general statement that a palette 'is accessible' — compute each pair, including pairs a human told you were fine.

proposed_change.summary: A gate that resolves the shipped Fluent theme (createLightTheme + the app's own overrides) and asserts every foreground/background token pair a component actually renders clears its WCAG floor: 4.5:1 for text pairs, 3:1 for UI-graphic pairs. src/code-apps/trustee-review-portal/src/theme.test.ts is a working per-app implementation of exactly this and could be lifted; the gap is that nothing requires it to exist in the next code app.

The repo-wide scripts/verify-brand-contrast.py this finding proposed was deliberately NOT built: the instance is already defended by theme.test.ts running in the code-app-coverage build step, and the residual gap ('the next code app') has a corpus of one, which cannot be measured against a corpus. what: src/test/harness.tsx rendered every component test inside <FluentProvider theme={webLightTheme}>, not the theme the app actually ships (brandTheme). cost: one ground-truthing pass; avoided shipping an unlicensed font file
what: Revitalise's brand handover named Aptos Display and Aptos as the heading and body fonts. Microsoft 365's inclusion of Aptos is NOT a webfont-embedding licence: it covers install and use on a licensed device and embedding inside documents, not self-hosting the font file for a portal served to trustees on their own devices. A separate commercial webfont licence exists via Monotype/MyFonts and is not procured under this engagement. So no .woff/.woff2/.ttf file was added and no @font-face rule was written; both stacks name Aptos first and fall through to 'Segoe UI Variable'/'Segoe UI'/system faces, which costs nothing and needs no licence.
expected: a brand handover that names a font is implementable by shipping that font
root_cause: a corporate font bundled with an Office/Microsoft 365 licence is licensed per-device for authoring, and the web-serving right is a separate SKU. Nothing in a brand guide distinguishes the two, so 'the brand font is Aptos' reads as an implementable instruction when the implementable part is only the font-stack NAME.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing — no gate or checklist asks whether a named brand font is licensed for web embedding, and the architecture's own extraction method (TAD 12.2) treats the font stack as a value to obtain rather than a right to obtain
lesson: Never bundle a font file that arrived with a brand handover without checking its web-embedding licence separately from the desktop one — an Office/Microsoft 365 font (Aptos, and the same applies to Segoe UI) is licensed for device install and document embedding, not for a site to serve. The compliant, zero-cost implementation is name-only in the CSS font stack with a full system fallback chain: the viewer's own installed copy is used where present, and nothing is served. Record the substitution rather than making it silently, because the rendered result differs per device.

proposed_change.summary: Add a brand-asset line to the checklist (or to a new brand-adoption skill): before shipping a font file, confirm a web-embedding licence exists for it; an Office/Microsoft 365 bundled font does not carry one. Name-only in the stack plus a system fallback chain is the default.

applied_by: Improvement review 34 change 10. skills/accessibility-checklist.md section 1.4 gains a brand-asset licence step: every font file shipped has a WEB-EMBEDDING licence, checked separately from the desktop one, because an Office/Microsoft 365 bundled font (Aptos, Segoe UI) is licensed for device install and document embedding and the web-serving right is a separate SKU. The compliant zero-cost default is named - name-only in the CSS stack with a full system fallback chain - and the checklist requires the substitution be RECORDED rather than made silently. Placed in 1.4 Distinguishable deliberately: the rendered face differs per device, so it is also a contrast-checking consideration, since the face you measured may not be the face that renders.

cost: 1 failed pac code push attempt, diagnosed and fixed in the same session by reading the platform's own error body; re-push succeeded and was proven idempotent by a second clean run
what: Closing A-LAND-2: `pa app add flow --flow-id 1242b7f9-14fc-4246-7c97-7a851e362dd2` (against the now-live REV | Portal | Round Statistics flow) wrote a `workflowDetails` object (workflowEntityId/workflowDisplayName/workflowName) into power.config.json's new `44f7e152-...` connectionReferences entry for the shared_logicflows connector. The immediately following `pac code push --solutionName RevitaliseGrantAutomation` (pac 2.4.1) failed outright: HTTP 400 InvalidRequestContent on PUT .../powerapps/apps/{id}, 'Could not find member workflowDetails on object of type AppConnectionReference'. Stripping that one member (keeping id/displayName/dataSources, matching the shape of the pre-existing Dataverse connectionReference entry) let the push succeed, and a second push with the same file was clean too.
expected: the file `pa app add flow` writes is the file `pac code push` accepts -- they are documented as the two-step mechanism for this exact scenario (TAD ADR-030, architecture doc L1017-1019) with no third step to reconcile them
root_cause: the two CLIs (`pa`, the @microsoft/power-apps-based tool that runs `add flow`, and `pac` 2.4.1, whose `code push` PUTs the app registration) disagree about the server-side AppConnectionReference schema for a logic-flow-backed connection reference: `pa` writes a `workflowDetails` sub-object that `pac`'s own PUT payload construction/the server's deserializer for api-version=1 does not recognise. `workflowDetails` is plausibly meant only as a local hint for future codegen (e.g. `pa app refresh data-source` deciding which workflow a data source maps to) and should never have reached the payload pac sends to the server, but nothing between the two tools filters it.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing -- this is the first time `pa app add flow` plus `pac code push` has been exercised together end-to-end against a live flow on this project; A-R37 in the architecture doc already flagged the mechanism as 'documented but unproven' for exactly this reason
lesson: After `pa app add flow --flow-id <id>`, before the next `pac code push`, check power.config.json's new connectionReferences entry for a `workflowDetails` member and delete it (keep id/displayName/dataSources only) -- pac 2.4.1's code-push PUT rejects it outright with HTTP 400 InvalidRequestContent naming `AppConnectionReference` as the type with no such member. Re-running `pa app add flow` or `pa app refresh data-source` later will rewrite the field back in, so this is a repeat-every-time step, not a one-off fix.

proposed_change.summary: Document the pa/pac interop defect: after `pa app add flow`, strip any `workflowDetails` member from the new connectionReferences entry in power.config.json before running `pac code push`, or the push fails HTTP 400 InvalidRequestContent (AppConnectionReference has no such member). Repeat after any re-run of `pa app add flow`/`pa app refresh data-source`.

what: Background dispatch a8c305c410fb67057 ('Push brand theme and loader to DEV') reported task status 'completed' with a final message stating 'I already have a Monitor watching for the idempotent re-run's completion (task bhkamkuhd). expected: a Task-tool dispatch that reports 'completed' has either produced its gate output (pipeline.log entry, Deployment Summary) or explicitly reports BLOCKED/STALLED -- not a third state where the agent describes itself as about to resume via a mechanism nothing in this system actually wires up
root_cause: a dispatched subagent has no way to be woken by a Monitor or background-task notification the way the top-level session is -- notifications route to the dispatching session, not to the dispatched agent's own (now-ended) context. The agent that set up the Monitor appears to have modeled its own execution the way the PARENT session works (react to a notification, continue the turn) rather than recognising that ITS turn ending IS the terminal state from the dispatcher's point of view, identical in effect to the three spend-limit deaths earlier this session (IMP-0172's class) even though no error was reported this time.
why_it_was_never_caught: agents/WORKFLOW.md's dispatch-death protocol covers a dispatch that dies to an external error (spend limit, timeout) but has no explicit case for a dispatch that ends its own turn voluntarily while describing unfinished work as pending on a mechanism that will not actually resume it -- the 'completed' task status looks identical to a genuinely finished dispatch from the parent's tool result alone
commercial_impact: none -- DEV-only, no billed hours claimed against unverified work
lesson: A background Agent-tool dispatch cannot resume itself from a Monitor or background-task notification it creates -- only the dispatching session receives those. If a dispatch's final message describes work as pending on 'I'll resume automatically when X completes,' treat that exactly like a spend-limit death: the dispatch has actually stopped, X will never be acted on by that agent, and the dispatcher must verify live state directly and do the smallest remaining reconciliation itself rather than waiting for a resumption that is not coming. A 'completed' task-notification status describes only that the agent's own turn ended with no live children -- it does not mean the agent's stated goal was reached.

proposed_change.summary: Extend the 'When a dispatch dies instead of finishing' section: a dispatch that ends with status completed but whose final message defers unfinished work to a self-created Monitor/background-task notification must be treated identically to a spend-limit death for reconciliation purposes -- verify on disk/live, do not wait for the described resumption, which cannot occur from a subagent context.

cost: one full failed 'npm test' run (7 suites failing) plus ~15 minutes spent patching node_modules' vendored @microsoft/power-apps package before the real cause was found
what: `npm test -- --coverage` in src/code-apps/trustee-review-portal failed 7 suites (App.test.tsx, DistributionChart.test.tsx, RoundStatisticsCharts.test.tsx, repository.test.ts, roundStatistics.test.ts, landing.test.ts, LandingPage.test.tsx) with 'Cannot find module .../dist/data/multiSelectPicklistUtils' — the exact symptom vitest.config.ts's own server.deps.inline comment already documents and already fixes by inlining /@microsoft\/power-apps\//. Deleting node_modules/.vite (vitest's dependency-optimization cache) and re-running made all 24 suites, 449 tests pass clean on the genuinely untouched node_modules — no source or config change was needed at all.
expected: the already-wired server.deps.inline fix in vitest.config.ts to hold on every run
root_cause: vitest/vite's dependency pre-bundle cache under node_modules/.vite can go stale relative to vitest.config.ts (e.g. after an npm install changed a dependency's installed files, as this session's tree already had pending package.json/package-lock.json changes adding recharts) and continue serving a pre-inline-fix optimization, reproducing the exact 'Cannot find module' Node ESM error the inline setting exists to prevent
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing clears or checks the vite dep-cache before a test run; the failure looks identical to a genuine upstream package defect (and IS a genuine upstream @microsoft/power-apps ESM defect — missing .js extensions on internal relative imports/exports — the inline setting works around, not fixes), so it is easy to misdiagne as unfixable rather than as a stale cache
lesson: Before treating a 'Cannot find module .../dist/data/multiSelectPicklistUtils' (or any @microsoft/power-apps/dist internal-import) failure in this app's test suite as a real defect, run `rm -rf node_modules/.vite` and re-run — vitest.config.ts's server.deps.inline already documents and fixes this exact class, and a stale dependency-optimization cache can reproduce the pre-fix symptom verbatim even when the fix is correctly in place. Never hand-patch node_modules to work around it — it is not tracked, does not persist to CI, and the real fix (or in this case, non-fix-needed) is one directory deletion.

what: Amendment A-02, Finding 1 recorded three whole categories as 'Correctly excluded - not a gap' (Financial Eligibility, the condition/illness checklist and health narrative, and helper/referee/emergency-contact details), citing SDD 7.1 and FR-036 as the justification. lesson: 'Correctly excluded - not a gap' is a claim about the schema and must be ground-truthed like any other. Verify exclusions against source with the same rigour as inclusions, and cite the evidence - an unevidenced exclusion is invisible at review, so nobody will ask for the evidence you did not gather.

proposed_change.summary: When a field-by-field comparison marks a source item as out of scope, require the same evidence citation the in-scope items carry - the column's IsSecured value and profile membership, not a prose classification tier. Exclusions are decisions and need a cited basis.

cost: would have failed the next build at the no-secured-columns-in-code-app step; caught at TAD stage instead
what: SDD Amendment A-05 (APPROVED) instructs the trustee Code App to bind 11 IsSecured=1 columns of REV_TrusteeRestricted, reasoning that binding is safe because 'the platform returns no value to a trustee whatever the app asks for'. Two things make that undeliverable as written: (a) the HARD build gate no-secured-columns-in-code-app derives its forbidden set from FieldSecurityProfiles.xml at check time and fails on ANY secured column the app references, so the build stops; (b) the safety premise is incomplete - parent TAD section 6.1 grants the PROCESS OWNER 'trustee portal (read)' and her REV Admins group team is an intended member of that profile, so the same query returns real helper/referee/emergency-contact names, benefit status and employment status when she opens the anonymous screen.
expected: an approved amendment's stated mechanism is buildable against the repository's own HARD gates
root_cause: A-05 Finding 1 reasoned about ONE persona (the trustee) on a screen that two personas open. Column security is per-principal, so 'the platform withholds it' is a statement about a reader, not about a query - and the app has two readers. The gate encodes exactly this, and its docstring states the process-owner case in prose, but the amendment was written from the profile XML rather than from the gate that guards it.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing - plan-agent does not run build gates, and no check compares an approved SDD amendment's prescribed mechanism against the build steps that would execute it. verify-tad-coverage.py checks that columns the TAD NAMES exist; it cannot check that a mechanism the SDD DESCRIBES is permitted.
lesson: Before designing to an approved requirement that says an app should READ a column, check whether that column is in a field security profile AND whether a build gate forbids referencing it - no-secured-columns-in-code-app fails on any secured column the Code App names, whatever the intent. cost: one draft rewritten before shipping -- caught by simulation before any live import, not a live defect
what: The workflow definition language's `if(<expr>,<valueIfTrue>,<valueIfFalse>)` does NOT short-circuit -- Microsoft's own function reference states 'Parameters are evaluated from left to right', meaning all three arguments are evaluated before one is selected. A first-draft percentage guard for a genuinely empty round -- `if(equals(population,0),0,mul(div(float(count),float(population)),100))` -- was written to avoid a division-by-zero, and still throws ZeroDivisionError-equivalent at runtime when population is 0, because the div(...) branch is evaluated regardless of which branch `if()` returns. Found by writing a small evaluator for the exact expression subset REVPortalRoundStatistics-...json's new actions use (scratchpad, not shipped) and running it against a synthetic zero-application round before the file was ever imported anywhere.
expected: an `if()`-style conditional guard prevents its untaken branch from being evaluated, the way most languages' ternary/short-circuit operators do
root_cause: Power Automate / Azure Logic Apps' workflow definition language evaluates function arguments eagerly, always, with no lazy/short-circuit special-casing for `if()` specifically -- confirmed directly from Microsoft's own docs (microsoft_docs_search, 'Reference guide to functions in expressions for workflows'), not inferred
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing in this repository's gates evaluates an expression's arithmetic -- verify-flow-definition-language.py checks for forbidden SHAPES, never numeric behaviour. This was caught only because this dispatch wrote a purpose-built evaluator for the exact functions its own new actions use, one level beyond what any existing gate does
lesson: Never rely on `if()` (or any WDL conditional) to guard a division, an array index, or any other operation that throws on the untaken branch's own inputs -- both branches are evaluated regardless of the condition. Use a divisor-safe rewrite instead: `max(<divisor>,1)` as the denominator (never a literal 0) gives the same correct answer whenever the true divisor is 0, because the numerator is then necessarily 0 too. The shipped fix -- `mul(div(float(count),float(max(population,1))),100)` -- is now the pattern for every future percentage-over-a-possibly-zero-population computation in this project's flows.

proposed_change.summary: Record that if() in the workflow definition language evaluates all three arguments eagerly (no short-circuit) -- cite Microsoft's own 'Parameters are evaluated from left to right' wording -- and that a division guarded by if(equals(divisor,0),...) still throws. Give max(divisor,1) as the safe pattern, with REVPortalRoundStatistics-...json's percentage expressions as the worked example.

cost: about 25 minutes of this session spent trying to keep app.module.css line-count-neutral above line 356 so three citations in another package's files would stay true, before abandoning that as worse engineering than reporting the drift
what: Three files written by the Package A dispatch cite this app's own layout stylesheet by LINE NUMBER, and two of the citations were already transposed before Package B touched anything: src/code-apps/trustee-review-portal/src/styles/ds.module.css:67-68, src/components/ds/Button.tsx:19 and src/styles/ds-tokens.test.ts:331-332 all say 'styles.tallTarget (app.module.css:171)' and 'styles.sortButton (:355-356)', but line 171 was `.table th .sortButton`'s min-height and 355-356 was `.tallTarget`'s - the two are swapped. Package B's restyle of app.module.css (the WBS 6.1/6.2 visual pass) then moved both declarations again, so all three citations now point at unrelated lines. No test asserts any of this; they are comments, and all three files are frozen Package A deliverables this dispatch was told not to edit.
expected: a source comment that cites another file by path:line to either stay true or be caught when it stops being true, particularly across a two-package split where each package owns a different one of the two files
root_cause: a path:line citation is a hand-maintained pointer with no derivation and no checker, and the two files sit in different dispatches of the same feature: the Package A pass wrote the citations against the stylesheet as it then stood, and the Package B pass is the one that edits that stylesheet - so neither pass is ever in a position to see the pointer break. CLAUDE.md's reporting rule requires freshly-grepped line-links in anything the REVIEWER reads, and that rule has been generalised in practice into source comments, where the cost profile is the opposite: a report is read once, a comment is read for the life of the file.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing. scripts/verify-derived-counts.py (built for IMP-0150, the same class) checks (file, pattern, derivation command) triples for COUNTS and has no notion of a path:line pointer; no gate opens a comment's citation and checks the target line still contains the named identifier. ds-tokens.test.ts asserts nine real properties of ds.module.css mechanically and the crossed citation sits in its own comment prose, untested by construction.
lesson: In a SOURCE comment, cite another file by the name of the thing (`app.module.css`'s `.tallTarget`) and never by line number - a grep finds the symbol forever, and a line number is stale the next time either file is edited by anyone. Reserve freshly-grepped path:line links for reviewer reports, which are read once. When a package split gives two dispatches one file each, a line citation across the boundary cannot be maintained by either of them: the pass that writes the pointer never edits the target, and the pass that edits the target is told not to edit the pointer.

proposed_change.summary: Extend the registry to a second claim kind: a `path:line` citation found in a tracked source comment, checked (SOFT) by opening the cited file at that line and confirming the line or its rule block still contains the identifier named beside the citation. Report file, citation, what was found instead. Pair it with a one-line convention in skills/how-to-report-to-the-reviewer.md distinguishing REPORT line-links (required, grepped fresh, read once) from SOURCE-COMMENT citations (name the symbol, never the line) - the rule is currently stated only for reports and is being generalised into source comments where it does not hold.

applied_by: improvement review 33 change 16 — skills/how-to-report-to-the-reviewer.md rule 1 now distinguishes a REPORT line-link (required, grepped fresh, read once) from a SOURCE-COMMENT citation (name the symbol, never the line), because the rule was stated only for reports and had been generalised in practice into comments where the cost profile is the opposite. Records the structural trap this finding identifies: when a package split gives two dispatches one file each, a line citation across the boundary cannot be maintained by either — the pass that writes the pointer never edits the target, and the pass that edits the target is told not to edit the pointer. The GATE half is deliberately not built and the reason is stated: it needs a registry of citations, and the three that exist sit in frozen deliverables nobody is authorised to edit, so the gate would open red on work no dispatch owns.

evidence_grep.contains: In a SOURCE COMMENT it inverts

cost: Caught during this dispatch's own verification pass, so nothing shipped wrong. Had it not been caught, the cost is the whole failure A-R38 was written to prevent: a later edit removing one import line, 600+ tests staying green, and a visually broken app discovered by a trustee.
what: TAD Revision 4's A-R38 named the highest-impact build-time risk correctly (a new global stylesheet imported only from main.tsx leaves the test harness asserting markup the app never produces) and prescribed a two-part mitigation: import it in harness.tsx, and add a disk-read contrast test in theme.test.ts's shape. Both were implemented exactly. Neither can detect the failure. Every token assertion reads ds-tokens.css OFF DISK, so deleting the `import "./styles/ds-tokens.css"` line from main.tsx leaves all 29 of them passing while the running app renders every var(--space-6), var(--radius-pill) and var(--text-heading) in seven components as nothing. The harness import is inert for the same reason the disk-read technique is necessary: vitest.config.ts sets no `css` option, so vitest processes no CSS import at all.
expected: A mitigation written against a stated risk should be able to fail when that risk materialises.
root_cause: The mitigation and the risk are about different things. The risk is about the stylesheet being LOADED; the mitigation asserts what the stylesheet CONTAINS. Both halves read the file directly, which is the only technique that works under this vitest config, and that same property is what makes them blind to whether anything imports it. The gap is invisible on inspection because the mitigation looks like it covers the case: it names the right file and runs in the right suite.
detected_by: development-agent verifying the sub-dispatch's work by mutation rather than by reading it — deleting the main.tsx import and observing that the suite stayed green.
why_it_was_never_caught: Nothing asserts that a side-effect CSS import exists. The three existing global stylesheets (brand.css, print.css, and now ds-tokens.css) are all guarded for content by disk-read tests and none is guarded for being imported, so the same blind spot already covered two files before this one.
lesson: A disk-read stylesheet test proves what a file SAYS, never that anything loads it — so it cannot see a deleted import, which is the exact failure the technique is usually adopted to guard. When a global stylesheet is added to this app, assert the side-effect import in main.tsx (and in test/harness.tsx) as well as the file's contents, and prove the assertion by deleting the import and watching it fail. Verified this dispatch: with the assertions added, deleting main.tsx's import fails 3 tests and deleting harness.tsx's fails 2; without them, zero.
proposed_change: Generalise rather than patch this one file: a check that every .css under src/code-apps/*/src/styles/ that is not a CSS Module (no .module.css) is side-effect imported by that app's composition root, wired as a build step beside no-secured-columns-in-code-app. brand.css and print.css have carried this same exposure since they were written; ds-tokens.css is the third instance, and the fix landed in this dispatch covers only the third.
applied_by: improvement review 33 change 2 — check A of scripts/verify-code-app-composition-root.py enumerates every non-module stylesheet under a code app's src/ from DISK and asserts src/main.tsx side-effect imports it, wired as build step 'code-app-composition-root'. Generalised rather than patched, as this finding asked: a hand-typed list of three filenames is replaced by an enumeration, which is C-TECH-067's own rule. Measured over the real tree: 1 app, 3 global stylesheets, all imported, 0 failures. The harness-divergence half is REPORTED and does not fail — brand.css and print.css are imported by main.tsx and not by harness.tsx, and since vitest processes no CSS nothing at runtime depends on it; the two source comments claiming all three are imported in the same change are the wrong half, and are handed to frontend-agent in review 33 §5.

cost: One implementation decision that had to be resolved by judgement and then flagged to the reviewer, on a value with a documented contrast figure and a pinned test behind it. No rework, because the conservative reading was taken.
what: TAD Revision 4 SS8.5 point 4 contains two statements that cannot both be followed. It says 'Exactly two things change: the .chartBar fill and the section chrome', and then four lines later 'The fill stays var(--colorCompoundBrandBackground)'. The dispatch brief inherited the first reading ('restyle its .chartBar fill'), so the contradiction propagated one level down before anyone met it. Separately in the same document, SS8.4.1 states the design system's warning-tone title at 3.18:1 where the WCAG 2.1 formula gives 3.16:1 over the same two hex values.
expected: An approved design document states each decision once, in one direction.
root_cause: SS8.5's per-point format is 'what changes' followed by 'the decision', and for this point the decision is that nothing changes about the fill. The lead-in sentence was written to the section's template rather than to its own content. The contrast figure is an independent transcription slip in the second decimal.
detected_by: development-agent, writing the dispatch brief for the consumption package and finding the two sentences disagreed while trying to state the instruction precisely.
why_it_was_never_caught: Nothing checks a design document for internal consistency, and both halves read as plausible in isolation. The contrast figure would have been caught by any recomputation, which is exactly what this dispatch did to all nine stated rows.
lesson: Resolve a contradiction inside an approved document in favour of the specific, reasoned sentence over the summarising lead-in, take the option that preserves an already-tested value, and report it rather than absorbing it. Here the explicit sentence was right on the merits independently: colorCompoundBrandBackground is brand[80] at 4.22:1 (clearing the 3:1 UI-graphic floor), its arithmetic is documented in app.module.css, it is pinned by theme.test.ts, and print.css forces it to black on paper — so 'changing' it would have moved a tested decision for no requirement.
proposed_change: Recompute every contrast figure an architecture document states, at development time, against the hex values the document itself names — this dispatch did so for all nine of SS8.4.1's rows and eight reproduced exactly. Worth a small script over the SS8.4-style tables rather than a habit, since the figures are the whole basis of an ADR that a later reader will trust without re-deriving.
applied_by: improvement review 33 change 7 — scripts/verify-design-doc-claims.py check (b) recomputes every contrast ratio a markdown TABLE ROW states from the hex values that row itself names, by the WCAG 2.1 formula. This finding's contrast half is reproduced INDEPENDENTLY by the gate: the stated 3.18 for #c47a00 on #fdf5e6 against a recomputed 3.1610. The shipped ds-tokens.css and ds-tokens.test.ts both carry 3.16, so the document is the wrong copy — instance handed to architect-agent, and the gate is red on it. Measured: 7 units in the first prose-inclusive form (1 true, 6 false — WCAG floors and a WBS id read as measurements); scoped to table rows, 2 findings (1 true, 1 false); one further narrowing removed the false one BY NAME — a row naming two hexes AND the word 'white' is UNCHECKABLE, because at L2136 the second figure is bolded together with trailing prose and does not parse, so the one figure that did got paired with the wrong two colours against a correct row. Final: 1 finding, 1 true, 0 false, 12 figures recomputing exactly, 4 rows declared UNCHECKABLE by name. This finding's OTHER half — S8.5 point 4's two statements that cannot both be followed — is a WORDING property no gate can read, and gets change 17's template rule instead.

cost: one wrong reading of a V2 reobservation, corrected within a minute by re-running through the project's own script path
what: Reobserving IMP-0352 at V2, 'npm --prefix src/code-apps/trustee-review-portal exec -- vitest run src/theme.test.ts' (invoked from the repo root) FAILED the whole suite with "SyntaxError: The requested module 'tabster' does not provide an export named 'createTabster'", pointing at theme.ts's createLightTheme import from @fluentui/react-components. The identical file run as 'npm --prefix src/code-apps/trustee-review-portal run test -- src/theme.test.ts' PASSED 26/26. The first form resolves vitest from the repo root and does not pick up the app's own vitest.config.ts, whose server.deps.inline entries exist precisely to fix this ESM-interop class (IMP-0365 added the @microsoft/power-apps entry for the same reason; @fluentui was already there).
expected: two ways of running the same test file against the same config give the same verdict
root_cause: 'npm --prefix <dir> exec -- vitest' sets the package resolution root but NOT vitest's own config discovery root, so vitest loads no config and every inline-deps workaround is silently absent. 'npm --prefix <dir> run test' executes the script inside the package directory, where config discovery finds vitest.config.ts.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing -- no gate compares invocation paths, and the build config only ever uses the run form (code-app-typecheck/lint/coverage/build all use 'npm --prefix ... run <script>'), so the failing form appears nowhere that executes. It is reachable only by an agent improvising a one-file test run.
lesson: To run ONE vitest file in this repo, use 'npm --prefix src/code-apps/trustee-review-portal run test -- <path>', never 'npm --prefix <app> exec -- vitest run <path>': the exec form does not discover the app's vitest.config.ts, so its server.deps.inline entries vanish and Fluent/tabster fails to load as ESM. A green or red result from an invocation path the build never uses is evidence about neither the code nor the build -- IMP-0026's rule (verify through the path CI actually uses) applied to a single-file run.

proposed_change.summary: Under Testing, record the one correct way to run a single vitest file and why the exec form silently loses the config. Cheap, and it stops the next agent reading a config-less failure as a real defect.

applied_by: improvement review 33 change 10 — knowledge/technology/code-apps.md, Testing section: the one correct way to run a single vitest file, and why the `exec` form silently loses vitest.config.ts and with it server.deps.inline. IMP-0026's rule applied to a single-file run.

what: Adding rev_ethnicgroup (IMP-0363) moved this solution's secured-column count 67->68 and the REV Trustee role's secured-column count 51->52. Add it as a SOFT step so a drifted count is reported by the build rather than discovered by whoever happens to run it. cost: one re-dispatch cycle; zero rework, caught before any ADR content was authored
what: architect-agent was dispatched at its default standard tier (Sonnet) for the superseding-ADR-030 TAD amendment (wbs:6.9). logs/routing.log's own last line, the ROUTED_TO:architect-agent entry timestamped 2026-08-28 09:51, carries no 'Escalated to strategic tier' language, unlike every one of the 4 prior architect-agent dispatches on this same TAD (2026-08-25 09:52, 2026-08-27 20:21, 2026-08-27 21:52, all explicit 'Escalated to strategic tier (opus)' citing the same two conditions). Both conditions independently apply to this dispatch for the same reasons the TAD's own header states they applied to every prior revision: (1) regulated data -- the mechanism being redesigned is the sole privileged read path over Art.9 columns (rev_gender, rev_careprovidedtype, wellbeing set); (2) custom security controls -- ADR-030 IS a custom disclosure-control mechanism ('a privileged read path whose output reaches a persona that cannot read its inputs'), and this dispatch's job is to redesign exactly that mechanism's transport (rev_roundstatisticsrequest write+poll replacing the direct PowerApps-trigger invoke), which raises new, undecided disclosure-relevant questions the concurrent session's code did not resolve: what stops one trustee's poll from reading a result computed for a different trustee's concurrent request against the single ever-present row, what write-access boundary stops a trustee client from writing rev_status/rev_resultjson directly instead of only rev_triggeredon, and whether the flow's written-back rev_resultjson can ever carry more than aggregate counts given trustees are now granted read on the row itself.
expected: per CLAUDE.md 'When Delegating to Another Agent' step 2 and agents/architect-agent.md's own top-of-file check, the dispatcher checks config/models.yml's escalate_to_strategic_when before the Task-tool call and passes an explicit model:opus override when a condition is met -- exactly as the dispatcher did on this same feature 4 times already (routing.log 2026-08-25 09:52, 2026-08-27 20:21, 2026-08-27 21:52)
root_cause: the escalation check is a manual step the dispatching agent (lead-agent) must remember to re-perform on every dispatch; it was performed correctly for revisions 1-4 of this exact TAD and lapsed on this one, most likely because the dispatch prompt frames the work as 'the decision is already made and built, author the ADR for the write-back side' -- a framing that reads as smaller/derivative and invites treating it as standard-tier documentation rather than as a fresh disclosure-mechanism design
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing mechanical -- there is no gate that inspects a Task-tool dispatch's parameters against config/models.yml before the call is made (same gap IMP-0290/IMP-0298 already found impossible to close with a script, since nothing in scripts/ sits between an agent and the Task tool). The only working mitigation is the dispatched agent's own self-check against its ROUTED_TO line and model identity, which is what caught this instance
commercial_impact: none billed -- caught before any TAD content was authored
lesson: Unlike IMP-0290 (rejected: that finding never actually checked routing.log and the escalation had in fact been applied), this is a genuine, verified instance of the same class -- confirmed by reading the exact ROUTED_TO line for this dispatch (routing.log's last line) and finding it silent on escalation where 4 sibling dispatches on the identical TAD are explicit. A request framed as 'formalise/document an already-built decision' is not evidence the escalation conditions no longer apply -- this feature's TAD has now been escalated 4 times running for the same two reasons (regulated data, custom security controls), and a 5th dispatch on the identical mechanism needs the same check applied with the same rigour, not waived because the code already exists.

proposed_change.summary: Where a dispatch brief frames work on an already-escalated feature as 'ratifying/documenting a decision another session already built', add an explicit reminder that a lower apparent authoring burden is not a signal to skip the config/models.yml escalate_to_strategic_when re-check -- re-check it against the feature's data/security profile, not against how much of the work reads as already decided.

cost: one extra dispatch round-trip (~15 min); no work product lost, since the target agent correctly declined to author under the unverified tier both times
what: Attempted to escalate an already-running architect-agent dispatch from standard to strategic tier by calling SendMessage with a model:'opus' parameter to resume it. SendMessage's own schema has no model parameter (only to/message/summary/notify_when_idle); the call nonetheless returned success with no validation error, and routing.log was written recording 'Escalated to strategic tier (opus)' before the target session's own next turn revealed its pin was unchanged.
expected: agents/WORKFLOW.md Session Boundaries states a model override is passed 'on the Task invocation' that spawns an agent; a model parameter supplied on any other call path should either take effect or be mechanically rejected, not silently accepted and logged as fact
root_cause: a model tier is pinned once, at the Task/Agent-tool call that spawns an invocation, and cannot be changed by a later SendMessage into that same running session -- SendMessage's schema has no model field, so passing one is a silent no-op rather than an error, and nothing checked that the resumed session's actual pin matched what routing.log then asserted
why_it_was_never_caught: no gate compares a routing.log 'Escalated to strategic tier' line against the target invocation's actual spawn-time model parameter; the only reason this surfaced is that the resumed architect-agent itself re-derived its own pin from first principles (its own model identity plus the routing.log entry for its own spawn) rather than trusting the coordinator's resume message
lesson: To correct an agent already dispatched at the wrong model tier, spawn a genuinely fresh Agent/Task-tool call with the right model: override -- never SendMessage a resume into the existing invocation expecting the pin to change. what: TAD section 1.2 (ADR-030) states 'The flow accepts no input parameters at all ... there is no round key, no filter and no column list a caller could steer, so the privileged read has no parameter surface to abuse.' cost: caught by mutation testing at authoring time; would have been a stale board figure presented as current
what: TAD section 5.3.1 argues that replacing request-identity freshness with an age bound 'removes the null-check trap BY CONSTRUCTION, rather than guarding against it', because 'an age comparison CANNOT express that bug - null fails the test and an old timestamp fails the test, for the same reason and in the same expression.' Built, then mutation-tested. Three of four mutations to the freshness predicate were killed. The fourth SURVIVED with 41 tests passing: making a null rev_computedon age as 0 instead of NaN, which reinstates exactly the bug the document says cannot be written. The claim is true of the COMPARISON OPERATOR and false of the helper that feeds it - ageInSeconds has a null arm, and that arm is where the bug reappears. Two further test cases (a parseable document WITH a bound but a null or unparseable stamp) kill it; without them the test suite could not see it, because the existing case carried no document either, so the bound was already NaN and the age never mattered.
expected: That an approved design document's 'this class of bug is structurally inexpressible' claim would hold over the implementation it specifies.
root_cause: The claim reasons about one expression - the `<=` - and the implementation is two: a comparison, and a function computing one of its operands. Structural-impossibility arguments are only as wide as the code they actually cover, and prose cannot tell where that boundary will fall before the code exists.
why_it_was_never_caught: Nothing, and nothing document-shaped could: the claim had been read by an architect writing it, a development-agent dispatching against it and a frontend-agent building to it, and all three found it convincing because it IS convincing. Only mutating the code found the gap. A green suite over a claim is not evidence for the claim.
lesson: When a design document says a class of bug is IMPOSSIBLE to express in the shape it specifies, mutate the shipped code to write that exact bug and confirm the suite goes red - before believing the claim, and before recording the claim as a control. A structural-impossibility argument covers the expression it reasons about and not the helpers feeding it; here the argument was sound about `now - computedOn <= S` and false about the function computing the age, whose null arm reinstated the bug with 41 tests still passing. This is the cheapest form of falsification available and it found in one run what three careful readings did not.

cost: one stale assertion silently green for a day; corrected here
what: src/code-apps/trustee-review-portal/src/dataverse/client.test.ts asserted 'five registered entity sets' and iterated a list of five names it wrote out itself, while READ_SERVICES had held SIX since 2026-08-27. It stayed green: the loop only ever visited the five it enumerated, so the sixth was invisible to it and the count agreed with the list rather than with the map. Corrected to seven this dispatch.
expected: A count assertion over a map to fail when the map grows - which is the entire reason this project accepts count-coupled tests (IMP-0005, IMP-0363: bump the number with a dated comment).
root_cause: The test derived its count from its OWN enumeration instead of from the subject. That inverts the whole point of a count assertion: it can only detect a REMOVAL (a listed name gone missing) and is structurally blind to an ADDITION. This is a different hazard from the five recorded instances of this class, which are all 'the number drifted and the test went red'. Here the number could not drift.
why_it_was_never_caught: Nothing. Every prior instance of this class announced itself by going RED on a legitimate change, which is how they were all found. This variant announces itself by staying GREEN, so no build, no review and no coverage figure could surface it.
lesson: A count assertion must take its count from the SUBJECT, never from a list the test writes out itself - `Object.keys(map).length` against a literal, not a loop over a hand-written array of names. A test that enumerates its own subjects can only detect a removal and is structurally blind to an addition, so it goes on passing while the thing it guards grows. Sixth recorded instance of the count-coupling class and the FIRST that fails by staying green: when you find one of these, check which direction it can actually detect.

proposed_change.summary: One line in the review checklist: for every count assertion, ask which direction of change it can detect. If the count comes from the test's own enumeration it detects removals only, which is the weaker half and usually not the half anyone wanted. cost: none - it is the step's own documented mechanism, used for the first time
what: Adding a table to a Code App has an unavoidable ordering constraint: READ_SERVICES must register its entity set for the app to compile and be tested, and `pa app add data-source` cannot declare it in the generated dataSourcesInfo.ts until the table EXISTS LIVE, because the verb reads the table's metadata from the environment. So the HARD `code-app-data-sources` gate is red for the whole interval between authoring the table and creating it. Its own docstring provides the answer and it had never been used: `--allow ENTITY=REASON`, verified working here - exit 0 with a printed 'exempt by --allow' line naming the entity and the reason. The two alternatives are both worse: hand-authoring an entry in dataSourcesInfo.ts fabricates platform-assigned connector metadata (C-TECH-051) in the one file whose whole value is that the platform wrote it; and deleting or skipping the step removes a gate whose defect is observable only at V4, because typecheck, lint, unit tests and build all pass with it present - a mock never resolves a data source.
expected: That a new table's app binding could be completed in the same pass as its schema, which it cannot on this platform.
root_cause: Not a defect: the CLI verb needs the live table, and TAD section 12.3 sequences schema creation at step 3 and the app binding at step 9 precisely because of it. The gate is correctly red in between and needs a way to say so that carries an owner and a clearing action.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing - a capability, not a defect. Recorded because the previous occurrence of the same interval (rev_roundfinance, 2026-08-26) was resolved by running the CLI verb immediately, which was possible only because that table already existed live. The next table-addition dispatch will hit this and its two tempting responses are both forbidden.
lesson: When a Code App registers an entity set whose table does not exist live yet, the sanctioned response is `--allow ENTITY=REASON` on the `code-app-data-sources` step, with an owner and a clearing action in the reason string - NOT hand-authoring an entry in the generated dataSourcesInfo.ts (that fabricates platform-assigned metadata, C-TECH-051) and NOT deleting the step (its defect is invisible below V4 because every local check passes with a mocked SDK). Delete the --allow line in the same change that runs `pa app add data-source`, and note that doing so closes the entity-set-name assumption in every place it was guessed at once.

proposed_change.summary: Record the ordering constraint and the --allow mechanism together, in the data-source section: registering an entity set, creating the table, and binding the app are three steps in a fixed order, and the middle one is a live action no build can perform. Name the two forbidden shortcuts explicitly, because both look like the obvious fix.

cost: 0 rework - caught by the activation step that requires verifying a finding against source. Had it been followed: one privilege revoked that every trustee needs, breaking Refresh Figures for all of them
what: The erratum dispatch brief restated two privilege facts rather than citing them, and got both wrong in the same sentence. It said A-R49 'currently names one stale grant (prvWriterev_roundstatisticsrequest on REV Trustee)' - the role is REV Service Automation (TAD A-R49; Roles/REV Service Automation/REV Service Automation.xml:166), and that privilege IS deliberately live on REV Trustee (REV Trustee.xml:252), because the trustee writes the ask. It also said prvReadWorkflow 'is still bound Global to REV Trustee in source's role XML' - it was REMOVED from source on 2026-08-27 (REV Trustee.xml:237) and is bound only in the LIVE environment, which is the entire mechanism of the finding it was summarising. Both errors were introduced by the brief; IMP-0407, the finding it summarised, states both facts correctly. Note this reuses baseline-restated-not-cited outside its commercial framing on purpose - see proposed_change.
expected: That a handoff summarising a finding either cites the finding and the source lines, or restates nothing. The dispatch's own instruction - 'verify both claims against current source yourself before writing, don't take the finding's word for it' - was correct and was what caught this; it just pointed at the wrong document, since the finding was right and the brief was wrong.
root_cause: The brief compressed a two-role, two-direction fact (privilege X stale on role A; privilege Y removed from role B's source but live in the environment) into one clause, and compression across a role boundary silently swapped the roles. The general mechanism is the one C-COM-008 already forbids for baseline figures: a restated fact has no line to check it against, so an error in the restatement is undetectable at the point of reading.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing - no gate reads a dispatch brief, and none can. The only control is the receiving agent's activation step requiring verification against source, which is exactly what fired here. That control is currently written per-agent in prose and applies to findings, not to briefs.
lesson: A privilege named in a handoff carries a ROLE, and the role is the half that gets swapped in compression - verify both halves against the role XML before acting. Specifically on this project: prvWriterev_roundstatisticsrequest is deliberately live on REV Trustee (the trustee writes the statistics ask, REV Trustee.xml:252) and stale only on REV Service Automation; prvReadWorkflow is absent from REV Trustee source since 2026-08-27 and stale only in the live environment. Revoking the first from the trustee role would break Refresh Figures for every trustee. More generally: C-COM-008's 'cite, never restate' is not a commercial rule - it holds for any fact a handoff carries, and a technical restatement is checkable against a line number exactly as a baseline figure is.

proposed_change.summary: Generalise C-COM-008 (or lift its mechanism into a technology/process constraint): 'cite the source line, never restate the figure' currently binds only contracted hours/fees/dates, and this is the 5th instance of class baseline-restated-not-cited - the first outside commercial content. A privilege+role pair, a trigger constant and a schema value are all restatable facts with a citable line, and the failure mode is identical. Per skills/how-to-promote-a-finding.md the altitude for a 5th instance is the general rule, not a 5th instance patch. Narrow companion, if the general form is refused: add to agents/lead-agent.md's delegation rules that a handoff naming a privilege names the role and the source line together, since privilege-without-role is the specific compression that failed here.

cost: the erratum had to correct 5 locations for one privilege, not the 1 the dispatch scoped; found by reading the document rather than by an incident
what: While correcting A-R49 to name the second stale privilege, found that prvReadWorkflow's withdrawal had been recorded in ADR-038's consequences, section 6.1.1 and the section 12.2 'closed as moot' row, while TWO section 12 prerequisite rows still listed it as a grant to MAKE: 'REV Trustee + prvReadrev_roundfinance + prvReadWorkflow ... environment_prerequisites' and 'The role privilege additions, including prvReadWorkflow ... Before app sharing and before the first invocation'. The second also still refers to a 'first invocation' under a design where nothing invokes a flow. So one revision withdrew the privilege in the sections that argue, and left it granted in the sections an operator executes. Verified that no automatic re-grant results: ensure-schema.ps1 builds its AddPrivilegesRole payload from the role XML on disk (ensure-schema-helpers.psm1:887-905, Get-RevRoleDefinitions), and the privilege is no longer in that XML - so the exposure is a human following the prerequisite table by hand, per environment, in TST/ACC and PRD where the grant is not yet bound at all.
expected: That withdrawing a privilege updates every section that names it - the ones that reason about it AND the ones an operator executes from - or that the executable sections derive from the reasoning sections rather than restating them.
root_cause: Revision 5 propagated the withdrawal along the axis it was thinking on (security argument -> risk -> verification) and not along the axis an operator reads (section 12.1 prerequisites -> section 12.3 steps). The prerequisite tables restate the privilege set as a literal list instead of citing section 6.1/6.1.1, so they cannot follow a change made there. Same shape as the A-R49 miss in the same document: a consequence propagated through the frame it was reasoned in, not through every frame that carries the fact.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing. verify-tad-coverage.py checks TAD columns against source and trustee-visible columns against role prvRead, and passes - it does not compare the TAD's own prerequisite tables against the TAD's own privilege tables. No gate reads two sections of one document against each other, which is what all 15 instances of approved-document-internally-inconsistent have in common.
lesson: When a privilege, column or connector is withdrawn from a design, grep the whole document for its identifier before closing the change - and check the EXECUTABLE sections (section 12 prerequisites and rollout steps) separately from the sections that argue, because they restate the same fact and will not follow a change made upstream. On this document: section 12.1 and the section 12 provisioning table list role privileges as literal lists, so every privilege change must touch them explicitly. Also: ensure-schema.ps1 derives its grants from the role XML on disk (ensure-schema-helpers.psm1:887-905), so a privilege removed from source is never re-granted by the script - the residual risk of a stale prerequisite row is a human hand-applying it, which is worse in TST/ACC and PRD where the privilege is not yet bound.

proposed_change.summary: Extend the existing TAD-vs-source gate with a document-internal consistency check: every prv* identifier named in a TAD's section 12 prerequisite/rollout tables must also be present in that TAD's section 6 privilege tables AND in the role XML on disk - and any prv* named in section 12 as a grant while absent from role source is an error, not a warning. This is the 16th instance of approved-document-internally-inconsistent and the class has no gate at all; a prv*-identifier set-comparison within one document is cheap, needs no live access, and would have caught both halves of this erratum (the stale grant rows here, and A-R49 naming one privilege where source-vs-live had two). Note the limit deliberately: it is a document-vs-document and document-vs-source check, so it can never see the live environment divergence that IMP-0407 records - that still needs the section 12.1 read-back.

cost: none here - change 15 was reshaped at application time. Standing cost: one disproved cause still rendering as authoritative on the digest's read path until this entry landed.
what: Improvement review 34 change 15 was approved as 'corrects is set on IMP-0010 as well as IMP-0079, so the digest's correction marker reaches BOTH entries carrying the disproved space-in-path cause'. It cannot be implemented as written: `corrects` is read as a SINGLE STRING by both consumers - scripts/verify-improvement-log.py:1466 (`str(row.get('corrects')).strip()`, which reports a list as 'not an entry in this log') and scripts/generate-known-failure-modes.py:411 (same coercion, which silently ignores an unresolvable target). So one entry can correct exactly one target, and IMP-0413 already names IMP-0079. Measured on the digest before this entry: IMP-0079's lesson at line 289 carried the CORRECTED marker and IMP-0010's at line 285 did not - and IMP-0010's lesson text LEADS with the disproved cause ('This repo's path contains spaces. pac solution check --outputDirectory silently writes nothing'), so the one entry a reader is most likely to meet first was the one rendering as authoritative. This entry carries corrects:IMP-0010 and thereby marks it, which is change 15's intent achieved through the schema as it exists rather than by editing two scripts a concurrently-applying review owns.
expected: that a single disproved root cause recorded across two findings could be marked in both, since the whole purpose of the marker is to stop a disproved lesson teaching.
root_cause: The field was designed for the one-to-one case it was introduced for (IMP-0314 correcting IMP-0287) and the many-to-one case was never considered: a cause re-confirmed several times produces several entries all carrying the same wrong mechanism, and disproving it once should reach all of them. Nothing in the schema or either reader anticipated a list.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing - the field is only four days old and this is its second use. Neither consumer validates the field's TYPE, so a list would not have errored loudly in the generator; it would have been coerced to a string, failed to resolve, and been silently ignored, which is the failure shape that hides itself.
lesson: `corrects` holds ONE id, as a string, and both readers coerce it with str() - scripts/verify-improvement-log.py:1466 and scripts/generate-known-failure-modes.py:411. A list does not work and does not error in the generator; it is coerced, fails to resolve and is silently dropped. So a root cause recorded in N findings needs N correcting entries to be fully marked, and the digest marker reaches only the entries actually named. When you disprove a cause that has been confirmed more than once, grep the log for the OTHER entries carrying it and say in `what` which ones you could not mark. Making the field accept a list is a two-line change in each reader plus a schema note, and is the right fix - it is not made here because both files were owned by another live dispatch.
commercial_impact: none
