cost: the batch trigger re-fires against work already analysed; a strategic-tier review has twice been dispatched at a queue whose true state nothing recorded (IMP-0183, IMP-0154)
what: By convention a review writes nothing to logs/improvement-log.jsonl until its keyword arrives, so between drafting and approval every entry it processed still reads `unread`. Measured during review 34's own application: verify-improvement-log.py reported 'Nothing records that anyone has looked at these' about 43 entries that improvement review 33 had already analysed in a full strategic-tier pass, and re-fired the batch trigger against them on every check. The `awaiting-approval` state exists precisely for this and is set by `reviewed_in`, so the state is reachable in principle and unused in practice. The gate itself already emits 58 WARNINGs of the form 'state unread, cited by N review document(s) and carries NO reviewed_in' - it can SEE the contradiction and cannot resolve it, because only the review can stamp and the review is waiting.
expected: that a queue gate's report of what nobody has looked at would not include 43 entries under active analysis by a named, on-disk document.
root_cause: Two rules that are each individually right: 'never apply a change before the keyword' (agents/improvement-agent.md's closing line) and 'an unread entry is one nobody has opened'. `reviewed_in` records only that a review READ the entry, which is true the moment the draft names it - so stamping it at DRAFT time would violate neither rule. Nobody separated 'read' from 'processed' when the convention was set.
why_it_was_never_caught: it was caught, twice, and both times as the COST rather than the cause: IMP-0154 and IMP-0183 are strategic-tier passes over settled work. Both were treated as the applying agent reading the queue wrongly, and the activation step was sharpened accordingly. Neither asked why the queue was misreporting in the first place.
lesson: A review parked at its gate is invisible to the queue gate, so `unread` cannot be trusted to mean 'nobody has looked at this' while any review sits unapproved. Before treating a batch trigger as real, check whether a review document already names the entries - verify-improvement-log.py prints exactly that as a WARNING per entry, and those warnings are the signal, not noise. Stamping `reviewed_in` at DRAFT time would fix it and is defensible, because that field records only that a review READ the entry; the trade-off is that every future review then writes to a shared append-only log earlier, and two live sessions on this synced path is IMP-0080's hazard - which review 34 met twice in one dispatch. It would NOT clear either blocker trigger: verify-improvement-log.py:123 counts `awaiting-approval` alongside `unread` for blockers, deliberately.
commercial_impact: none

what: Review 34 change 4 rejects a build step whose comment block asserts the step currently fails. Measured before wiring, the NAIVE phrase match returned 2 findings on the CORRECTED working-tree file and 1 on the DEFECTIVE `git show HEAD:` version - a POLARITY INVERSION - because the correction quotes the old sentence in order to withdraw it, and quotes it twice ('It currently FAILS on six live instances...' plus the explanatory clause 'whose config says it is EXPECTED to be red'). Naive total across the config corpus: 3 findings, 1 true, 2 false. A retraction guard (skip a comment block containing CORRECTED / 'this comment read' / 'has not been true') removed both false positives by name and left the true positive standing: 1 finding, 1 true, 0 false. This is the FOURTH measured occurrence of the same shape in this repository: review 33 measured one at 7 findings 0 true, and review 34 measured three more (cluster B's naive form, cluster E's sibling inference at 7 findings 1 true, cluster H's privilege-pair check at 24 raw findings and at best 1 true).
expected: that a phrase-presence check over documentation prose would score a corrected file BETTER than the file it corrects.
root_cause: A correction in this repository's documentation style RETAINS the withdrawn wording so a reader can see what changed - a delta TAD does it deliberately with a supersession note, and a config comment does it by quoting the sentence it is retracting. So the corrected text contains strictly MORE instances of the offending phrase than the defective text did. Proximity cannot distinguish an assertion from its own retraction, and negation compounds it: two of the false positives across these four attempts were negations the pattern could not read, one because the word 'no' was wrapped in markdown emphasis.
why_it_was_never_caught: the fixtures always pass. A gate's fixtures are written by the same author, in the same sitting, from the same mental model as the regex, so they encode the assumption rather than testing it - and verify-build-config.py's own negative-test check accepts a --selftest exit 0, which is a can-it-fail proof and nothing more. Only running the candidate against the real corpus, including the pre-correction version in git, exposes the inversion.
lesson: A prose-proximity gate cannot tell an assertion from its own retraction in this repository, and four measured attempts across two reviews now say so. ASSERT ON VALUES, NOT ON PHRASES, wherever a value exists. Where only prose is available: (1) measure the candidate against the CORRECTED file specifically, not only against a known-bad one - if it scores the corrected file worse, the polarity is inverted and the design is wrong, not the wording; (2) carry an explicit retraction guard and declare it as a phrase list with both failure directions named; (3) treat a fixture-green gate as unmeasured. A future review proposing a fifth attempt should read this entry before starting.

So the claim and the evidence it cited were invalidated by one change, and the document retained both. root_cause: a verbatim quotation of source inside a document is a snapshot with no link back to the file it came from, so it survives every later edit to that file. The quotation made the false claim MORE credible to each subsequent reviser - it read as already ground-truthed - which is the opposite of what a citation is supposed to do. Nothing re-reads a quoted description to confirm the quote still exists.
why_it_was_never_caught: no gate compares a document's quoted source text against the file it names; design-doc-claims checks the CLAIM against Entity.xml but never the document's own QUOTATION of Entity.xml, so the dangling quote would have survived even a green gate
lesson: When you correct a false claim in a document, correct the EVIDENCE IT CITED in the same pass - the proof may have expired with the claim, and a stale verbatim quotation of source is the most persuasive form a false claim can take, because it reads as already ground-truthed and each reviser trusts it harder than a bare assertion. Concretely: grep the quoted sentence against the file the document names before repeating it. Here S3.4 quoted rev_gender's description as proof rev_ethnicgroup was never built, and that description had been rewritten to say the opposite in the same change that built the column. Corollary for risk registers: a risk that prescribes CREATING an artefact must have its prescription re-checked against source too - A-R24 asked for 'a new secured column' that already existed, so the mitigation, not just the risk statement, was the thing that would have cost delivery time.

This is the third instance of wrong-artefact-cited-as-evidence (after IMP-0305, IMP-0341), so per skills/how-to-promote-a-finding.md it is due generalisation rather than another instance patch; the general property is that verbatim source quotations in documents are uncheckable snapshots today, and a mechanical version (grep every quoted sentence naming a repo path against that path) is a plausible fourth-instance gate if this recurs.

Reproduced on a copy of the script with the guard reverted, against the real log: it raises AttributeError, prints ZERO verdict lines, and exits 1. cost: one blocked closure and a judgement call while applying improvement review 5: check_reobservation() correctly refused IMP-0423's closure because the truthful re-observation stamp read EARLIER than the finding it re-tested.
detected_by: agent-self - the gate fired on correct work while improvement review 5 was being applied.
what: logs/improvement-log.jsonl carries timestamps from at least two clocks that are ~4h apart on 2026-08-28. IMP-0423 is stamped 17:58 and the concurrent architect entries IMP-0428/0429/0430 are stamped 14:05-14:09, while `date` on this machine returned 13:36 at the moment improvement review 5 was applied. scripts/verify-improvement-log.py's check_reobservation() asserts an ordering BETWEEN two fields - reobserved.ts must not predate the entry's own ts - so a re-observation stamped from the wall clock (13:36) against an entry stamped 17:58 is reported as 'a copy of the original report, not a re-test of it', which is exactly the right rule reaching the wrong conclusion about honest work. Resolved here by stamping the re-observation on the entry's own clock (18:05) and stating the skew in reobserved.result rather than silently picking a number that passed.
expected: two entries in one append-only log are comparable in time, so a gate asserting an ordering between them is asserting something about events rather than about whose clock wrote them.
root_cause: nothing normalises or records a timezone: `ts` is a free-text local-time string with no offset (IMP-0423 '2026-08-28T17:58', IMP-0390 '2026-08-27T23:23:29+02:00' - one of the few entries that DOES carry an offset). Sessions on this synced SharePoint path write with whatever local convention they used, so the field is only reliably ordered within one session.
why_it_was_never_caught: the only check that compares two timestamps is check_reobservation(), and V2+ closures needing a reobserved stamp are rare - every earlier one happened to be written by the same session that wrote the entry, where one clock is used throughout.
lesson: A `ts` in logs/improvement-log.jsonl is NOT comparable across sessions: stamps ~4h apart were written the same afternoon, and one entry in a hundred carries a UTC offset while the rest carry none. When you close an entry needing `reobserved`, stamp it on the SAME clock as the entry's own `ts` and state the wall-clock reading in `reobserved.result` - do not pick a number that merely passes the gate, and do not rewrite another session's ts. The mechanical fix, if this recurs, is to require an ISO-8601 offset on `ts` for new entries (forward-bound, like the evidence_grep needle in IMP-0181) so the ordering the gate asserts is about events rather than about clocks.
commercial_impact: none
revisit_when: the next V2-or-higher closure whose reobserved.ts is refused, or any new gate that compares two entries timestamps

what: seed-round-statistics-test-data.ps1 read $before.rev_resultjson from a keyed GET ?$select=rev_resultjson. The Dataverse Web API OMITS a null-valued column from the response body rather than returning it as null, so on the first run after seed-round-statistics-result.ps1 the response carried no rev_resultjson property at all — and under Set-StrictMode -Version Latest that access is a TERMINATING PropertyNotFoundException, not $null. root_cause: two contracts multiplied. (a) Dataverse omits null columns from a response body — $select names what you want, not what you get. (b) Every provisioning script here sets Set-StrictMode -Version Latest, which turns a missing property from $null into a terminating error. Either alone is benign; together, the ABSENT-VALUE case — the normal first-run state — throws.

lesson: The Dataverse Web API OMITS a null-valued column from a response body — $select names what you asked for, not what comes back — and under Set-StrictMode -Version Latest (which every provisioning script sets) reading that absent property is a TERMINATING error, not $null. Guard every optional-column read with ($response.PSObject.Properties.Name -contains 'col'), never a bare $response.col. And when mocking it in a test, make the fake OMIT the property rather than set it to $null: a null-valued fake passes while the real API throws, so the mock must reproduce the absence.

what: IMP-0425 asked for verify-tad-coverage.py's --design-docs default to cover docs/plans, on the stated ground that one plan document 'carries the classification table two findings in improvement review 33's batch are about' and another carries the 'rev_providerid is not built in this slice' row. expected: that a finding naming specific content in a specific document, as the reason a gate should read that document, would have checked that content against the gate's actual subject.
root_cause: a gate's NAME and its SUBJECT are different scopes, and a finding about scope naturally reasons about the name. 'The gate over design-document claims does not read docs/plans' is true; 'therefore it is missing findings in docs/plans' does not follow, because check (c) reads one narrow cue and not design-document claims in general. Nothing in the finding's own prose distinguishes 'this directory is unread' from 'this directory contains unread instances'.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing checks a finding's stated premise before a review acts on it, and this premise reads as already-verified because it names a real table in a real document. Only running the check with the proposed argument settles it, which is exactly the discrimination IMP-0426 records and review 36 change 3 turned into an activation clause.
lesson: A scope-mismatch finding must be measured with the PROPOSED ARGUMENT before the change is designed: 'gate G does not read directory D' and 'directory D contains findings G would catch' are two claims, and the second is the one that sizes the change. verify-tad-coverage.py's assertion (c) reads only items of a bolded 'deliverable now / ships now' list, so pointing it at docs/plans yields 0 items in 0 claims across 3 documents - a real scope repair with zero measured effect. Make the repair, and report it as a repair rather than as a coverage win; a review that reports the zero is what stops the next one re-deriving the same expectation.

what: Dropping the rev_status write made the three attribute <Description>s on rev_roundstatisticsrequest true, and left THREE other artefacts in the same ADR-038 blast radius still saying the answer lives on that table: the entity-level <Description> of rev_roundstatisticsrequest ('the flow writes rev_status, rev_resultjson and rev_computedon when it finishes' — shipped metadata, contradicting its own attributes eight lines below), the global option set rev_roundstatisticsrequeststatus's <Description> ('State of the single rev_roundstatisticsrequest row's most recent computation cycle'), and the flow's notes.md section 5 ('rev_roundstatisticsrequest.rev_status documents DefaultValue=2 ... that is the seeded row's resting state'). expected: an ADR that moves columns between tables leaves no shipped prose asserting the old location, and a TAD claim about what a shipped <Description> says is true of that description
root_cause: the ADR-038 sweep was scoped to the moved COLUMNS — their attribute descriptions, the roles, the flow's write actions, the app's select lists — and prose that describes the TABLE's role names the columns without being a write or a read of them. So neither the authoring pass nor scripts/verify-superseded-column-writers.py (which resolves entity-set-plus-column co-occurrence in .ps1 and Workflows/*.json only) had any reason to look at an entity-level description, a global option set's description, or a notes.md. The TAD half has the same shape one level up: verify-design-doc-claims.py checks that a design document's deliverable-now items name columns that EXIST, not that a quoted artefact contains the words the document says it contains.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing. verify-superseded-column-writers.py checks the writers of a marked column and explicitly defers the read half; no gate reads the entity-level <Description> or an OptionSets/*.xml <Description> at all, and verify-shipped-content.py's description check looks for a description naming a DELETED column — these columns are retained, which is the whole point of ADR-038 and the reason every source-vs-source gate passes.
lesson: When an ADR moves columns off a table but retains them, sweep the artefacts that describe the TABLE, not only the ones that write or read the columns: the entity-level <Description>, the global option set's <Description>, and the flow's notes. On rev_roundstatisticsrequest all three still said the flow writes the answer there three days after ADR-038, inside the same file whose attribute descriptions now carry 'Written by nothing and read by nothing' — a shipped artefact contradicting itself eight lines apart. The mechanical form is one grep per moved column against Entities/*/Entity.xml entity-level descriptions and OptionSets/*.xml, and it is the natural second half of verify-superseded-column-writers.py. And never cite a shipped <Description> as saying something without grepping the description: TAD section 3.9.2 claimed this option set's description recorded the naming mismatch, and it did not.

proposed_change.summary: Extend the gate that already parses UNUSED FROM REVISION markers: for every marked column, no <Description> anywhere in the solution — entity-level, attribute-level, or in OptionSets/*.xml — may assert that column is written on the entity that carries the marker. what: scripts/verify-provisioning-step-convergence.py tells you to add "'# -- <n>. ' step markers", and its parser is STEP_MARKER = re.compile(r'(?m)^# ── (.+?) ─*$') — box-drawing U+2500, not two ASCII hyphens, and a trailing rule is required. expected: a gate's remediation sentence can be followed literally

Nothing is wrong with the parser: the box-drawing marker is a real convention every provisioning script already follows.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing, and no gate can catch it: this is a gate correctly reporting a real gap in prose a human has to act on. Its own selftest fixtures build markers in the true format, so they can never disagree with the message the way a reader does.
lesson: scripts/verify-provisioning-step-convergence.py's step marker is `# ── <n>. <title> ────` with BOX-DRAWING U+2500 and a trailing rule — not the `# -- <n>. ` its own UNCLASSIFIABLE message and docstring show. Copy the shape from a script that already passes (ensure-schema.ps1's `# ── 1. Global option sets ────`) rather than from the gate's advice. And the general form, for anyone writing a gate: a remediation sentence that ASCII-flattens the exact token it demands is an instruction that cannot be followed — print the literal bytes, or point at a file that already has it right.

proposed_change.summary: In the UNCLASSIFIABLE message and the docstring, print the marker in the exact form the parser accepts (`# ── <n>. <title> ───`), or name a file that already carries one. One string, no logic change. Not proposed as a constraint or a new gate: the gate is right and only its advice is unusable.

Measured rather than assumed: an entry of that shape in `deferrals` makes the gate exit 1 with 'TD-EXPERIMENT: defers nothing: no absent TAD 3.1 column on rev_roundstatisticsresult matches it', which is its own _stale_entries_fail rule working correctly. The three gaps were recorded in a new `undelivered_requirements` key instead, which the gate ignores by construction and which says so in its own text.
expected: The register a defect report and a dispatch brief both name as the place to record a TAD-vs-source gap can hold the gap they are about.
root_cause: The register and its gate were built for one shape of gap - a column TAD 3.1 names and Entity.xml lacks (IMP-0159) - and the matcher, the required fields and the staleness rule are all column-shaped. Nothing was wrong with any of them. What was missing is that the file's own _purpose says 'columns the approved TAD 3.1 names' while being the ONLY register of its kind, so an agent holding a non-column gap reads a file that names its own boundary and still has nowhere else to go. Two readers - test-agent writing D-11 and lead-agent writing the brief - both routed a response-field gap there, which is the measure of how strongly the file reads as general.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing, and no gate could: the gate is correct and its refusal is the designed behaviour. This is the first non-column TAD-vs-source gap this project has had to record, so the boundary had never been reached. The closest thing to a check is the gate's own failure message, which names what does not match but not where the entry should go instead.
lesson: contract/tad-deferrals.json's `deferrals` array holds ABSENT TAD 3.1 COLUMNS ONLY - every entry is matched against one, and an entry matching none FAILS the HARD tad-coverage gate as a dead promise. Do not put a response-document field, a requirement, or any other non-column gap in it, however directly a defect report names the file: run `python3 scripts/verify-tad-coverage.py --deferrals <your copy>` on a scratch copy BEFORE editing the tracked file. Non-column gaps go in the `undelivered_requirements` key added 2026-08-28, and that key is read by no gate - it is a dated written record, not a control, so it only works while a corrected Appendix A row and a 11 risk row point at it.

(1) Cheap and certain: make the gate READ the `undelivered_requirements` key and validate the same seven fields plus the expiry it already validates on `deferrals`, so those entries expire loudly instead of silently - it need not resolve the response field to make that worth doing. (2) Coordinate with IMP-0451, which proposes resolving each Appendix A requirement row against the implementing artefact and failing on a literal null with no register entry; that is the half that would have caught D-11 in the first place, and the two proposals are the same gate seen from the document side and the register side. Also one string: add the destination to the 'defers nothing' failure message, since that message is what an agent in this position actually reads.

cost: five findings unreachable by any session across two reviews, plus a HARD build step red on a problem whose printed remedy would have made it worse
what: IMP-0440 through IMP-0444 each carried BOTH `appended_by` and `reviewed_in` naming docs/improvements/2026-08-28-improvement-review-6.md, and that document mentions none of them — `grep -c 'IMP-044[0-4]'` against it returns 0. Review 36 APPENDED those five; it did not process them. `appended_by` was true and `reviewed_in` was not. Because a resolvable `reviewed_in` classifies an entry as `awaiting-approval`, verify-improvement-log.py instructed every later review to 'read the document each one names and send the keyword; do not re-derive' — against an already-applied document that names them nowhere, so no keyword could dispose of them. Review 37 then cited IMP-0443 as a PRECEDENT in a cluster's Cites: line, which check_citation_stamps() read as processing, and the gate went red demanding the stamp move to review 37. IMP-0445 is a sixth instance from review 37 itself.
expected: a finding a review wrote and did not process reads as `unread`, and a gate's printed remedy fixes the defect it names
root_cause: two mechanisms. (1) `appended_by` exists precisely to separate 'a review WROTE this' from 'a review PROCESSED this' (verify-improvement-log.py L439-L445, added by review 29), and a review appending its own findings set both fields to itself — the writing is recorded twice and the processing claim is fabricated. Nothing checked the claim, because no check asked whether the named document contains the id. (2) The stamp check's remedy sentence assumes the stamp is merely STALE and tells you to move it forward. When the stamp is FALSE rather than stale, moving it forward points at another document that also never processed the entry — here an already-applied one — so following the instruction preserves the defect and clears the error.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing asked whether a document named by `reviewed_in` mentions the entry, which is a string containment test over files already on disk. check_citation_stamps() deliberately warns rather than fails because it cannot prove a citation implies processing — a sound reason that does not apply to this question, and the absence of the stronger check left the weaker one to produce a wrong remedy on the shape it does not model.
lesson: A review that APPENDS its own findings must set `appended_by` and NOT `reviewed_in`. Setting both makes the entry read as `awaiting-approval`, which tells every later review to send a keyword against a document that never mentions it — a state no session can clear, and the queue reads as handled. The fix is always to DROP the false `reviewed_in` and keep `appended_by`; never to move the stamp forward, which is what the gate's own message used to advise. scripts/verify-improvement-log.py now fails on this via check_self_stamps(). And the general shape, which is the more valuable half: when a gate's finding is real but its printed REMEDY is wrong, the remedy is part of the defect — measured 31 findings unnarrowed (26 historical entries with no `appended_by`, which would have made the gate permanently red), narrowed to 6 findings / 6 true / 0 false with 9 true negatives.

proposed_change.summary: APPLIED in review 38 change 9 as check_self_stamps(): an ERROR when a document named by both `appended_by` and `reviewed_in` does not mention the entry. Built on ONE instance by explicit reviewer decision against the ladder's two-instance rule, because the failure is silent, self-concealing and disables the learning loop for every entry it touches.

applied_by: Improvement review 38 changes 8 and 9. Change 8 dropped the false `reviewed_in` from all six entries (IMP-0440..IMP-0445), keeping `appended_by`; the queue moved from 5 awaiting-approval and 8 unread to 0 and 0. Change 9 is the gate that stops it recurring.

cost: nothing — the design was measured and discarded before it was wired. The entry is the record that stops a seventh attempt
what: SIXTH measured instance of the shape IMP-0422 documents, and the first to measure not INVERTED but BLIND. IMP-0448 proposed extending verify-superseded-column-writers.py to shipped <Description> prose: no description may assert a marked column is written on the entity carrying the marker. Measured against the two texts of the same description — defective 'the flow writes rev_status, rev_resultjson and rev_computedon when it finishes' and corrected 'the flow writes rev_status, rev_resultjson and rev_computedon ON rev_roundstatisticsresult, never on the table it triggers on' — it scores 3 findings and 3 findings. Identical. IMP-0441 recorded instances 1-5 as 'the record that stops a sixth attempt'; the sixth happened anyway, from a different direction.
expected: a prose gate scores the corrected text better than the defective text
root_cause: this repository's documentation style CORRECTS by retaining the withdrawn wording and appending the negation, so the corrected text contains every token the defective text did plus more. Instances 1-5 were assertion-versus-retraction and scored the corrected file WORSE; this one scores it the SAME, because the discriminator is a prepositional phrase 60 characters downstream of the matched tokens. And unlike the earlier five there is no value-asserting reformulation available: the subject is prose making a claim about prose, so there is no value in the artefact to compare against.
why_it_was_never_caught: it WAS caught, by the mandatory real-corpus and corrected-vs-defective measurement in agents/improvement-agent.md. Recorded because a discarded design that leaves no trace is how a seventh attempt gets designed — which is exactly what happened to IMP-0441's record between review 36 and review 38.
lesson: Before proposing a gate over shipped PROSE, ask whether a VALUE exists to assert on instead — and if none does, the honest answer is a human checklist, not a weaker regex. Six measured attempts across four reviews now say a prose gate cannot survive this repository's correction style: five scored the corrected file worse (IMP-0422, IMP-0428) and this one could not distinguish the two texts at all. The specific trap here is that a correction's discriminator can sit far from the matched tokens, so proximity windows do not rescue the design. Where the requirement is real and no value exists — 'this shipped description must be true' — the durable form is the checklist in knowledge/technology/dataverse.md naming the four artefacts an ADR's retain-in-place column move has to sweep, with the ADR as the trigger rather than a build step.

proposed_change.summary: APPLIED in review 38 change 7: the four-artefact checklist plus the measurement table, so the discarded design is on the record where the next author of that sweep reads it rather than in a review nobody re-opens.

applied_by: Improvement review 38 change 7, and IMP-0448's own applied_by carries the same measurement.

cost: one wrong implementation caught before wiring, by the rule that exists to catch it
what: The first implementation of verify-tad-coverage.py's new assertion (d) walked properties.definition.actions recursively to find the action composing each literal-null response key. It reported 0 null response keys against a flow containing 8, because the OK document (Compose_response_body) is nested inside a Scope inside a condition and the walk did not reach it. The second attempt brace-matched action blocks instead and attributed every key to the OUTERMOST enclosing block — 'properties' — whose status set is every status the flow can emit, so all ten keys were misfiled as non-ok and the count read 0 again. Only attributing each key to the NARROWEST enclosing block gave the measured-correct answer: 8 OK-document nulls in Compose_response_body, 2 non-ok.
expected: a gate reporting 0 findings against a corpus known to contain 8 is treated as broken, not as clean
root_cause: a structural walk over a Power Automate definition has to know every nesting key that can carry actions (actions, else, cases, foreach, a Scope's own actions), and the shape it does not know is invisible rather than an error. The brace-matching replacement removed that dependency and introduced the opposite one: block containment is nested, so 'the block containing this key' is ambiguous until you say WHICH — and the outermost always matches.
why_it_was_never_caught: it was caught immediately, by agents/improvement-agent.md's rule that a gate reporting 0 findings against a corpus you know contains an instance is the tell rather than a clean run — the null keys had been measured independently at 8 before the gate was written, so the 0 was recognisable. Nothing mechanical would have caught it: the gate exited 0 and its selftest fixtures would have been written from the same wrong mental model.
lesson: Measure the quantity a new gate depends on BEFORE writing the gate, with a throwaway probe, so the gate's first run has a number to be wrong against. Two independent implementations of the same extraction reported 0 against a flow containing 8, and both exited 0 — the only reason either was caught is that 8 had already been measured. Two concrete traps for Power Automate definitions: (1) a recursive walk over `actions` misses an action nested in a Scope inside a condition, and misses it silently; (2) when attributing a match to an enclosing JSON block by brace matching, take the NARROWEST enclosing block — the outermost one is `properties` and always matches, which turns a per-action classification into a whole-file one. Prefer classifying by a VALUE the block itself carries (here: the action composes "status":"ok") over classifying by the action's NAME — the name regex would have treated three of this flow's four non-ok documents as the OK one.

proposed_change.summary: No rule change. agents/improvement-agent.md already carries the rule that caught it ('where a gate reports 0 findings against a corpus you know contains an instance, that is the tell'), and it worked. Recorded as the concrete worked example, because the two Power Automate traps are reusable and the next gate over a flow definition will meet both.

applied_by: Improvement review 38 change 1. The shipped implementation attributes each null key to the narrowest enclosing action block and classifies OK-versus-non-ok by the status VALUE that block composes; verified at 8 OK-document nulls and 2 non-ok, matching the independent pre-measurement.

what: The dispatch instruction for wbs:6.9's D-11 fix asserted as settled ground truth that if() 'evaluates only the branch it takes in this runtime, proven on this project by TD-07/TD-08 (IMP-0124), so the guard is real', and specified if(empty(coalesce(openedOn,'')),'null',concat(...ticks(openedOn)...)) for FR-058's applicationsPerDay. why_it_was_never_caught: nothing - no gate reads an expression for a throwing call on an untaken if() branch, and verify-flow-definition-language.py's seven checks do not include one
lesson: IMP-0124's lesson ends with a 'Related:' clause claiming if() evaluates only the branch it takes; IMP-0378 (APPLIED) and IMP-0412 say the question is OPEN. cost: caught inside the dispatch that created it; would otherwise have shipped three undelivered FR-060 measures behind a green HARD gate
what: verify-tad-coverage.py's assertion (d) classifies a literal-null response key by the set of "status" literals composed inside the NARROWEST enclosing action block (IMP-0458's fix): statuses == {'ok'} means the OK document, anything else is a non-ok document and is correctly ignored. A STATUS-FREE helper Compose matches NEITHER — its status set is the empty set, which is != {'ok'} — so it was filed as non-ok and dropped. When wbs:6.9 built FR-059/FR-060, the response document stopped being composed by one action: Compose_response_body now interpolates outputs('Compose_breaktype_rows'), outputs('Compose_breaktype_total') and outputs('Compose_exceptional_funding_summary'), and the four money-average nulls that are STILL genuinely undelivered live in those three helpers. Measured: before the fix the gate saw 4 OK-document nulls and reported averageCost/averageAmountRequested/percentageOfCost as 'nulled only in a non-ok document, correctly ignored', i.e. it read breakTypeProfile as delivered while three of FR-060's four measures were null one action away. After the fix it sees 7 and acquits three against register UR-002/UR-003.
expected: that a gate asserting 'every null response key is declared somewhere' keeps working when the document it reads is composed from fragments rather than from one action
root_cause: the classifier is a two-way test (ok vs non-ok) over a three-way world (ok document, non-ok document, status-free fragment), and the third case defaults to the silent branch. The premise 'every null is in the one action that composes the status' was true of the artefact when the gate was written and stopped being true the same day, because splitting a long concat into helper Composes is ordinary refactoring that nothing flags as gate-relevant.
detected_by: the HARD gate exiting 1 on a dead-promise assertion (f) for dotted-path response_fields, which forced a read of how it actually matches keys; the blind spot was found on the way, not by the failure itself
why_it_was_never_caught: assertion (d) was added hours earlier by improvement review 38 against a flow where all ten nulls sat in Compose_response_body, so the status-free-fragment case did not exist in the corpus it was falsified against. Its own selftest fixtures compose a status literal in every document.
lesson: In verify-tad-coverage.py, a status-free Compose is a FRAGMENT, not a non-ok document: attribute it to the action(s) that interpolate outputs('<name>') from it, transitively, with a cycle guard. Fixed in flow_null_response_keys. Two residual weaknesses are REPORTED NOT FIXED: (1) assertion (d) silently SKIPS a null key that no Appendix A row mentions at all, so removing both the register entry and the row's key names passes — three of four mutants passed for this reason, and only 'register removed AND a row that names the keys but reads delivered' fails; (2) matching is by LEAF KEY NAME, not path, so registering averageAmountRequested once satisfies both its FR-059 and FR-060 occurrences. Generally: when a gate keys on 'the action that composes X', splitting that action into helpers is a gate-relevant refactor, and the tell is a null count that DROPS while the artefact gains nulls.

proposed_change.summary: Two additions beyond the fragment-attribution fix already applied: (a) make assertion (d) FAIL, not skip, on an OK-document null that neither the register nor any Appendix A row accounts for — a null nobody has written down anywhere is the exact state this gate exists to end, and it currently passes; (b) track null keys by PATH (metric.field) rather than by leaf name, so a leaf shared between two metrics cannot be acquitted once and counted twice. Both are improvement-agent's to weigh: (a) may need a baseline pass for pre-existing unmentioned nulls.

cost: four approved requirement-measures cannot be delivered by the approved mechanism; discovered only when someone tried to build them
what: TAD S5.1 states the flow 'reads the round's rows and tallies them with array expressions (length(filter(...)) and equivalents)', and TAD S3.3's contract specifies four money-average measures on that basis: exceptionalFundingSummary.averageAmountRequested, and breakTypeProfile's averageCost, averageAmountRequested and percentageOfCost. THERE IS NO EQUIVALENT FOR A SUM. Read this session from Microsoft's own workflow-definition-language function reference: the math set is add, div, max, min, mod, mul, pow, rand, range, sub, and add takes exactly two operands. A sum over a FIXED operand count is expressible by nesting add() — which is why FR-060's five-operand total-row COUNT is deliverable — and a sum over a variable-length array is not expressible at all. The same document already ground-truthed that FetchXML aggregate is unsupported by List rows and that ADR-030 rejected a Custom API as outside the language palette, so the design closed off every route to a mean and then specified four of them.
expected: that a response contract specifying an average over a filtered subset names the mechanism that computes it, in a design that has already ruled out server-side aggregation
root_cause: the phrase 'and equivalents' generalised from a verified fact (length() counts a filtered array) to an unverified one (some expression totals it), inside the same sentence and with the same apparent authority. The counts were built first and worked, which confirmed the sentence's first half and left the second half untested until the money measures were attempted.
detected_by: attempting to implement FR-059/FR-060 and looking up the math-function list before writing an expression rather than after
why_it_was_never_caught: no gate reads a design document's claim about what the platform's expression language can do; verify-flow-definition-language.py checks for constructs that are PRESENT and wrong (select(), filter(), nested item), never for a capability a document assumes and the language lacks. And the four fields were literal nulls, so nothing downstream ever exercised the missing mechanism.
lesson: The workflow definition language has NO sum over an array. add() is strictly binary, so a total is expressible only over a FIXED, known operand count (nest add() n-1 deep — this is how FR-060's five-break-type total-row count ships) and never over a filtered subset of unknown length. Before a design specifies any mean, total or ratio-of-totals computed 'in flow expressions', check the math-function list: the three candidate mechanisms all cost something real (Apply to each + variables is proven but turns a declarative tally into ~900 sequential action executions and breaks a 'figures read as seconds old' claim; xpath(xml(...),'sum(...)') is one action but unverified here and a silent 0 on malformed input puts a WRONG money figure on a board pack; a Dataverse Custom API reopens ADR-030). More generally: a design sentence of the form 'X and equivalents' is two claims, and the second one is the unverified one.

proposed_change.summary: Record the negative platform fact: the WDL math set is add/div/max/min/mod/mul/pow/rand/range/sub, add is binary, there is no sum() over an array, and List rows supports neither $apply nor FetchXML aggregate — so any average/total over a variable-length collection needs an explicit mechanism decision with a latency or verification cost, and the three candidates with their costs. This is the file an architect or automation agent reads before specifying an aggregate, and it currently says nothing about it.

cost: prevented - measured before any expression was authored, rather than after a wrong money figure reached a board pack
what: XPath 1.0 sum() has two silent-wrong-answer modes on exactly the data this project would feed it, measured against a conformant XPath 1.0 engine on the XML shapes a Dataverse money column produces: sum() over an EMPTY node-set returns 0 (indistinguishable from a real total of zero), and sum() over a node-set containing ANY non-numeric leaf - an empty element from a null money value, or a formatted '1,200.50' - returns NaN for the WHOLE sum. NaN is not valid JSON, so a single blank money value in a flow that writes its aggregate as a JSON string makes the entire document unparseable and takes every metric off the screen, not just the affected one. All three money columns on rev_application are RequiredLevel None (rev_costs Entity.xml:1391, rev_amountrequested:1316, rev_additionalamountrequested:1599), so blanks are certain in real data rather than hypothetical.
expected: a documented aggregate function returns either a correct total or an error - not a plausible zero on absent input and a document-destroying NaN on one blank cell
root_cause: XPath 1.0 defines sum() over a node-set by converting each node's string-value with number(), where the empty string converts to NaN and NaN propagates through addition; and it defines the sum of the empty node-set as 0. Logic Apps inherits both because it evaluates xpath() with the .NET XPath library. Neither behaviour is a Power Automate quirk and neither is going to be fixed.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing - verify-flow-definition-language.py has seven checks and none of them reads inside an xpath() expression, so an unguarded sum() over a nullable column would pack, import, activate and run green while emitting either a wrong figure or an unparseable document
lesson: NEVER sum a nullable Dataverse column with xpath(...,'sum(...)') unguarded: XPath 1.0 returns 0 over an empty node-set and NaN over any non-numeric leaf, NaN is not valid JSON, and one blank money cell therefore destroys the whole aggregate document. Filter the nulls OUT before projecting to XML (that filter's length() is also the measure's honest denominator - coercing a null to 0 while still counting the row biases the mean), and guard the empty case with if(empty(...), null, ...). Do not coerce; exclude.

proposed_change.summary: check 8 - an xpath() expression containing 'sum(' must draw its node values from a Select whose source is a Filter array testing the summed column for null, and must sit inside an if(empty(...), null, ...) guard. Needs a known-bad fixture and a negative test per C-TECH-057. Proposed, not applied: the altitude is improvement-agent's to decide

what: check_citation_stamps() in scripts/verify-improvement-log.py warned that IMP-0465, IMP-0466, IMP-0467, IMP-0468 and IMP-0469 were 'cited by 1 review document and carry NO reviewed_in' when improvement review 39's section 9 named them precisely to declare they were NOT processed. SCOPE_DISCLAIMER did not match 'Five findings left unread for the next review, deliberately' (the pattern has 'left unprocessed' but not 'left unread'). After rewording to 'have NOT been processed in this review', IMP-0465 cleared and IMP-0468/IMP-0469 STILL warned, because a disclaimer governs ONE paragraph by design and those two ids were also named in a later paragraph giving context about a reviewer decision that had superseded another finding's lesson. Clearing them needed the same disclaimer repeated in that second paragraph.
expected: a review that goes on record naming what it did not process is not warned as though it had made a processing claim — the rule the check's own docstring states, and the whole point of IMP-0196
root_cause: the check recognises a declaration of non-scope by MATCHING A PHRASE against a fixed cue list, per paragraph. Both halves fail in normal use: the cue list cannot enumerate the ways a human says 'not this time' (it has 'left unprocessed' and not 'left unread'), and the per-paragraph unit — correct for suppression safety, since one table row's NOT APPLIED must not excuse its neighbours — means a document must repeat its disclaimer in every paragraph that names a deferred id, including paragraphs whose purpose is context rather than disposition.
detected_by: agent-self, applying improvement review 39: the warning count went 4 -> 9 on writing section 9, and only reached 4 again after three rewordings
why_it_was_never_caught: the two prior instances were each fixed by ADDING a cue or a position to the same phrase-matching design — IMP-0196 added the heading rule, improvement review 19 change 7 added the paragraph rule — so each fix widened the recogniser rather than replacing it, and the next unmatched phrasing was inevitable. Nothing measures the check against a review document that is deliberately explicit about its own caps.
lesson: THIRD instance of this check over-firing on an honest review (after IMP-0196's heading and improvement review 19's paragraph rule). Two things a review author needs today: SCOPE_DISCLAIMER matches 'left unprocessed' and NOT 'left unread', and a disclaimer governs ONE PARAGRAPH — so every paragraph that names a deferred finding id needs its own 'not processed in this review' clause, even one whose purpose is only context. And the general shape: a gate that decides INTENT by matching a phrase list will keep meeting phrasings the list lacks, and each instance-level widening guarantees the next one. Assert on a VALUE instead — the review's own explicit disposition per finding — rather than on the prose around the id.

The general form is to stop inferring disposition from prose: have a review declare its dispositions in ONE machine-readable position that already exists — the CLUSTER block's own fields, or a required 'Deferred:' line listing ids — and have check_citation_stamps() read that instead of scanning paragraphs for cues. what: ADR-039's literal expression, xpath(xml(concat('<r><v>', join(body('Select_x'), '</v><v>'), '</v></r>')), 'sum(/r/v)'), returns NaN whenever the presence subset is EMPTY - because join() over an empty array yields '' and the XML becomes <r><v></v></r>, a node set containing one empty element. Measured against libxml2: <r></r> -> 0, <r><v></v></r> -> NaN, <r><v>10</v><v></v></r> -> NaN.
expected: TAD S0.9 point 3 and ADR-039 both state the two failure modes as 'sum() over an EMPTY NODE-SET returns 0' and 'sum() over a node set containing one empty element returns NaN', and present the presence Filter array as removing the NaN case at source. It does not: the presence filter removes blank VALUES, and the empty-ARRAY case is a different thing that the literal shape converts into the NaN case.
root_cause: Two distinct emptinesses were treated as one. A blank money value inside a non-empty subset is removed by the presence filter; an entirely empty subset makes join() produce '', which the surrounding '<v>'...'</v>' literals turn into exactly the empty element the NaN case needs. And the NaN ESCAPES the per-measure guard: the total row sums the five per-type sums with a nested add(), so one break type with no costed application makes rev_resultjson unparseable and takes all thirteen metrics off the screen, not one.
why_it_was_never_caught: Nothing. No gate evaluates a flow expression's arithmetic, and TAD S12.2 seeds exactly this case ('one break type has zero applications') for a LIVE run - so the first observation would have been on a real round with a real board waiting.
lesson: XPath 1.0 sum() is 0 over an empty node set and NaN over a node set containing ANY empty element, and NaN is not valid JSON - so build the XML so an empty collection produces NO element at all: concat('<r>', if(empty(body('S')), '', concat('<v>', join(body('S'), '</v><v>'), '</v>')), '</r>'). join() over an empty array is '', which the surrounding element literals turn into the NaN case, so 'a presence filter removes the NaN case' is only true of blank values INSIDE a non-empty collection. And check where a NaN can escape to: a nested add() over per-group sums carries one group's NaN into a total, so a single empty group takes every metric in the document off the screen rather than one.

cost: two Pester runs
what: Three new Pester assertions of the form `$x | Should -BeLike "*item()?['rev_costs']*"` failed against a subject that plainly contained the needle. -BeLike is WILDCARD matching, and item()?['rev_x'] contains [ and ], which the wildcard engine reads as a character class.
expected: a substring match, the way -BeLike is used everywhere else in this suite - where no needle happens to contain a bracket.
root_cause: Every other -BeLike needle in this file matches an action name or a JSON key, none of which carries a bracket. The moment an assertion matches an ITEM-ACCESSOR expression - which is most of what a flow definition is made of - the wildcard metacharacters in item()?['x'] silently change the meaning of the pattern.
why_it_was_never_caught: Nothing, and the direction matters: `Should -BeLike` with a bracketed needle fails LOUDLY, which is how this was found. `Should -Not -BeLike` with the same needle would PASS VACUOUSLY - a test asserting the absence of something it can never match. Grepped: no existing assertion in src/tests/ is in that state today.
lesson: In Pester, use `Should -Match ([regex]::Escape(...))` and never `-BeLike` when the needle contains a flow expression - item()?['rev_x'] carries [ ] and -BeLike reads those as a character class. -BeLike fails loudly and -Not -BeLike passes vacuously, so the dangerous half is the negative assertion: an absence test whose needle can never match is a test that cannot fail.

proposed_change.summary: Add one line to the testing section: -BeLike is wildcard matching, so any needle containing [ ] - which every item()?['column'] flow expression does - must use -Match with [regex]::Escape instead. Name the -Not -BeLike vacuous-pass direction explicitly, because that is the half no failure will reveal.

cost: one Pester run
what: A Pester assertion written as `$x | Should -Contain $y `\n -Because "..." +\n '...'` sent the piped variable as $null: the trailing + binds to the -Because ARGUMENT and splits the statement, so Should ran against nothing and reported 'collection $null'.
expected: a two-part -Because string, and the pipeline intact.
root_cause: Identical binding trap to IMP-0142, in a different cmdlet: a string concatenation continued across a line break inside a parameter argument re-parses the whole statement. The fix is the same one - build the whole string first, inside one set of parens, or keep it on one line.
why_it_was_never_caught: IMP-0142 recorded this for Write-Output with -f and the lesson was written about -f specifically. It is a PowerShell parsing property, not a Write-Output property, and the digest entry names the cmdlet rather than the property.
lesson: Never continue a PowerShell string concatenation across a line break inside a cmdlet parameter argument - the + binds to that argument and re-parses the statement, so a piped subject arrives as $null and the assertion reports on nothing. This is IMP-0142's property, not its cmdlet: it holds for Should -Because exactly as it holds for Write-Output -f. Build the whole string inside one set of parens first, or keep it on one line.

proposed_change.summary: Generalise IMP-0142's lesson from Write-Output/-f to the underlying parse rule, in the same line as the -BeLike entry above: a string concatenation continued across a line break inside any cmdlet parameter argument re-parses the statement.

applied_by: Review 40 changes 11+12. cost: a false CONTESTED marker stood under a correct, APPLIED, gate-enforced lesson in the generated digest; found and removed within one review of the mechanism being built
what: The `contests` edge kind, built by improvement review 39 and shipped the same day, was set WRONGLY on its first use outside that review. IMP-0476 set `contests: IMP-0142`, and logs/known-failure-modes.md L404 then rendered '⚠ CONTESTED by IMP-0476 — a later finding disputes a claim in this lesson and NEITHER has been re-tested' beneath IMP-0142's lesson. Both clauses are false: IMP-0476 does not dispute IMP-0142, it GENERALISES it from Write-Output/-f to the underlying PowerShell parse rule (both lessons are true, one is broader), and IMP-0476's own detected_by is 'tool', so it was tested.
expected: an edge kind whose meaning an agent reads off the skill and applies correctly, or a gate that catches the misuse — the digest is the read path every other agent depends on, so a false marker there is worse than a missing one
root_cause: `contests` was defined by its STRENGTH relative to `corrects` (weaker: disputed rather than wrong) and not by the case it excludes. 'The earlier lesson is true but too narrow' is neither wrong nor disputed, and a reporting agent widening a lesson reaches for the only edge available to express a relationship at all. The skill's table had two rows where the domain has three, so the third case fell into the nearest one.
detected_by: agent-self, applying improvement review 40: the regression check on review 39's own change 1 read the rendered marker against the two entries' actual lessons
why_it_was_never_caught: review 39 measured whether the edge RENDERS (1 finding, 1 true, 0 false, digest byte-identical without the edge). Nothing measured whether an agent would SET it correctly, and no fixture can: the author of a new schema field and its first outside user are different agents with different information. A new field is a new instruction, and its first outside use is the only test that counts.
lesson: A new log schema field is an instruction to every future agent, and shipping it measured-as-rendering-correctly is only half a proof — the other half is whether the next agent sets it right, which no fixture written by its author can test. Define a field by the case it EXCLUDES, not only by its strength relative to its neighbour: `contests` means the earlier lesson is WRONG ABOUT SOMETHING, and 'true but too narrow' is a WIDENING that takes no edge at all. Concretely, for anyone reading a digest marker: '⚠ CONTESTED' asserts BOTH that a claim is disputed AND that neither entry has been re-tested, so it is a false statement to leave standing over a correct lesson — check the two lessons against each other before trusting it. verify-improvement-log.py now requires a `contests_clause` quoting the disputed clause verbatim, which forces the author to the step at which 'there isn't one' becomes obvious.

proposed_change.summary: APPLIED by improvement review 40 change 12: `contests` requires a `contests_clause` quoting the clause it disputes, validated for PRESENCE only (semantics are prose and no gate will read them); the false edge on IMP-0476 removed; the pre-existing legitimate edge on IMP-0412 backfilled with IMP-0124's 'Related: if() evaluates ONLY the branch it takes here' clause; and skills/how-to-log-an-improvement.md gains a third table row for the widening case plus the test. cost: one live query; caught before the disclosure control was reported as in force. Observable only at V5 - the withheld screen needs a completed run.
what: TAD Revision 6 / ADR-039 make k=5 the minimum population at which a money average is published, and RoundStatisticsMoneyMeasureMinimumPopulation is seeded with 5 in all three provisioning/deploymentSettings files with a Pester assertion covering all three. I queried rev_setting live in REV-GrantApplications-DEV for rev_name like 'RoundStatistics%' and got NO ROWS AT ALL - neither the k row nor the freshness bound exists in any environment. The flow's fail-safe then yields k=999999999, so every one of the four money measures is withheld on the first live run while status stays 'ok'.
expected: a disclosure control described in an approved ADR, seeded in every settings file and asserted by a test, is present in the environment it governs
root_cause: seeding is a post_deploy pipeline step (TAD 12.3) that has not run, because the feature's own table (rev_roundstatisticsresult) does not exist in DEV yet either. Nothing between the settings file and the environment is a gate: DeploymentSettings.Tests.ps1 asserts the FILE contains the key with value 5, which is a source-side fact, and no check compares it against a live rev_setting row.
why_it_was_never_caught: every existing check on this setting is source-side. The build asserts the key is in three JSON files; the flow asserts it reads the key; the contract test asserts the filter string. No gate reads the environment, and the flow's own fail-safe is silent - it withholds correctly and emits status 'ok', so a misconfigured environment and a genuinely small round render identically.
lesson: A disclosure threshold seeded in every settings file is not a control until a row exists in the environment - query the setting live (rev_setting, by key) before reporting a minimum-cell-size rule as in force, because an unseeded threshold and a genuinely small population produce the same screen and the same 'ok' status.

cost: one grep; no rework, but a diagnostic state the app implements is unreachable
what: TAD 3.3 enumerates five status values including 'threshold-unset'. The shipped flow definition contains ZERO occurrences of that string - it emits ok, no-open-round, ambiguous-round, truncated and error. The Code App fully implements the value (types.ts:304, landing.ts:143, covered by three test files including a LandingPage assertion on its wording), so the producing side and the consuming side disagree in the direction that leaves a diagnostic permanently dead. verify-tad-coverage.py reports '6 status value(s) produced against 5 enumerated' and exits 0.
expected: every value in a declared enumeration has a producer, or is marked as reserved
root_cause: the gate counts the two populations rather than comparing them as sets, so a declared-but-unproduced value and an produced-but-undeclared value cancel out numerically. The flow's own notes.md states 'the last not yet emitted by this first version', so the gap is known and disclosed - it just is not checked, and nothing schedules its closure.
why_it_was_never_caught: the previous test cycle recorded the same enumeration mismatch in the opposite direction (five declared, seven produced) as a P3. The gate was subsequently extended to reach Appendix A and to count status values, which made the mismatch VISIBLE as a number while still not failing on it - so the count grew and the verdict stayed green.
lesson: A status enumeration is a two-way contract: check that every declared value has a producer as well as that every produced value is declared, because a gate that COUNTS values on each side passes over a diagnostic state nothing can ever emit.

proposed_change.summary: Compare the produced and enumerated status sets by MEMBERSHIP, not by count, and report each direction separately: an undeclared produced value is a contract breach, a declared unproduced value is either a dead diagnostic or must carry an explicit 'reserved' marker in the contract block.

root_cause: the correction pattern this project uses for narrative sections - append a dated update, retain the prior text so a reader can see what changed - was applied to a TABLE CELL, where it has the opposite effect. proposed_change.summary: Add to the 'conclusion first' rule that it binds TABLE CELLS as well as sections: the retain-the-superseded-text convention is for narrative, and inside a matrix cell the current verdict is rewritten in place with the history moved after it or into the revision log.

cost: invalidated the evidentiary basis lead-agent used to justify this re-dispatch as safe (WORKFLOW.md 'fourth case'); no actual data damage this instance, because the discovered prior writes happened to be complete and converged rather than partial
what: Before executing TAD Revision 5 steps 3/4a/4b/8 myself, live queries showed all four already done in DEV: rev_roundstatisticsresult table + all 4 attributes + alternate key + both role privilege grants (ensure-schema.ps1 -Env dev reported 100% EXISTS, 0 CREATED except the routine publish); its table auditing (ensure-auditing.ps1 -Env dev, 100% EXISTS); its CURRENT row (seed-round-statistics-result.ps1 -Env dev, 'nothing to seed'); and the two stale privileges from STEP 8 already revoked (both read back NOT BOUND). logs/pipeline.log has zero entries between 2026-08-27 21:01 and this dispatch's own first write, and config/revitalise-grant-automation-pipeline.yml's own text for these steps carries no DONE annotation. Lead-agent's 09:00 STALLED entry in routing.log concluded, from that same log absence plus the deployment-summary's unchanged mtime and no PREFLIGHT/WRITE ATTEMPTED markers, that the 2026-08-28 23:58 pipeline-agent dispatch 'died before Stage 0 produced any output -- no live write was attempted, nothing to reconcile'. That conclusion is contradicted by live state: substantial live writes against DEV plainly occurred after the pipeline config was last edited on 2026-08-28 and before this dispatch's first script call.
expected: agents/WORKFLOW.md's 'fourth case' (a dispatch that stalls without erroring) treats an absent pipeline.log entry, an unchanged Deployment Summary mtime and absent PREFLIGHT/WRITE ATTEMPTED markers as sufficient evidence that 'nothing happened' and there is 'nothing to reconcile' -- i.e. that log absence is proof of write absence
root_cause: agents/pipeline-agent.md's own Logging section instructs 'Append to logs/pipeline.log after each stage' -- one entry per STAGE, not per operation -- while the PREFLIGHT/WRITE ATTEMPTED markers required by C-TECH-065's report-back rule are written 'into your logs/pipeline.log entry', i.e. batched into that same end-of-stage line. A dispatch that performs several live writes (schema creation, auditing, seeding, a privilege revoke) and then dies for an external reason (spend-limit, credit exhaustion -- the same class as IMP-0172/IMP-0357) before reaching the point where it composes and appends that end-of-stage entry leaves a complete, correct set of live changes with ZERO log trace of any kind. Log absence in this design is consistent with both 'nothing was attempted' and 'everything was attempted and succeeded, but the session died before writing it down' -- the two are indistinguishable from the log alone, and WORKFLOW.md's fourth case currently assumes only the first.
why_it_was_never_caught: no gate compares a pipeline-agent dispatch's log silence against a live spot-check of the target environment before a lead-agent session concludes 'nothing to reconcile' and re-dispatches fresh. verify-provisioning-report.py checks that a WRITE ATTEMPTED marker is paired with a PREFLIGHT marker; it does not and cannot check the inverse (a live change with no markers at all), because it only reads the log, which is exactly the artefact this failure mode is silent in.
commercial_impact: none -- DEV only, no billed hours claimed against unverified work; this dispatch is standard tier and the discovered prior state was complete and correct, not damaging
lesson: A dispatch death (spend-limit, credit exhaustion, or any other external kill) can occur AFTER real live writes and BEFORE that dispatch appends its own end-of-stage pipeline.log entry, because pipeline-agent logs once per stage rather than once per operation. This means log absence proves only 'no entry was written', never 'no write was attempted' -- the two are the same signal today. Before any session concludes a stalled pipeline-agent dispatch 'died before Stage 0' or otherwise attempted nothing, it must run at least one live spot-check against the target environment for the specific components that dispatch's stage would have touched (e.g. does the new table exist, are the new privileges bound) -- log-file absence alone is not sufficient evidence, per this dispatch's own instruction from lead-agent to treat the log-based inference as unverified until confirmed live, which is exactly what surfaced this gap.

proposed_change.summary: Strengthen the 'fourth case' (a dispatch that stalls without erroring) to require a live spot-check of the specific components/state the stalled stage would have touched, not merely log-file absence (pipeline.log entry, Deployment Summary mtime, PREFLIGHT/WRITE ATTEMPTED markers), before concluding 'nothing happened, nothing to reconcile'. Separately, consider whether agents/pipeline-agent.md's Logging section should require an incremental append after each individual live operation rather than only after each stage, so a mid-stage death leaves partial evidence instead of none.

root_cause: Two different things are both plausibly 'the slug' when a build config is shared across features: the build CONFIG FILE's own feature name (config/revitalise-grant-automation-build.yml) and the DISPATCHED feature's own name (trustee-portal-visual-refresh). agents/build-agent.md's activation steps use one bare placeholder, <slug>, for both the config path (step 1, correctly the shared config's name) and the artifact-dir feature argument (step 3, which must be the dispatched feature's own name) without ever saying they can differ.

cost: one warning read and adjudicated; nothing rework-able, but the warning's own remedy is wrong and following it would have written a false disposition into the log
what: scripts/verify-improvement-log.py's citation-stamp WARNING reports 'IMP-0489: state unread, cited by 1 review document(s) (2026-08-29-improvement-review.md) and carries NO reviewed_in'. Review 41 names IMP-0489 exactly once, at L373, as a NUMERIC WATERMARK inside a note about id allocation -- "the max read `IMP-0489` at that moment, with zero duplicates". Review 41 did not process IMP-0489, does not cite it in any CLUSTER block or change-table Cites cell, and its `**Deferred:**` line (which is the machine-readable non-scope declaration) does not name it either, because a watermark is not a disposition. Obeying the warning would stamp IMP-0489 with a document that says nothing about it, making it read `awaiting-approval` against a review whose keyword cannot resolve it.
expected: the citation-stamp check treats an id in a PROCESSING position as a processing claim, and an id quoted as a value -- a maximum, a count, a range endpoint -- as neither a claim nor a deferral
root_cause: the predicate's substantive set is `(elsewhere & known) | processed`, where `elsewhere` is every id in the document minus the ids under a non-scope declaration. An id quoted as a NUMBER is in neither excluded position, so it lands in `elsewhere` and reads as a claim. The function's own docstring (L1469-1474) records that deciding substantiveness by SUBTRACTION 'grows one exemption per shape forever and is wrong by construction on the shapes nobody has met yet' -- this is one of those shapes, and the docstring predicted it.
detected_by: agent-self, drafting improvement review 43: read the warning against review 41 L373 before acting on it
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing measures this check's precision against the review corpus after each new review shape appears; the check is a WARNING, so a false positive costs nothing visible and never fails a run. Review 41 is the first review document in this repository to quote a finding id as an allocation watermark, a habit introduced by the id-allocation rule in agents/improvement-agent.md step 8 itself.
lesson: Before obeying verify-improvement-log.py's citation-stamp WARNING, open the review document it names and check WHERE the id appears: an id quoted as a value -- 'the max read IMP-nnnn at that moment', a range endpoint, a count -- is not a processing claim, and stamping the entry with that review writes a false disposition that makes it read `awaiting-approval` against a document whose keyword resolves nothing. Stamp only where the review actually processed the finding. The durable fix is to decide substantiveness POSITIVELY (a CLUSTER block, a Cites: line, a change-table row) rather than by subtracting known non-scope positions, which the function's own docstring already argues for.

proposed_change.summary: DEFERRED by improvement review 43, not proposed: narrow the citation-stamp check's substantive set from `(elsewhere & known) | processed` to processing positions only, measured against all 47 review documents first. One instance; the check is a WARNING; and the same function's docstring records four prior narrowings, so a fifth exemption shape needs a second instance to justify the regression risk of dropping the `elsewhere` half.

deferred_reason: One instance, and it is a WARNING that resolves itself the moment this review stamps IMP-0489. verify-improvement-log.py L1469 records four prior narrowings of this exact predicate and argues against adding a fifth exemption shape; dropping the `elsewhere` half is the right fix and it risks losing IMP-0154's original coverage, which needs a corpus measurement across all 48 review documents to settle. ANNOTATED AT APPLY TIME (2026-08-30), per the rule that an approved revisit_when is applied verbatim while the current state is recorded here: the warning is confirmed GONE — verify-improvement-log.py --check now reports citation-stamp warnings for IMP-0290, IMP-0298, IMP-0320 and IMP-0437 only, and none for IMP-0489. The corpus figure is also now measurable rather than estimated: verify-review-document.py reports 48 documents, so the entry's own proposed_change, which says 47, is the stale number of the two. The mechanism that mis-fired is untouched and will mis-fire again on the next review that quotes a finding id as a value.

Four pages checked (expression-functions-reference#result, logic-apps-exception-handling's 'Get context and results for failures' walkthrough, the Switch and Condition how-to guides, and the control-workflow-action schema reference): every worked example and every prose description names only Scope, For_each and Until as result() targets. Calling result() with a Switch or If action's own name is neither confirmed nor denied anywhere in first-party documentation.

cost: one review document reasoned from a false premise about a gate's behaviour, and the error survived drafting, the reviewer's read and the keyword; caught only because the applying dispatch ran the gate instead of re-reading it. NOTE ON STATE: the verify-tad-coverage HALF of this finding is already fixed (improvement review 43 change 2, deviation 3, recorded in IMP-0481's applied_by). This entry deliberately carries NO evidence_grep, because a needle pointing at that fix reports the whole finding as shipped — the validator caught exactly that on first append — and the SECOND half is open: no gate anywhere calls Baseline.unused / note_claimed, so a baseline whose debt has been paid is reported by nobody and merely waits to fail on its expiry date.
what: Improvement review 43 section 6 justified baselining two verify-tad-coverage findings on the ground that 'the register suppresses the FAIL and never the report'. That is config/gate-baselines.json's stated promise and scripts/lib/gate_baseline.py provides Baseline.cite() to keep it. Measured at apply time: verify-tad-coverage.py called .cite() ZERO times (git show HEAD confirms 0), so a baselined status value was dropped from output entirely -- the run said only '6 status value(s) produced against 5 enumerated' and named neither the suppressed `error` finding nor its owner. Fixed in the same change: suppressed status findings now print by name with owner, expiry and clearing action. SECOND, WIDER HALF, also measured: Baseline.unused / note_claimed exist precisely so a gate can report a baseline whose debt has been paid, and grep across scripts/ finds ZERO callers outside the library itself -- all four gates that load baselines (verify-tad-coverage, verify-code-app-data-sources, verify-provisioning-test-presence, verify-superseded-column-writers) leave it unused. So a stale baseline is reported by nobody and simply waits to fail on its expiry date.
expected: A shared library that encodes a promise ('suppress the FAIL, never the report') either enforces it on its callers or something checks that each caller keeps it. A capability the library offers and no caller invokes is dead code wearing the appearance of a control.
root_cause: gate_baseline.py is opt-in by design and says so ('It is opt-in, like every helper in this directory, and nothing forces a new gate to consult it'). The reporting half is opt-in too, but nothing records that: the file's _not_a_waiver key states the promise as though it were a property of the register rather than an obligation on each caller. A gate can therefore load baselines, suppress correctly, report nothing, and look compliant.
detected_by: improvement-agent applying review 43 change 2, running the gate to verify the review's own factual premise before writing it into the durable record (agents/improvement-agent.md step 8: where an assertion is about a script's BEHAVIOUR, EXECUTE it)
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing -- no gate reads the gates. verify-build-config.py checks that a step exists, can fail and has its inputs; it does not check that a gate honouring an opt-in register also reports through it.
lesson: A promise stated in a shared library's docstring is not a property of the system; it is an obligation on every caller, and it holds only where a caller implements it. Where a helper exposes both a suppress path and a report path, the report path is the one that gets skipped, because skipping it costs nothing visible.

proposed_change.summary: TWO candidate altitudes, and the second instance decides between them. (a) Cheap: have each of the four gates call note_claimed() with the keys it actually consulted and print baseline.unused, so a paid-off baseline is reported the run after it stops matching rather than on its expiry date. (b) Structural: make load_baselines return an object whose citation set MUST be drained -- e.g. the gate's summary builder takes the Baseline and renders suppressed findings itself -- so the report path cannot be silently skipped. Not proposed for immediate action: verify-tad-coverage's instance is fixed, the other three gates DO call cite(), and the unused-baseline gap has produced no incident yet. Log-note altitude until it does.

cost: none observed - the work this dispatch produced is verified correct - but the session boundary this dispatch's own dispatch instruction named was not honoured, which is the exact pattern IMP-0143 exists to prevent
what: This dispatch's own opening instruction read: 'This dispatch is flow-authoring work - fan out to automation-agent per your own sub-agent table for the actual Power Automate flow-definition editing, per your own agent file's procedure.' development-agent did not do this: the flow JSON edit (REVPortalRoundStatistics's Describe_the_failure descent), the gate script edit (verify-flow-definition-language.py's _CHECK7_EXCEPTIONS entry removal and two stale-count corrections) and the new Pester regression test were all written directly inside this development-agent session, with no Task-tool dispatch to automation-agent at any point.
expected: agents/development-agent.md's own Sub-Agents section: 'each spawn is a Task-tool dispatch to .claude/agents/<sub-agent-name>.md... not a section of your own turn. Running four of these as inline exploration inside your own conversation instead of four separate dispatches is the sub-agent version of the mistake agents/WORKFLOW.md -> Session Boundaries exists to stop.'
root_cause: the work required reading four Microsoft Learn pages, the flow's own JSON structure, the gate script's algorithm, two prior improvement reviews and the existing REVIntakeWordPressToDataverse precedent all in the same continuous line of reasoning before a single character of the fix could be written safely - the platform-contract ground-truthing and the construction it justified were not separable into a 'development-agent researches, automation-agent implements' handoff without re-deriving the same context twice. That is a real cost, not an excuse: WORKFLOW.md's Session Boundaries rule does not carve out an exception for tightly-coupled research-then-implement work, and this dispatch did not stop to ask whether one applied.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing catches this class mechanically - a Task-tool dispatch is a prompt, never a file, so no gate can assert one occurred (agents/development-agent.md's own IMP-0470 note makes the identical point about a different instance: 'a dispatch instruction is a Task-tool prompt, never a file, so there is nothing for a script to read'). The only check is the receiving agent (or the reviewer) noticing the sub-agent report never arrived.
lesson: When a dispatch instruction names a specific sub-agent fan-out and the work turns out to be one continuous chain of ground-truth-then-construct reasoning, STOP and either (a) do the fan-out anyway, passing the ground-truthed platform fact and the exact construction to write as the sub-agent's brief, or (b) if genuinely inseparable, say so explicitly in the gate output rather than silently completing the work in the parent session. Silence is what makes this class expensive: the same operator lesson IMP-0143 records ('two full days of Haiku/Sonnet-tier work on Opus because nothing ever actually dispatched a separate, pinned session') recurs every time a session judges its own case that a fan-out was unnecessary.

proposed_change.summary: Add one sentence to the Sub-Agents section: when a dispatch names a specific sub-agent and development-agent judges the work inseparable from its own research, that judgement itself must be stated in the gate output (one line: 'sub-agent fan-out not performed - reason'), not left implicit in the absence of a HANDOFF line naming that sub-agent.
