what: agents/build-agent.md L251 declares the build manifest's warnings block as exactly {total, resolved, accepted, untriaged}. Measured across all 22 TRACKED manifests under build/artifacts/**/manifest.json: the block takes FIVE different shapes - 6 with `warnings: null`/absent, 6 with `warnings.detail` as a LIST, 4 with `warnings.detail` as a STRING, 3 with counts only, 3 with a separate top-level `warnings_detail[]` - and uses NINE distinct key names inside `warnings{}`: accepted, accepted_preexisting, accepted_reviewer_soft, accepted_this_dispatch, detail, notes_triaged_not_warnings, resolved, total, untriaged. Separately: `warnings_detail[]`, the only field structured enough to diff a build's warnings against a Dev Summary table, is NOT in the declared schema at all, yet build-agent has improvised a near-miss version of it in 3 manifests.
expected: A schema declared in an agent file is either followed by the artefacts it governs or something reports the divergence. verify-build-manifest-note.py runs against the manifest each build and asserts the build-note half; nothing asserts the warnings half.
root_cause: The manifest is hand-composed prose written by build-agent at the end of a long run, and the only gate reading it (verify-build-manifest-note.py) checks the note, not the warnings block. Each build-agent session invented whatever key names its own run needed - `accepted_preexisting` and `accepted_reviewer_soft` are both individually sensible and collectively make the field unparseable.
detected_by: improvement-agent drafting review 44, measuring the input of the gate IMP-0323's revisit_when asked for BEFORE designing it (agents/improvement-agent.md L406: run the candidate against the real corpus, never the fixtures)
why_it_was_never_caught: no gate reads the manifest's warnings block. C-TECH-055 is checked by build-agent against the Dev Summary during the run, and the manifest is written afterwards as a record of that check - so the record has never itself been an input to anything, and an unread field has no pressure to keep a shape.
lesson: Before designing a gate, measure the INPUT it would read, not just the defect it would catch. The obvious mechanical home for untriaged-tool-warning (x6) is a diff of each build's warnings against the current Dev Summary's C-TECH-055 table, and it is unbuildable today for two independent reasons: the raw warning stream is gitignored (build/artifacts/** except manifest.json), and the one tracked surrogate is free-form prose in five shapes. The one integer that IS well-formed, warnings.untriaged, is disqualified for a different reason - it records build-agent's own conclusion about its own work, so a gate asserting it is 0 would be reading the answer rather than checking it (the gate-reassures-wrongly shape IMP-0497 recorded in the same batch).

cost: one dispatch: a browser reproduction plus one CSS line
what: A reviewer's screenshot showed StatTile values that wrap to two lines (long currency figures like £50,000.00) with their second line spilling past the tile's bottom border, overlapping content below. Reproduced live with a real Chromium render of RoundFinancePanel (playwright, not jsdom): `.statTileValue` (ds.module.css) never declared its own `line-height`, so it inherited FluentProvider's root value of 22px (lineHeightBase300, tuned for 16px body text). At this class's own 32px (--text-2xl) display size, 22px per line is shorter than the glyphs need, so a wrapped value's two lines painted on top of each other instead of stacking, and the bottom line visually spilled past the tile.
expected: IMP-0486 already added `overflow-wrap: break-word` to this exact class for this exact currency-wrapping case, and its own comment reasoned carefully about wrapping vs truncating. Nothing in that fix, or since, considered the class's line-height, so the wrap it enabled was never given room to render without overlapping itself.
root_cause: `overflow-wrap: break-word` controls where a line breaks; it says nothing about how much vertical space a line box gets. `.statTileValue` set font-size but not line-height, so it inherited the nearest ancestor's value rather than one sized for its own type scale. `FluentProvider`'s root sets `line-height: 22px` for Fluent's 16px body face, and that value reaches every descendant that doesn't override it -- including a converted design-system component set at 32px. The box model (grid track, tile height, `<dd>`'s own bounding rect) was correct throughout; only the painted glyphs exceeded their line box, which is invisible to any assertion on element geometry and only visible in an actual rendered screenshot.
why_it_was_never_caught: jsdom (this app's only test environment before this entry) computes no CSS at all -- ds-tokens.test.ts's own header says so explicitly -- so no existing test could see an inherited line-height, an overlap, or a spill. ds-tokens.test.ts's IMP-0486 test asserted the wrap property existed but never asked whether the wrapped result had room to render without colliding with itself.
lesson: A font-size change to a shape borrowed from a host framework (Fluent, or any design system whose root sets typography on `body`/its provider root) needs an explicit line-height alongside it -- inheriting the host's line-height tuned for its own base font-size silently produces overlapping wrapped lines at any size larger than that base, and this is invisible to jsdom-based tests, clean type-checks, and clean lint, because it is a paint-time collision, not a box-model defect. When a CSS class changes font-size away from the ambient body size, grep the same rule for line-height in the same change, and verify by rendering (not by reading the box model) whenever the property can wrap.

proposed_change.summary: Add an item: any class setting font-size larger than the ambient/inherited body size must also set an explicit line-height in the same rule -- especially where the value can wrap (overflow-wrap/word-break) -- because jsdom cannot catch a wrapped-line overlap and it is otherwise only found by a human looking at a screenshot.

deferred_reason: The class fix shipped and is measured: change 4/5 of 2026-08-31-improvement-review.md wire scripts/verify-css-line-height.py and C-TECH-076, and the gate's polarity was proven against this very defect — run over HEAD~1 it reports .statTileValue at 32px as a third finding, and over the current tree it does not, because the specific fix landed in commit 6ae5bf6. .statTileValue now carries line-height: var(--leading-tight) at styles/ds.module.css, alongside overflow-wrap: break-word from IMP-0486 and a clamp() font-size. IT STILL DOES NOT CLOSE: observable_at is V4 and the only proof that a wrapped tile value no longer overlaps is a rendered screenshot, which no session in this repository can produce. jsdom computes no layout — that is the whole reason this defect reached a human eye first. NOTE, and it is why this entry stays useful: the same gate reports TWO OTHER rules still defective on this surface today, .panelHeading (20px, ratio 1.10) and .cardTitle (24px, ratio 0.92), both open.

cost: the entire round-statistics feature has been unable to show a computed result to any user since it shipped, despite the flow itself working correctly
what: src/code-apps/trustee-review-portal/src/dataverse/roundStatistics.ts's isCurrent() computes `ageInSeconds(computedOn, now) <= (staleAfterSeconds ?? NaN)`. OQ-042 (the RoundStatisticsStaleAfterSeconds rev_setting value) has never been answered/seeded, so staleAfterSeconds is null in every response document the flow produces (confirmed live: 2026-08-30 rev_roundstatisticsresult.rev_resultjson carries "staleAfterSeconds":null despite a genuinely fresh, Complete, real-data computation). Any comparison against NaN is false in JavaScript, so isCurrent() NEVER returns true -- not at mount time, and not during the poll loop that runs immediately after the app's OWN trigger write. The reviewer reported seeing the flow compute real figures (confirmed live) while the app never shows them -- exactly this mechanism.
expected: docs/architecture/trustee-portal-visual-refresh-architecture.md#L2149 states the unseeded default is safe and 'makes S null and reproduces Revision 2's behaviour exactly -- every mount recomputes,' framing it as equivalent to always-recompute-and-show. The code does not do that: it recomputes but can never accept ANY resulting document as current, including one it just triggered and watched complete within the same poll loop, so the practical effect is always-recompute-and-NEVER-show -- a much more severe outcome than the architecture's own description of the fail-safe.
root_cause: isCurrent() uses one comparison for two different questions that need different null-handling: (1) 'should I skip recomputation and reuse an existing document' -- correctly fail-safe as false when staleAfterSeconds is null, and (2) 'should I accept the document my own poll just observed as complete' -- which should not depend on staleAfterSeconds at all, since a document computed after this cycle's own trigger write is definitionally current regardless of any staleness window. The NaN-comparison trick collapses both into one expression, which is elegant for question 1 and wrong for question 2.
why_it_was_never_caught: no test or live check ever ran the full write-then-poll cycle against a real, unseeded environment and asserted that a freshly-completed result is actually returned -- unit tests presumably mock the timing/staleness math directly. The architecture's own prose description of the fail-safe was taken as correct without tracing the actual NaN-comparison consequence through the poll loop specifically.
lesson: When a freshness/staleness bound is deliberately allowed to be unset as a fail-safe default, trace its effect through EVERY code path that uses the same comparison, not just the primary one it was designed for. Here, a bound meant to prevent 'skip recomputation and show something stale' also silently defeated 'accept the recomputation I just triggered and watched finish' -- because both checks shared one expression. Either seed a real value for RoundStatisticsStaleAfterSeconds now, or (durable fix) give fetchRoundStatistics's poll loop its own acceptance test -- a document whose computedOn is strictly after the moment this cycle wrote rev_triggeredon is current, independent of staleAfterSeconds -- rather than reusing isCurrent() for both purposes.

proposed_change.summary: Correct OQ-042's description: the unseeded default does not reproduce 'every mount recomputes and shows the result' -- it reproduces 'every mount recomputes and never shows any result, ever, including its own.' Either seed a real RoundStatisticsStaleAfterSeconds value as the immediate fix, or give the poll loop in roundStatistics.ts its own current-document test independent of the reused isCurrent() staleness check.

cost: one attempted live push to DEV did not complete; the config-file half of the urgent IMP-0511 fix is done and verified, the live-seed half is not
what: Dispatched to push RoundStatisticsStaleAfterSeconds=300 live to DEV via `pwsh provisioning/dataverse/seed-settings.ps1 -Env dev` (the existing, correct script per its own header). This is not the Auto Mode classifier refusal IMP-0245/IMP-0313 describe — no live call was even attempted, the script's own guard fired first because this interactive session simply has no PROVISION_APP_ID / PROVISION_CERT_THUMBPRINT exported at all.
expected: provisioning/README.md and agents/pipeline-agent.md both describe these as CI secrets, exported before the script runs; this session has no mechanism to hold or receive them (correctly, per C-TECH-001/C-TECH-002 — they must never be hardcoded or committed).
root_cause: development-agent (and any interactively-dispatched agent) runs in a session with no route to the CI secret store. Live Dataverse writes via seed-settings.ps1-class scripts are only ever runnable from a CI pipeline context (pipeline-agent's normal deploy) or a human's own shell holding the cert — not from a development-agent dispatch, no matter how narrow the change. docs/development/revitalise-grant-automation-dev-summary.md L171/L187 already recorded exactly this outcome for an earlier rev_setting seeding fix, so this is a second occurrence of the same class, not a first.

lesson: A development-agent (or any non-pipeline-agent) dispatch cannot complete a live Dataverse write itself, even for a one-row config seed — it has no route to PROVISION_APP_ID/PROVISION_CERT_THUMBPRINT and should not be given one. cost: ADR-036/ADR-042 spent multiple TAD revisions treating 'real font files or a licence' as an unmet external dependency (A-R21) waiting on the reviewer, when a redistributable copy of the exact named typeface was one npm install away
what: ADR-042 (Revision 7) closed by self-hosting Playfair Display for --font-display. The real font files were sourced from the npm package @fontsource/playfair-display@5.3.0 -- the canonical Google Fonts-published distribution of the SAME typeface, under the SIL Open Font License 1.1, which explicitly permits embedding/redistribution. Two static weights (400, 700, latin, normal style -- the only ones any --font-display call site in this app actually renders) were copied from that package into src/assets/fonts/playfair-display/ (with the OFL licence text alongside them) and re-encoded as base64 data: URIs directly inside styles/ds-tokens.css's own @font-face rules -- never a relative url() to a separate built asset file, per the A-BRAND-1 precedent that this Power Apps Code App host does not reliably resolve a second fetched file.
expected: A-R53 (TAD Revision 7, section 11) recorded this as 'certain until supplied' -- an external dependency on the reviewer providing files or a licence, with no route named for obtaining either independently. The TAD's own external-dependencies table (section 12) listed the font files as 'NOT YET SUPPLIED... blocking for ADR-042 only'.
root_cause: Nobody had checked whether the specific typeface named by the design system (Playfair Display, a real published Google Font) was itself available under a redistribution-safe licence via a standard package registry -- the TAD's framing treated 'the reviewer supplies files' as the only route, when for any typeface that is ALSO a published open-source Google Font (as opposed to a proprietary/commercial face like Aptos, where this genuinely does not apply), an @fontsource/<name> package already IS that supply, at a known npm registry, with the licence text included in the package itself.
why_it_was_never_caught: nothing in this project's font-handling knowledge (knowledge/technology/code-apps.md) or the ADR-036/ADR-042 chain named the @fontsource distribution pattern as a thing to check before declaring a named open-source typeface an unmet external dependency.
lesson: Before recording a NAMED typeface as an unmet external-dependency blocker, check whether it is a published Google Font available via an @fontsource/<slug> npm package (SIL OFL 1.1, redistribution-safe) -- this closes the dependency immediately for any open-source face, and is a different, far cheaper route than waiting on the reviewer to supply proprietary files (which remains the only route for a face like Aptos that is not open-source). When bundling the result for a Power Apps Code App, follow the A-BRAND-1 precedent: embed the font bytes as a literal base64 data: URI inside the CSS @font-face rule itself, never as a relative url() to a second built asset file -- this host does not reliably resolve a second fetched file at runtime, the same defect A-BRAND-1 found for the logo image.

proposed_change.summary: Add a font-self-hosting procedure: for any typeface named by a supplied design system that is a published Google Font, check @fontsource/<slug> on npm (SIL OFL 1.1) before treating the file as an unmet external dependency; embed the resulting woff2 as a base64 data: URI directly in a local @font-face rule (never a relative url() to a separate built asset), per the A-BRAND-1 precedent for this Code App host.

cost: 1 failed live write, reviewer had to hand-fix DEV schema directly to unblock IMP-0511's urgent seed
what: development-agent's field-length-limits check (verify-field-length-limits.py, C-TECH-060) passed the RoundStatisticsStaleAfterSeconds setting row's 629-character description against Entities/rev_setting/Entity.xml's declared MaxLength=1000. The live write still failed with Dataverse error 0x80090429 (String or binary data would be truncated, rev_settingBase.rev_description) -- live DEV's actual column was narrower than 1000 at write time, meaning source's MaxLength=1000 was never actually applied to DEV by any ensure-schema run. The reviewer fixed it by manually widening the live column to 2000, directly in the environment, outside any provisioning script.
expected: A HARD gate reporting PASS on a field-length check should mean the write will not be rejected for length. Instead it verified the value against a declared metadata file that live never actually matched, and the write failed anyway.
root_cause: verify-field-length-limits.py checks a value's length against SOURCE's declared MaxLength, not against the live column's actual MaxLength. Nothing in this project's build or pipeline sequence asserts that a MaxLength declared in Entity.xml was ever successfully applied live via ensure-schema.ps1 -- the same class of gap IMP-0122 named for adding a column at all ('Adding a column is TWO deployments, not one'), but for WIDENING an existing column's MaxLength specifically, which is a metadata PATCH rather than a create and may be silently skipped by a create-only provisioning step (IMP-0259's class).
why_it_was_never_caught: verify-field-length-limits.py has no live-state check at all -- it is a pure source-vs-source comparison. No gate anywhere in this project's pipeline confirms a MaxLength widening in Entity.xml actually reached the target environment before a value depending on that width is written.
lesson: A field-length gate that checks a value against a DECLARED MaxLength is not evidence the live column accepts that value -- widening MaxLength is a metadata PATCH that a create-only provisioning step (per IMP-0259's established pattern) may silently skip on a column that already exists. Before writing a setting value close to or dependent on a recently-widened MaxLength, verify live via EntityDefinitions(...)/Attributes(...)?$select=MaxLength, not by reading Entity.xml alone.

proposed_change.summary: Add an optional live-reconciliation mode (or a paired script) that reads each checked attribute's actual live MaxLength via the Dataverse metadata API and flags any column where source's declared MaxLength exceeds the live value -- the exact drift this incident hit.

Review 18's 285-line live verifier — written by an improvement review into provisioning/, never executable because it assigned the read-only $pid automatic variable — is the precedent for why. The requirement and the query are handed to pipeline-agent or the reviewer's own shell as warranty rework inside WBS 6.9. THE HOLE IS OPEN AND IS STATED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER: until that live reconciliation exists, verify-field-length-limits.py keeps reporting PASS on source values that the live column will reject, because it is a source-vs-source check and cannot be anything else. C-TECH-060 was examined for retirement or replacement on exactly this ground and deliberately kept — the row is correct about what it claims, and deleting a working source-side gate because a live-side gate is missing would remove coverage and add none.

cost: would have been an indefinitely halted build: C-TECH-061 red at step 3 of 68 on every future build-agent dispatch, with no agent able to diagnose why approving the review did not clear it
what: Review 45 (docs/improvements/2026-08-30-improvement-review-2.md) section 8 disposes of IMP-0511 (blocker, observable_at V5) as: stays NEW on approval, gains a revisit_when, is NOT closed because the re-observation cannot be made here. That reasoning is correct. But simulated against scripts/verify-improvement-log.py --check with review 45 applied exactly as written, all three TRIGGERs survive: IMP-0511 classifies as 'awaiting-approval' (its reviewed_in names a document that exists), and the blocker rung fires identically on 'unread' and 'awaiting-approval'. classify() at scripts/verify-improvement-log.py:992 places deferred_reason AHEAD of awaiting-approval in precedence, and revisit_when alone affects no state at all. So the approved remedy leaves C-TECH-061 permanently red.
expected: Sending APPROVE IMPROVEMENTS against a review that fully and correctly processes the only blocker in the queue should clear the blocker rung of C-TECH-061 and let build-agent proceed.
root_cause: A review that correctly declines to CLOSE a V5 entry has exactly two states available that discharge the blocker rung - APPLIED/REJECTED, or NEW with a deferred_reason - and 'NEW with only a revisit_when' is neither. Nothing in agents/improvement-agent.md's step 8 says so: it tells a review to leave the entry NEW with a revisit_when (L293) and separately tells it that reviewed_in goes on at draft time (L255), and the combination of those two correct instructions is precisely the state that keeps the gate red. The two instructions were written for different purposes and never checked against each other.
why_it_was_never_caught: no review had previously declined to close its only blocker. Reviews either closed the blocker (clearing the rung) or the queue had other unread entries masking the effect. Nothing simulates a review's own disposition against the gate before the keyword is sent, so a review's remedy is never tested against the gate it exists to clear.
lesson: Before parking a review at its gate, SIMULATE the disposition against scripts/verify-improvement-log.py --check on a scratch copy of the log and confirm the triggers the review exists to clear actually clear. 'NEW plus revisit_when' does NOT discharge the blocker rung - only APPLIED/REJECTED, or NEW plus an explicit deferred_reason, does. A V5 entry that honestly cannot be closed therefore needs a deferred_reason recording that decision, not merely a revisit_when; the gate's own message names deferred_reason as the second legitimate discharge.

root_cause: Step 8's re-verification is scoped to what the review writes into agents/, constraints/, skills/ and knowledge/, plus deferred_reason prose. A routed item is neither: it changes no file in this review, so nothing in the step points at it, yet it is the highest-consequence output a review has - it becomes a delivery dispatch against src/ or against a live environment. The routed table is also where a review's diagnosis is most likely to be stale, because it names defects the review deliberately did NOT fix, so they sit unfixed across exactly the interval in which someone else may fix, decide or supersede them.
why_it_was_never_caught: No gate reads a review's routed-work table, and nothing can diff a routed sentence against a tree. Step 8's own list of what to re-verify is prose, and routed work is absent from it - so an agent following the step literally and completely still misses this.
lesson: At apply time, re-verify every item in a review's 'work this review routes rather than performs' table exactly as you re-verify a proposed change's premise - and check specifically whether the thing being routed has since become a CLOSED DECISION rather than an open defect. A routed item is the only review output that becomes an instruction to another agent, and it names defects the review chose not to fix, so it is the output most exposed to the drafting-to-keyword interval that IMP-0405 identified. Where a routed item is disproved, withhold it and say so in the applied section, exactly as for a disproved change.

what: Closing IMP-0518 required a 'reobserved' block, and verify-improvement-log.py rejects one whose ts predates the finding's own ts. The finding was stamped 2026-08-31T12:20 by build-agent; `date` on the host applying the review returned 12:08. So the true wall-clock time of a re-observation that genuinely happened AFTER the defect was reported still failed the check, by ~13 minutes of skew between two agents' clocks. Recorded 12:21 with the skew noted inline in the reobserved.result rather than back-dating the finding or disabling the check.
expected: that recording the actual current time as a re-observation timestamp would satisfy a monotonicity check, because the re-observation really did happen after the finding
root_cause: the check compares two timestamps written by DIFFERENT agents on possibly different hosts, and treats their difference as evidence about event ordering. That inference only holds under a shared monotonic clock, which a multi-agent system running dispatches across sessions does not guarantee. The check's own error text states the intended invariant correctly ('a re-observation recorded before the defect was is a copy of the original report, not a re-test of it'), but the quantity it measures is clock skew plus ordering, and it cannot separate the two.
why_it_was_never_caught: every prior closure happened to be on a host whose clock was at or ahead of the finding's stamp, so the skew never crossed zero. It only surfaces when the closing session's clock lags the reporting session's by more than the gap between report and closure - which shrinks as the loop gets faster, so a QUICKER turnaround makes this MORE likely, not less.
lesson: A timestamp comparison across agents is a clock comparison, not an ordering proof. Where a gate needs ordering, prefer a monotonic source both parties share (a commit sha, a sequence number, the log's own append position) over wall-clock stamps written independently.

proposed_change.summary: Consider allowing a small negative tolerance (or comparing append ORDER in the file rather than ts values) for the reobserved.ts monotonicity check, so that inter-agent clock skew cannot block an honest closure. Deliberately NOT proposed as a change in review 47: it is a one-instance finding, the workaround is a one-line note, and loosening a check that currently catches genuine copy-paste closures needs its own measurement against the corpus first.

cost: 3 concurrent build-agent dispatches for the same feature (wbs:6.9), two killed manually, ~500k tokens burned across dead/looping attempts before one completed genuinely
what: Three consecutive build-agent dispatches for the same build each ran a real, long-running OS process (npm ci / vitest / pester / pac solution check) in the background, then ended or looped their own turn saying 'I'll continue once it completes' / 'waiting for the background process to complete, it will notify me automatically.' Two of the three produced no completion at all after several such turns and had to be stopped with TaskStop; live checks (ps aux, build-run.log tail) showed the OS process itself was gone each time, well before the declared work was done. Only the third instance (dispatched with an explicit 'do not end your turn while a background step is running, actively wait/poll synchronously' instruction) completed with a real, complete gate output.
expected: agents/WORKFLOW.md's 'fifth case' already documents that a dispatched Agent-tool invocation cannot be woken by a background-task notification once its own turn ends, and that this reads as success when it is actually a death. That guidance was known and cited in this session's own dispatch briefs, and still recurred twice more after being explicitly warned against in the dispatch prompt for the second attempt.
root_cause: A subagent that runs a long shell step via its own backgrounded process, then ends its turn expecting a later notification to resume it, both (a) cannot actually be resumed (the WORKFLOW.md fifth case) and (b) appears to lose the OS process itself once its harness turn ends -- the child process does not survive past the dispatching turn. The dispatch prompt has to explicitly forbid backgrounding and require synchronous/blocking execution of long steps, every time, or the agent defaults to a plausible-sounding but nonfunctional wait-and-resume pattern.
why_it_was_never_caught: WORKFLOW.md's fifth case names the SYMPTOM (a dispatch claiming it will resume) but does not instruct the DISPATCHER to preempt it by explicitly forbidding backgrounded/detached execution of long steps in the dispatch prompt itself -- so each new dispatch re-derives the same failure independently unless the prior lesson happens to be remembered and stated
lesson: When dispatching any agent for a task with a long-running step (npm ci, a full test suite, a live solution-checker call), the dispatch prompt must explicitly state: run every long step as a synchronous, blocking call within the current turn; do not background it and do not end the turn expecting a later resumption, because a dispatched agent's background child process does not survive its own turn ending, and the dispatcher cannot wake it either way. State this preemptively in every such dispatch, not just after the first failure.

proposed_change.summary: Add to the 'fifth case' section: the dispatcher's own responsibility is to preempt this failure mode by explicitly instructing every dispatch with a long-running step to run it synchronously/blocking, never backgrounded, in the dispatch prompt itself -- not just to react to it after the fact.
